Course No: AE5510
Course Name: Security of safety-critical systems
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course will provide an overview of the security challenges and approaches to overcome them in safety-critical
systems such as unmanned aircraft systems, autonomous cars, intelligent transportation systems, etc.
Course Content:
Introduction to safety-critical systems, system architecture of a typical safety-critical system, security vulnerabilities
and attack vectors including side-channel attacks, different types of intrusion/attack detection systems,
hardware-based and software-based attack mitigation strategies, attack-resilient system design, learning-based
approaches for attack detection and mitigation, decision and game-theoretic approaches to security, randomisation
and moving-target defence.
Text Books:
1. Yu, Huafeng, Xin Li, Richard M. Murray, S. Ramesh, and Claire J. Tomlin, eds. Safe, autonomous and intelligent
vehicles. Springer, 2018.
2. Wolf, Marilyn, and Dimitrios Serpanos. Safe and secure cyber-physical systems and internet-of-things systems.
Cham: Springer, 2020.
3. Lin, Chumg-Wei, and Alberto Sangiovanni-Vincentelli. Security-aware design for cyber-physical systems.
Springer, 2017.
4. Song, Houbing, Glenn A. Fink, and Sabina Jeschke, eds. Security and privacy in cyber-physical systems:
Foundations, principles, and applications. John Wiley & Sons, 2017.
Reference Books:
1. Sun, Yunchuan, and Houbing Song, eds. Secure and trustworthy transportation cyber-physical systems.
Springer Singapore, 2017.
2. Lee, Edward A, and Sanjit A Seshia. Introduction to embedded systems: A cyber-physical systems approach.
MIT Press, 2016.
3. Guo, Song, and Deze Zeng, eds. Cyber-Physical Systems: Architecture, Security and Application. Springer
International Publishing, 2019.

Course No: AE5520
Course Name: Verification of cyber-physical systems
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course will provide an overview of the different types of approaches for verifying safety-critical cyber-physical
systems such as unmanned aircraft systems, autonomous cars, intelligent transportation systems, etc.
Course Content:
Brief introduction to automata and formal methods, modelling cyber-physical systems, requirements specification
using a formal language, compositional reasoning, deductive verification, SMT-based model checking, reachability
analysis, data-driven verification, stress testing of safety-critical systems, falsification techniques, runtime
monitoring, contract-based design, verification of learning-based components.
Text Books:
1. Mitra, Sayan. Verifying Cyber-Physical Systems: A Path to Safe Autonomy. MIT Press, 2021.
2. Platzer, André. Logical foundations of cyber-physical systems. Vol. 662. Cham: Springer, 2018.
3. Garoche, Pierre-Loïc. Formal verification of control system software. Vol. 67. Princeton University Press, 2019.
Reference Books:
1. Yu, Huafeng, Xin Li, Richard M. Murray, S. Ramesh, and Claire J. Tomlin, eds. Safe, autonomous and intelligent
vehicles. Springer, 2018.
2. Lee, Edward A, and Sanjit A Seshia. Introduction to embedded systems: A cyber-physical systems approach.
MIT Press, 2016.

Course No: AM 5
Course Name: Analytical methods in applied mechanics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The goal of this course is to offer broad physical and analytical concepts that are important in engineering
mechanics understanding and application. This course will provide a platform to review and learn a combination of
analytical and modeling tools needed for a graduate engineer.
Course Content:
First Principles: Equations in mechanics, Conservation laws; modeling, dimensional analysis; Review of
Differential equations: ordinary and partial; linear and nonlinear; classification; simple solution techniques;
Functional analysis, Calculus of variations; Thermodynamic principles, Lagrange and Hamiltonian methods;
linearization, asymptotic and perturbation methods; Modeling complex engineering systems - preliminary and
detailed modeling; decomposition methods and mathematical transforms with engineering examples.
Text Books:
1. Howison, Sam. Practical applied mathematics: modelling, analysis, approximation. Vol. 38. Cambridge
university press, 2005.
2. Fowler, Andrew Cadle. Mathematical models in the applied sciences. Vol. 17. Cambridge University Press,
1997.
Reference Books:
1. Tayler, Alan B. Mathematical models in applied mechanics. Vol. 4. Oxford University Press, 2001.
2. Segel, Lee, and G. H. Handelman. Mathematics applied to continuum mechanics. Vol. 52. Society for Industrial
and Applied Mathematics, 2007.
3. Mei, Chiang C. Mathematical analysis in engineering: how to use the basic tools. Cambridge University Press,
1997.
Course No: AM 5016
Course Name: Numerical methods in Biomedical Engineering
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course attempts to cover concepts of numerical methods from a biomedical engineering perspective. It will
introduce the student to the nature and behavior of physiological systems, and how to apply mathematical
modeling techniques to these systems in order to develop models that may be used to simulate their behavior.
Course Content:
Review of Linear Algebra, Solution of nonlinear algebraic equations: Specifically, Gauss elimination, Gauss-Jordan
reduction, and Gauss-Seidel substitution methods for linear systems, and linear interpolation, Newton-Raphson,
and Newton's methods for simultaneous nonlinear systems will be discussed with example application in Force
balance in biomechanics, Biomedical imaging and image processing, Friction factor in a catheter,
Michaelis-Menten kinetics, Ventricular pressure measurements
Review of Finite difference methods- Interpolation, Differentiation, and Integration; PDE and ODE with application
in Pharmacokinetics: the drug absorption problem, Laser ablation, etc.
Monte-carlo methods and applications such as polymerization of biomolecules and others. Stochastic differential
equations. Gillispie's direct method with applications such as mechanochemical force-generation and others.
Measurements, Errors and Uncertainty, Descriptive Statistics, Inferential Statistics, Least Squares Modeling,
Curve Fitting with applications in Computing statistics of MRI and CT image intensities, Analysis of mass spectra
data, Separating EEG frequency components, etc.
Text Books:
1. Stanley M. Dunn, Alkis Constantinides, Prabhas V. Moghe, Numerical Methods in Biomedical Engineering,
Academic Press, 2006.
Reference Books:
1. Numerical Recipes, W. H. Press., S.A. Teukolsky, W.T. Vetterling, B.P. Flannery, Cambridge University Press,
1992. ISBN: 0-521-43064-X
2. Numerical Methods for Engineers, Chapra et al. (any edition)
3. Stochastic Differential Equations: An Introduction With Applications . Author: BerntØksendal. Publisher:
Springer; 6th edition
4. An Introduction to Stochastic Processes with Applications to Biology. Author: Linda J.S. Allen. Publisher:
Chapman and Hall/CRC. 2nd Edition. "
Course No: AM1010
Course Name: Introduction to Physiology for Engineers
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Compare homeostasis mechanisms in different environments.
Summarize the physiology of bone formation and skeletal muscle contraction..
Relate muscle properties (e.g., elasticity) to engineering materials science.
Distinguish between neuromuscular junction dysfunction and muscle pathology.
Describe the structure of the heart, blood vessels, and respiratory system.
Interpret the cardiac cycle and gas exchange processes in the lungs.
Calculate cardiac output and blood pressure using physiological formulas.
Correlate blood composition changes with clinical conditions (e.g., anemia).
Compare respiratory volumes in athletes vs. sedentary individuals.
Label the major components of the brain, spinal cord, and neurons.
Outline the process of nerve impulse transmission and synaptic communication.
Investigate how CNS damage affects motor or sensory function.
Recall the structure of the nephron and skin’s role in temperature regulation.
Predict how dehydration affects nephron function and blood composition.
Compare thermoregulation strategies in different environmental conditions.
Assess the efficiency of dialysis machines relative to natural kidney function.
Course Content:
Cellular and Membrane Physiology:
Cell – Cell Structure and organelles - Functions of each component in the cell. Cell membrane – transport across
membrane - Action potential (Nernst, Goldman equation), Homeostasis. Tissue: Types, functions.
Musculoskeletal Physiology
Skeletal: Types of Bone and function – Physiology of Bone formation – Division of Skeleton -Types of joints and
function – Types of cartilage and function. –Types of muscles – Structure and Properties of Skeletal Muscle-
Changes during muscle contraction- Neuromuscular junction.
Cardiovascular and Respiratory Physiology
Cardiovascular System: Structure – Conduction System of heart – Cardiac Cycle – Cardiac output.
Blood: Composition – Functions - Hemostasis – Blood groups and typing. Blood Vessels – Structure and types -
Blood pressure
Respiratory system: Parts of respiratory system – Respiratory physiology – Lung volumes and capacities –
Gaseous exchange.
Central Nervous system: Structure and function of nervous tissue – Brain and spinal cord – Functions of CNS –
Nerve conduction and synapse – Reflex action
Excretory System
Structure of nephron - mechanism of urine formation - skin and sweat gland - temperature regulation
Text Books:
Guyton & Hall: Physiology, Latest edition
Costanzo, Physiology, Latest edition
Reference Books:
Berne & Levy: Physiology. Latest edition
Joseph Feher: Quantitative Human Physiology, Latest edition
Course No: AM1011
Course Name: Introductory Physiology Lab
Course Type:
Lab
Description:
To practically understand human physiology by measuring some basic physiological parameters
Course Content:
Analysis of ECG and Heart Rate Characteristics During Stress Test Exercise- Bruce Protocol
Valsalva Manoeuvre to Test the Autonomous Control of the Heart
Comparison of Heart-Rate Variability (HRV) Between ECG and PPG
Respiratory Analysis Using Spirometer
Audiometric Assessment of the Hearing Function
Skin Conductance Response to VR Simulation
Physiological pH Measurement
Real Time Recording of Various Physiological Parameters Using Patient Monitoring System
Biocompatibility Assay – MTT Assay
Synthesis of Hematite Nanoparticles and Characterisation

Course No: AM1100
Course Name: Engineering Mechanics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
---
Course Content:
Equilibrium of rigid bodies, free body diagram, Analysis of beams and trusses, Equilibrium of continuous systems
-derivation of relation between load, shear force and bending moment. Energy conservation in rigid bodies
-potential energy and elastic energy. Virtual work in multibody assemblies. Lumped mass models in Dynamics
-Particle motion in cylindrical c0ordinates, engineering applications of central force motion. Kinetics of rigid bodies
-translation and rotation motion of a rigid body, relative motion with translating and rotating axes and Coriolis
acceleration. Kinematics of rigid bodies -3-D properties of sections, angular momentum of rigid bodies and energy
relations for rigid bodies. Mechanical vibrations of single degree of freedom systems -free vibration of rigid bodies,
general equations of motion and response to forced sinusoidal loading.
Text Books:
---
Reference Books:
1. Beer F.P. and Johnston E.R., Vector Mechanics for Engineers - Volume I - Statics, Volume II - Dynamics,
McGraw Hill, New York.2. Merlam J.L and Kraige L.G., Engineering Mechanics, Volume I - statics, Volume 11-
dynamics, John Wiley & Sons, New York. 3. Shames L.H., Engineering Mechanics, Prentice HaII, New Delhi

Course No: AM2200
Course Name: Strength of Materials
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The following are the objectives for the course.
1. Understading stress and strain
2. Determining principal stress and strain and their directions
3. Application of stress and strain for axial, bending and torsional members
4. Understanding deformation and determining deformation for axial, torsional and beams.
5. Understanding stability of columns.
6. Failure theories.
Course Content:
The course content is as follows:
1. Definiation of stress and strain in 1D, 2D and 3D
2. Transformation of stress and strain in 2D, Mohr's Circle
3. Constitutive relations, understanding of plane stress and plane strain phenomenon
4. Stress, strain, deformation of determinate and indeterminate axial members
5. Stress, strain, rotation of determinate and indeterminate torsional members
6. Bending stress and strain in beams
7. Composite beams, equivalent theory
8. Shear stresses in beams
9. Unsymmetric beams
10. Deflections in beams, Compatability conditions for indeternminate beams
11. Stability in columns
12. Introduction to strain energy and determination of deflection
13. Introduction to failure theories
Text Books:
1. Mechanics of Materials, 8th Edition | Russell C. Hibbeler | Pearson Education
2. Elements Of Strength Of Materials | SP Timoshenko |
Reference Books:
1. An Introduction to Mechanics of Solids, 3ed Edition | SH Crandall, NC Dahl, TJ Lardner, MS
Sivakumar | Mc Graw Hill
2. Lecture notes
Course No: AM2530
Course Name: Foundations of Fluid Mechanics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Introduce fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics to Undergraduate students.
Course Content:
1 Introduction
Reynolds Transport Theorem
2 Fundamental Equations of Compressible Flow
(a) In-depth understanding of the physics of the basic governing equations
(b) Mathematical nature of the governing equations
(c) Non-dimensional parameters
3 Solutions to Newtonian Viscous Flow Equations
(a) Couette Shear Flow
(b) Steady Fully Developed Duct Flows
(c) Unsteady Duct Flows
(d) Compressible Flow Solutions
(e) Linearized Creeping Motion
4 Laminar Boundary Layers
(a) Solutions of 2D Steady Flow
(b) Thermal Boundary Layers
(c) Flow in the inlet of ducts
(d) Unsteady Laminar Boundary Layers
(e) Free-Convection Boundary Layers
5 Stability of Laminar Flows
(a) Small-perturbation stability
(b) Linearized Stability of Parallel Viscous Flows
(c) Parametric effects in Linear Stability Theory
(d) Transition to turbulence
6 Introduction to turbulence
(a) Reynolds Equations for Incompressible Turbulent Mean Flow
(b) 2D Incompressible Turbulent Boundary Layer Equations
(c) Incompressible Turbulent Boundary Layers on a Flat Plate
(d) Compressible Turbulent Boundary Layer Equations
(e) Compressible Turbulent Boundary Layers on a Flat Plate
Text Books:
G. K. Batchelor, “An Introduction To Fluid Mechanics”
Reference Books:
• Frank M. White, “Viscous Fluid Flow”
• G. K. Batchelor, “An Introduction To Fluid Mechanics”
• John C. Tannehill, Dale Anderson & R.H. Pletcher,
“Computational Fluid Mechanics And Heat Transfer”
• John D. Anderson Jr., “Modern Compressible Flow”
• H. Schlichting & K. Gersten, “Boundary Layer Theory”

visualization of stress field by photoelasticity; b) Evaluation of stress field in four point bending by photoelasticity

Course No: AM4020
Course Name: Non equilibrium Gas Dynamics and Molecular Simulation
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course focuses on the molecular description of the physical and chemical processes on gases and introduce
the students to the methods of simulation. Essentials of kinteic theory of gases, quantum mechanics and statistical
mechanics are combined in order to study the nonequilibrium processes in gases. Direct Simulation Monte Carlo,
a numerical technique for nonequilibrium gas flows, is also covered in detail.
Course Content:
Kinetic theory of gases: Particle model, molecular collisions, molecular transport processes, velocity distributions,
Boltzmann equation, Maxwellian velocity distribution function, equilibrium collision properties, kinetic based
analysis of nonequilibrium flows.Basic ideas of quantum mechanics,atomic structure and structure of diatomic
molecule.
Molecular statistical methods, distribution of energy states, partition functions, dissociation-recombination
systems.Finite rate processes: equilibrium processes, vibrational relaxation, finite rate chemistry.
Chapman-Enskog analysis of transport properties.Evaluation of collision crosssections and transport. DSMC
basics,models for viscosity, diffusivity and thermal conductivity, internal energy transfer modeling,introduction to
models for nonequilibrium thermochemistry
Text Books:
1. Iain D.Boyd and T.E.Schwartzentruber, Nonequilibrium gas dynamics and molecular simulation, Cambridge
University Press (2017).
2. G.Bird, Molecular Gas Dynamics and Direct Simulation of Gas flows, Oxford University Press(1994)
Reference Books:
1. Chapman,S and Cowling, T.G. The mathematical theory of non uniform gases, Cmabridge University Press
(1970)
2. F.Sharipov, Rarefied Gas Dynamics: Fundamentals for Research and Practice, Wiley-VCH (2016).
3. Carlo Cercignani, Rarefied Gas Dynamics: From basic concepts to actual calculations. Cambridge University
Press (2000)
Course No: AM4105
Course Name: Foundations of Data Structures and Algorithms
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course will introduce the data structures necessary for implementing algorithms into a high level language
code. The course will develop the necessary foundation for scientific problem solving.
Course Content:
Section 1: Fundamentals: Scientific Computing Tools, Quick Revision of C programming, Compilers, Basic
structure of compilation process; Structured (vs) Objective oriented programming practices, Recursive Paradigm,
Memory hierarchy, Memory management, Code optimization, Software development life cycle.
Section 2: Data Structures: Basic Data Structures with emphasis on sorting and searching, Arrays, Pointers,
Structures, Self referential structures, Linked lists, Stacks and Queues
Tree data structure, Tree Traversal (breadth first vs depth first), AVL trees, Red-Black trees,
Graph data structure, Directed and Undirected Graphs, Applications on short path algorithms.
Hash functions; collision avoidance
Section 3: Algorithms : Algorithmic complexity, Growth of functions, Recurrences, Analysis of Algorithms,
Algorithmic design techniques, Analysis of various sorting methods.
Section 4: Applications: Data structures and algorithms for mesh based and mesh free methods, Analysis of
various data structures and algorithms for Searching and Sorting (Insertion, Selection, heap, quick, Shell, Radix
etc. ), Analysis and implementation aspect of algorithms for data compression, page rank, stable matches,
Graham’s scan, Bower-Watson’s, random number generators etc.
Section 5: Miscellaneous: Introduction to computational complexity, Broad overview of P, NP and NP hard
problems.
Text Books:
1. A.V. Aho et al., Data Structures and algorithms, Pearson (2002).
2. J.A. Storer, An Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, Springer (2001).
Reference Books:
1. T.H. Cormen et al, Introduction to Algorithms, 3rd Ed., MIT Press (2009).
2. M.A.Weiss, Data structures and algorithm analysis in C, 2nd Ed., Pearson (1997).

Course No: AM5001
Course Name: Engineering Simulations in Fluid Dynamics
Course Type:
Lab
Description:
Objectives:
Learn fluid dynamics simulation using a CFD software package.
Course Content:
Course Contents:
1) Module 1
Basic user interface and file structure (Fluent/OpenFOAM).
2D mesh generation.
Solve a 2D steady diffusion (heat) equation and visualize the (temperature) contours.
Effect of mesh properties (orthogonality, skewness, aspect ratio) and convergence criterion on solution.
2) Module 2
Understand the concept of false diffusion by solving a pure convection equation (2D).
Study the influence of mesh refinement, mesh type (body fitted vs unstructured) and bounded schemes on false
diffusion.
3) Module 3
Simulating a 2D laminar flow through a pipe/channel.
Study the axial domain length influence to achieve a fully developed flow.
Obtain fully developed flow on a short domain using periodic boundary conditions and imposed pressure gradient.
4) Module 4
Unsteady laminar flow past a cylinder.
Record velocity time history and calculate shedding frequency using a Matlab script.
Study sensitivity of outflow boundary condition (reflective vs non-reflective).
Exploring temporal schemes: Implicit vs explicit, CFL number
Text Books:
Text Books:
1) Jiyuan Tu, Guan yeoh, Chaoqun Liu, Computational fluid dynamics : A practical approach, Elsevier, 2012.
2) H. Versteeg, W. Malalasekera Introduction to Computational Fluid Dynamics, An: The Finite Volume Method,
2nd
Edition, PHI, 2007.
Reference Books:
Reference Books:
1) ANSYS Fluent Software Manual
2) C. Pozrikidis, Introduction to Theoretical and Computational Fluid Dynamics, Oxford University Press, 1997

Course No: AM5004
Course Name: Computational Linear Algebra in Mechanics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
To provide a deep understanding of linear algebra concepts with computational techniques using MATLAB for
solving engineering and scientific problems.
Course Content:
1. Introduction to Linear Algebra and MATLAB (5 hours)
? Fundamentals of linear algebra, introduction to the MATLAB environment, basic MATLAB commands for linear
algebra, matrix generation, and manipulation.
2. Matrices and Linear Equations (5 hours)
? Detailed matrix operations, solving systems of linear equations using direct methods, LU decomposition.
? Applications in engineering mechanics, such as equilibrium equations in statics, truss analysis, and thermal
expansion models
3. Vector Spaces (5 hours)
? Deep dive into basis, dimension, subspaces, linear independence, orthogonal and orthonormal sets,
Gram-Schmidt process.
? Application of vector spaces in dynamics, vibration analysis, and the modeling of mechanical systems
4. Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (5 hours)
? Calculation methods, including power method, applications in stability analysis, and dynamic systems.
? Applications in stability analysis of mechanical structures, natural frequencies, and modes of vibration in
dynamic systems
5. Singular Value Decomposition (5 hours)
? SVD concepts, computational techniques.
? Applications in modal analysis for mechanical systems, signal processing for mechanical measurement
systems, and image techniques for materials science
6. Iterative Methods for Linear Systems (5 hours)
? Detailed study of Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel, Newton Raphson and conjugate gradient methods, comparison of
convergence properties.
? Application to iterative solution of large-scale mechanical system simulations, including finite element analysis
(FEA) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD).
7. Applications of Linear Algebra (5 hours)
? Network analysis in fluid flow systems, optimization in design and manufacturing, data compression techniques
for simulation data, introduction to graph theory applications in gear train analysis, and assembly planning.
? Case Studies: Specific examples illustrating the use of linear algebra in analyzing mechanical systems,
optimizing mechanical components, and improving manufacturing processes.
8. Advanced Topics in Linear Algebra (5 hours)
? Introduction to tensor operations and their applications, sparse matrices and their uses in large-scale
computational problems, principal component analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction in data science.

1) Strang, Gilbert. "Linear Algebra and Its Applications 4th ed.", Cengage India Private Limited, 2012.

Course No: AM5006
Course Name: Computational Methods in Mechanics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Objectives:
To equip students with numerical methods for differentiation, integration, and solving differential equations using
computational tools.
Course Content:
Course Contents:
1. Review of Calculus and Introduction to Numerical Methods (4 hours)
? Fundamentals of differential and integral calculus, introduction to numerical analysis, error sources in numerical
computation.
2. Numerical Differentiation (4 hours)
? Forward, backward, and central difference formulas; higher-order differences; error analysis; applications in
gradient
calculation.
? Applications of gradient calculation for stress and strain analysis in materials and thermal gradient calculations in
heat transfer problems.
3. Numerical Integration (4 hours)
? Trapezoidal rule, Simpson's rule, Gaussian quadrature, adaptive quadrature methods; error estimation.
? Applications in calculations of areas and volumes in engineering design, integral solutions for work, and energy
problems in dynamics.
4. Initial Value Problems for Ordinary Differential Equations (4 hours)
? Euler's method, Runge-Kutta methods (including higher-order); Fourier and Laplace Transforms, stability
analysis;
applications to physics and engineering problems.
? Applications in modeling and simulation of mechanical systems, such as spring-mass-damper systems and
thermal
systems.
5. Boundary Value Problems and Partial Differential Equations (6 hours)
? Finite difference method for elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic equations; method of lines; introduction to finite
element methods.
? Applications in stress analysis, fluid flow, and heat transfer problems
6. Systems of Differential Equations (4 hours)
? Numerical methods for linear and nonlinear systems; stability and stiffness.
? Applications in dynamic systems and control theory in robotics and mechanism design.
7.Optimization Techniques in Calculus (6 hours)
? Gradient descent, Newton's method; introduction to constrained optimization
? Optimization in engineering design, such as minimizing the weight of structures while maintaining strength and
stability, optimizing energy consumption in thermal systems.
8. Advanced Topics in Numerical Methods (8 hours)
? Spectral methods for differential equations; introduction to numerical methods for stochastic differential
equations;
machine learning algorithms for data fitting and prediction.
? Advanced modeling and simulation techniques for complex mechanical systems, predictive maintenance using
machine learning.

Course No: AM5010
Course Name: Biomechanics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Understanding basic terminologies in biomechanics
Solving simple problems in statics and dynamics of human body
Understanding mechanical properties of bones, muscles, their anatomical and physiological significance
Course Content:
1. Terminologies used in Bio-mechanics, Classification of Bones, Joints etc.
Anatomical terminology, motion in the human machine, the standard human scaling relationships (Anthropometry),
Classification of bones, Classification of Joints, Movements about joints, Skeletal Muscles structure and function,
Sliding Filament theory, length tension relationship, Hills muscle model.
2. Statics of Human Body
Review of forces, torques, and equilibrium, motion in one plane and levers, statics in the body, Statics analysis of
elbow, shoulder, spine, hip, knee, ankle etc. Static analysis of different postures.
3. Mechanical Property of the Human Body
Material components of the body and their elastic properties, time-independent deviations in Hookean materials,
static equilibrium of deformable bodies, time-dependent deviations from elastic behavior: viscoelasticity,
viscoelasticity in bone, bone fractures, common sports injuries, avoiding fractures and other injuries.
4. Study of Muscles
Skeletal muscles in the body, the structure of muscles, passive muscles, activating muscles, a macroscopic view,
the effect of exercise on muscles and their coordination, active/tetanized muscles, a microscopic view, hill
force–velocity curve, the sliding filament model, a nanoscopic view.
5. Advanced topics: Kinematics of human motion
Text Books:
1. Nihat Ozkaya and Margareta Nordin. Fundamentals of Biomechanics: Equilibrium, Motion, and
Deformation.
2. Joseph Hamill and Kathleen Knutzen. Biomechanical Basis of Human Movement.
3. Susan J. Hall. Basic Biomechanics.
4. Margareta Nordin and Victor Frankel. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System.
5. David Winter. Biomechanics and Motor Control of Human Movement.
6. Irving P. Herman, Physics of the Human Body, Springer, New York, NY, November 2006
Reference Books:
1. Zatsiorsky, Vladimir M. Kinetics of human motion. Human Kinetics, 2002.
2. Zatsiorsky, Vladimir M. Kinematics of Human Motion. Human Kinetics, 2002.
3. Zatsiorsky, Vladimir, and Boris Prilutsky. Biomechanics of skeletal muscles. Human Kinetics, 2012.

Course Name: Industrial Fluid Dynamics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course attempts to provide the participants with an in depth understanding on the principle of fluid dynamics
applied to industrial systems. They may, at the end of the course, be able to analyze and diagnose
engineering/research problems which are likely to be seen in their professional field. They would be able to apply

Course No: AM5014
Course Name: Microhydrodynamics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
To teach students fundamentals of low Reynolds number flows and suspension dynamics. The course will
introduce the physics of highly viscous flows, exact solutions to single particle dynamics, effects of particle shape
anisotropy, colloidal forces and hydrodynamic interactions.
Course Content:
• Introduction to viscous flows – Stokes approximation
• Properties of Stokes’ flow – Linearity, reversibility, reciprocal theorem
• Single particle dynamics I – Sphere in Stokes flow – Rotation, translation and extension, Fundamental
singularities, Faxen’s laws
• Single particle dynamics II – Anisotropic particles, Multipole expansion, Boundary integral method, Slender body
theory
• Hydrodynamic interactions – Resistance-Mobility formulation, Far-field (method of reflections), Near-field
(lubrication)
• Macroscopic properties – Calculation of suspensions viscosity – Einstein and Batchelor
• Applications in dynamics of swimming microorganisms
• Effect of fluid inertia – Oseen approximation
• Introduction to colloidal physics – Electrostatic and dispersion forces, Diffusion
• Statistical microhydrodynamics - Coagulation
Text Books:
• E. Guazzelli and J. Morris – A physical introduction to suspension dynamics, Cambridge
• S. Kim and S. J. Karilla – Microhydrodynamics: Principles and selected applications, Dover
Reference Books:
• G. K. Batchelor – An introduction to fluid dynamics, Cambridge
• W. B. Russel, D. A. Saville and W. R. Schowalter – Colloidal dispersions, Cambridge

verification and validation, design transfer and changes - The design history file - Risk management - Failure Mode
and Effects Analysis - Fall Tree Analysis - Hazards and Critical Control Points - Redesign and Renunciation -
Design control regulation.
Unit III - Pathway to Market - Regulatory requirements for Premarket application - Premarket submissions and
approvals - Device registration and Listing - Clinical trials - Post-Market Regulations, audits and inspections -
Introduction to mandatory medical device reporting.
Unit IV - Case Studies and Special Topics - Regulatory approaches for mobile medical applications -Emerging
Regulatory Framework for mHealth - Representative guidelines on calibration and maintenance of medical devices
- Case of software as a medical device.
Text Books:

Course No: AM5016
Course Name: Numerical methods in Biomedical Engineering
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course attempts to cover concepts of numerical methods from a biomedical engineering perspective. It will
introduce the student to the nature and behavior of physiological systems, and how to apply mathematical
modeling techniques to these systems in order to develop models that may be used to simulate their behavior.
Course Content:
Review of Linear Algebra, Solution of nonlinear algebraic equations: Specifically, Gauss elimination, Gauss-Jordan
reduction, and Gauss-Seidel substitution methods for linear systems, and linear interpolation, Newton-Raphson,
and Newton's methods for simultaneous nonlinear systems will be discussed with example application in Force
balance in biomechanics, Friction factor in a catheter, Michaelis-Menten kinetics, Ventricular pressure
measurements. PDE and ODE with application in Pharmacokinetics: the drug absorption problem, Laser ablation.
Monte-carlo methods and applications such as polymerization of biomolecules and others. Stochastic differential
equations. Gillispie's direct method with applications such as mechanochemical force-generation and others.
Text Books:
1. Stanley M. Dunn, Alkis Constantinides, Prabhas V. Moghe, Numerical Methods in Biomedical Engineering,
Academic Press, 2006.
Reference Books:
1. Numerical Recipes, W. H. Press., S.A. Teukolsky, W.T. Vetterling, B.P. Flannery, Cambridge University Press,
1992. ISBN: 0-521-43064-X2. Numerical Methods for Engineers, Chapra et al. (any edition)3. Stochastic
Differential Equations: An Introduction With Applications . Author: BerntØksendal. Publisher: Springer; 6th

Course No: AM5017
Course Name: Statistics for Biomedical Engineers
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Introduction of Biostatistics, data representation and analysis. Brief insight into probability theory and statistical
inference methods. Design and analyze statistical and mathematical models to evaluate research studies and
programs pertaining to health services. Design testable hypotheses for wide pathological needs.
Biostatistics is a discipline that develops and applies methodology for quantitative studies in public health and
biomedical research. The methodology focuses on the design and analysis of health surveys, clinical trials,
prevention trials, intervention studies, longitudinal studies, and laboratory studies
The objective of this course is to provide a comprehensive knowledge on these aspects to the M.Tech, MS and
Ph.D. students, primarily to enhance their analysis and employability skills.
Course Content:
Introduction to Biostatistics
Biostatistics, importance, significance, biological variables, data inference and display mechanisms, Role of
biostatistics in public health and biomedical research, Disease specific case studies.
Descriptive Statistics
Definition, Data preparation approaches - Ordered array and Grouped data, Measure of Location, Measures of
Central Tendency, Measures of Dispersion, Measure of Spread, Properties of Arithmetic mean, Properties of the
variance and standard deviation, Coefficient of Variation, Graphic methods, Algorithms to obtain Descriptive
Statistics, Case study - Effects of Lead Exposure on Neurological and Psychological Function in Children,
Probability Theory
Definition of Probability, Multiplication law of probability, Addition law of Probability, Discrete Probability
Distributions, Moments, Permutations and Combinations, Sampling Distributions, Estimation, Randomized Clinical
Trials, Estimation of the Mean of a Distribution, Conditional Probability, Bayes’ Rule, Hypothesis Testing:
One-Sample Inference, Two-Sample Inference, The Relationship Between Hypothesis Testing and Confidence
Intervals, One-Sample Inference for the Binomial Distribution, Poisson Distribution, p-values - interpretation,
one-sample, two-sample and non-parametric approaches, ROC Curves
Regression and Correlation Analysis
Regression Model, Regression Equation - Evaluating and Application, Fitting Regression Lines, Interval
Estimation, Correlation Model, Correlation Coefficient, Statistical Inference for Correlation Coefficients, Multiple
Regression and Multiple Correlation Models, Partial and Multiple Correlation, Rank Correlation, Interval Estimation
for Rank Correlation Coefficients, ANOVA, One-Way ANOV A—Fixed-Effects, Hypothesis Testing in One-Way
ANOVA, Two-Way ANOVA, The Kruskal-Wallis Test, Model Power Analysis, Chi Square Distribution, Non
Parametric Distribution- Signed test, Wilcoxon Signed test
Design of Experiments
Design of Experiments - Principles - Design Methodology, Survival Analysis - Kaplan - Meier Procedure - Cox
Regression, Epidemiological Designs - Study Design, Standardization, Power and Sample Size Estimation,
Meta-Analysis, Clinical Trail Design, Case Study - 5
Text Books:
1. Biostatistics: A foundation for analysis in the health sciences, Daniel, W. W. and C, L. Cross 9ed Wiley. 2013
2. Biostatistics for the Biological and Health Sciences, Triola and Triola, Pearson Addison Wesley
Reference Books:
1. The Cartoon Guide to statistics - Gonick & Smith - Haper & Collins

Course No: AM5030
Course Name: Linear Dynamical Systems
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This is intended to be a first level course for students interested in the area of dynamics and vibrations. The
objective of this course is to introduce students first to the basic fundamentals of mathematics involving linear
algebra and differential equations that are essential for analysis of dynamical systems. Subsequently, these
methods will be used in analysis of linear vibrating systems. This course will prepare students to take up advanced
courses in dynamics, including nonlinear dynamics, computational structural dynamics and other related courses.
Course Content:
Second order differential equations in science engineering; Modelling vibration problems; Review of linear ordinary
differential equations; Single degree of freedom systems and their analysis in time and frequency domain;
Multi-degree-of-freedom systems; Solutions of coupled ordinary differential equations; Concepts of linear algebra,
eigenvalues, eigenspaces and their implications in solving vibrating systems;Decomposition methods and
transforms.
Text Books:
1. Gilbert Strang, Differential Equations and Linear Algebra, Wellesley-Cambridge Press, 2014, ISBN:
978-0-9802327-9-0.

2006 edition (June 3, 2006)

Theory
Description:

Course Content:

Course No: AM5113
Course Name: Atomization and Sprays
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
the goal of this course is to provide an overview of physics of liquid atomization, spray formation and propagation.
The course will introduce the student to the theoretical models pertaining to jet breakup and drop formation. The
application of multiphase models for studying spray transport will also be discussed. Finally, the course will present
an overview of the design aspects as they pertain to spray nozzle and atomizers and discuss potential applications
incombustion systems.
Course Content:
Theoretical modeling of drop formation and atomization: Various regimes of jet breakup will be discussed with
Relevance to the non-dimensional parameter space. This part of the course will discuss linear instability as well as
nonlinear stability based theoretical models for drop formation in both cylindrical jet and annular and planar sheet
geometries will be delineated. The course will discuss experimental evidence in support of such theoretical models
as
proof of validation. Finally, theoretical models of “prompt” atomization will be presented.
Drop size distribution models: The second part of the course will consider a stochastic description of the spray
formation and propagation process while paying attention to the physical origins of such distributions. The various
existing models for drop size distribution will be discussed. The coupling of these models into a multiphase
transport
framework for studying spray propagation will be presented. Finally, the various experimental techniques that are
employed to interrogate sprays will also be presented.
Spray applications: The third part of the course will discuss various applications of sprays including spray
combustion and spray drying. A general overview of the physical processes underlying each application will be
presented and an overview of the design process for each application will be discussed.
Text Books:
1) Atomization and Sprays, Arthur H. Lefebvre, Taylor & Francis Press, 1989.
2) Liquid Atomization, L. Bayvel and Z. Orzachowski, Taylor & Francis Press, 1993.
Reference Books:
1) Atomization and Sprays Journal, Begell House, 2000.

Course No: AM5114
Course Name: Flow and Transport in Heterogenous Porous Media
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The goal of this course is to provide an overview of physics of flow and transport in porous media. In first part
basics of saturated and unsaturated flow in porous media will be covered. In this part we will derive the governing
equations from the physics of mass and momentum balance and discuss various numerical techniques to solve
them. In second part the focus will be on the effect of heterogeneity in natural porous media. This part will start
with a brief introduction to the random field mo
Course Content:
Introduction to porous media – Concept of porosity and permeability – Effect of grain size distribution – Volume
averaging and Darcy equation for saturated flow.
Capillary action and drainage hysteresis – Capillary pressure vs saturation models: Brook-Corey and Van
Genuchtan model – Relations between relative permeability and water content – Derivation of unsaturated and
multiphase flow equations – Richard’s Equation – Approximate solution schemes: Green Ampt model, Kinematic
wave theory.
Gas and vapor transport in porous media – Forced and free convective heat transport in porous media – Solute
transport with adsorption and desorption.
Random field modeling – Spatial auto-correlation and spectral density function of random hydraulic conductivity
field – Effective hydraulic conductivity – Spectral and Lagrangian methods – Scale dependent macrodispersion.
Text Books:
• Dynamics of Fluids in Porous Media, Jacob Bear, Dover Publication, 1988
• Groundwater Hydraulics and Pollutant Transport, Randall J. Charbeneau, Prentice Hall, 2000.
• Flow and Transport in Porous Formations, Gedeon Dagan, Springer-Verlag 1989.
• Stochastic Subsurface Hydrology, Lynn W. Gelhar, Prentice Hall, 1993
Reference Books:
• Unsaturated Zone Hydrology for Scientists and Engineers, James A. Tindall and James R. Kunkel, Prentice Hall

Course No: AM5116
Course Name: Structural Control
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The objective of this course is to introduce a new subject on structural control from mechanical sciences
perspective. The subject will include linear vibrations, structural dynamics, stability criteria, open loop and closed
loop control aspects of linear systems, passive, active and semi-active control of structures.
Course Content:
Introduction and Motivation to the subject
Mathematical preliminaries: ODEs, numerical techniques, Laplace transform, linearization. Review of linear
dynamical systems: Analysis of single degree of freedom systems, multi-degree of freedom systems, distributed
parameter systems, base excited systems, state space representation, time response of linear systems in state
space form, frequency domain analysis, modal analysis, Effect of damping and stiffness on structures. Linear
control system design: Review of classical control systems, pole placement design, modern control design,
stability, controllability and observability of linear systems, Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) theory and its
extensions. Lyapunov stability theory. Structural control: Passive structural control, DVA, passive dampers, base
isolations, active base isolation, hybrid base isolations, semi-active structural control devices and design, MR
dampers, active structural control, hybrid structural control.
Text Books:
• D. J. Inman, Engineering Vibrations, Pearson Education, Third Edition, 2009.
• B. Friedland, Control System Design, McGraw Hill, 1986.
• L. Meirovitch, Dynamics and Control of Structures, Wiley, 1990.
Reference Books:

• N. Nise, Control Systems Engineering Wiley 4th Ed. 2004.

Education India: New Delhi, 2008.
• T. T. Soong, Active structural control: theory and practice, Longman Scientific & Technical, 1990.

Course No: AM5131
Course Name: Advance Techniques and Models in Regenerative Medicine
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course has a broad spectrum of subjects, ranging from the foundational principles of regenerative medicine to
cutting-edge technologies and experimental models used in the field. The syllabus delves into essential areas
such as biomaterial design, tissue engineering technologies, controlled delivery systems, cellular studies using in
vitro models, and various experimental models for regeneration. The course delivers the pivotal role of
experimental systems and the utilization of emerging equipment, highlighting their importance in driving innovation
and research advancements in this field. Subsequently, the course addresses advanced technologies in tissue
engineering, encompassing pivotal methodologies like electrospinning, 3D bioprinting, Holographic tweezers, and
the use of decellularized extracellular matrix hydrogels as natural scaffolds. Furthermore, highlights the controlled
delivery systems, in vitro cellular models, and diverse experimental animal models for regeneration. Additionally, it
addresses preclinical models and the crucial phases of clinical trials in regenerative medicine, along with the
regulatory framework governing cellular therapies. Overall, the course aims for a solid understanding of the
principles, techniques, and experimental models essential in the field of regenerative medicine.
Course Content:
Introduction to Regenerative Medicine and Experimental Systems (5 hours)
• Overview of Regenerative Medicine
• Importance of Experimental Systems
• Emerging Equipment in Regenerative Medicine
Advanced Technologies in Regenerative Medicine (8 hours)
• Electrospinning for Scaffold Fabrication
• 3D Bioprinting: Shaping the Future
• Holographic Tweezers for Precision Cell Manipulation
• Decellularised Extracellular Matrix Hydrogels: A Natural Scaffold
Delivery system for Regenerative Medicine (5 hours)
• Non-Viral Gene Delivery: Transfecting Without Viruses
• Controlled Release of Biopharmaceuticals for Targeted Regeneration
In Vitro Models for Cellular Studies (7 hours)
• Invitro Cell Culture Techniques, Primary Cell Isolation, Stem Cell Culture
• Investigating Cell Migration and Invasion
• Exploring 3D Cell Culture Approaches
• Biochips: Engineering Microenvironments
Experimental Models for Regeneration (10 hours)
• Ex Vivo Chick Embryo Model
• Drosophila Model: Tiny Organisms, Big Discoveries
• Hydra Regenerative Model: Masters of Regeneration
• C. Elegans Model: Unveiling Cellular Mysteries
• Zebrafish Model: From Development to Regeneration
• Mammalian Models (Rat, Mice, Rabbit): Bridging the Gap
Preclinical Models and Clinical Trial Phases (5 hours)
• Preclinical Models in Regenerative Medicine
• Navigating Clinical Trial Phases
• Regulatory Framework in Cellular Therapies

Course No: AM5132
Course Name: Artificial Organs & Biodevices
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Artificial organs are bioengineered devices or tissues that scientists create and integrate into the human body to
replace, duplicate, or augment functional, naturally occurring organs. They pose a solution to organ donor
shortages, and can also be used as medical training tools. This course will be devoted to teaching bioengineered
devices (material selection, fabrication, implantation, and regenerative engineering). In addition to scientific details
on artificial organs and assistive devices, this course will discuss the opportunities & challenges in the clinical
translation of such devices/biomaterials. This course will enable the promotion of translational science. Several
other concerns, including socioeconomic, ethical, and regulatory issues, will also be discussed. Therefore, this
course offers a different flavor than the existing courses like Biomaterials (AMBE) and Tissue Engineering (BT).
Objectives:
Introduce students to the world of artificial organs, their emergence and implementation
Introduce multidisciplinary approaches to create biomimetic bioengineered devices
Explore emerging trends and technologies in the area of biofabrication or biomanufacturing
Learn about risks and challenges involved in the clinical translation of artificial organs and implantable devices
To make students aware of socioeconomic, ethical, and regulatory considerations of artificial organs
Learning Outcomes:
Students will be made aware of opportunities and challenges in the field of translational bioengineering to design
and develop more sustainable solutions in the future.
Course Content:
Unit 1: Introduction to artificial organs (7 hours)
Overview and classification of synthetic organs
Evolution and emergence of artificial organs or biodevices
Clinical case studies
Unit 2: Artificial assistive devices and biodevices (9 hours)
Ventricular assist device
Mechanical heart valve
Cardiac pacemaker
Implantation, and pre & post-operative measures
Unit 3: Introduction to regenerative engineering (8 hours)
Tissue repair and regenerative processes
Cell fate processes
Role of scaffold
Chemical, mechanical, electrical, and physical properties of soft (i.e., skin) and hard (i.e., bone) tissues
Unit 4: Advances in the biomanufacturing (10 hours) Additive manufacturing methods
Stimuli-responsive smart materials
Bioprinting techniques
Introduction to organ-on-chip
Unit 5: Practical limitations of artificial organs (8 hours)
Socioeconomic issues with biodevices
Ethical & regulatory consideration
Challenges in clinical translational
Text Books:
Anwarul Hasan, Tissue Engineering for Artificial Organs: Regenerative Medicine, Smart Diagnostics and
Personalized Medicine, WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, 2017
Joseph D Bronzino, The Biomedical Engineering hand Book Vol-11, CRC Press, 2000.
Jacob Segil, Handbook of Biomechatronics, 2018, 1st Edition, Hardback ISBN: 9780128125397, eBook ISBN:
9780128125403
Reference Books:
Joseph P. Vacanti, Robert Langer, Robert Lanza, Principles of Tissue Engineering. Elsevier Science. 2000.
Larry L. Hench and Julian R. Jones, Biomaterials, Artificial Organs and Tissue Engineering, Woodhead Publishing
2005.

Course No: AM5199
Course Name: DIY Inelastic Modeling, Analysis and Design
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
To be able to translate design or real life problems of structures, components and processes that undergo inelastic
deformations into simplified/idealized problems and be able to analyze and obtain results that are meaningful for
making design decisions related to their failure, life, processing, etc
Course Content:
This course offers hands on experience in understanding situations that involve inelastic deformations, translate
into idealized problems, analyze and solve them to obtain meaningful information for making design decisions.
The situations could be failure, life prediction or materials processing.
------------
1. What is inelasticity
2. Identify the real life situations in which inelasticity is important and what kind of inelastic deformation are we
looking for
3. What kind of failures are we trying to predict
4. Given a real life problem, how do I systematically simplify the problem
5. Modeling and solving specific inelasticity problems – case studies incl.
6. how to make decisions given the results from the plastic analysis
---------
Simple demos to understand and distinguish between elastic and inelastic deformations;
Classification into rate dependent and independent behavior, linear and nonlinear modeling; physical mechanisms
leading to inelastic deformations; association with shear;
Real life situations in which inelastic deformations occur; simplistic identification models; classification of
applications using critical parameters into structural, forming and smart applications. Simplifying and Idealizing of
real life problems;
Treatment for structural type problems – fatigue and collapse; treatment for forming / moulding problems; lower
and upper bound limit analysis methods for first level solutions;
Generating governing equations in a IBVP form. Use of standard computational packages to solve. Setting up
problem for standard analysis packages.
Case studies in design decision making. Strength failure, stiffness failure, fatigue failure, formability and ageing.
Text Books:
Srinivasa, A.R. and Srinivasan, S.M. Inelasticity of Materials, World Scientific, 2009.
Lemaitre, J. and Chaboche, J.L., 1994. Mechanics of solid materials. Cambridge university press
Simo, J.C. and Hughes, T.J., 2006. Computational inelasticity (Vol. 7). Springer Science & Business Media.
Reference Books:
Billington and Tate, Physics of Deformation and Flow, 1975 (available at the Central Lib)
Lubliner, J. Plasticity Theory, Macmillan Publishing Company, New York, 1990. (available at Central Lib)
Prager W, Hodge PG (1951) Theory of perfectly plastic solids. John Wiley and Sons, New York, 1951 (available at
the cenlib)
Jirásek, M. and Bazant, Z.P., 2002. Inelastic analysis of structures. John Wiley & Sons

Theory
Description:
Introduce the concept of uncertainties in engineering applications and train students into methods of uncertainty
quantification and analysis based on probabilistic approaches. The students will be trained both on the
mathematical and theoretical background as well as on implementation of these methods in computational
framework.
Course Content:
Introduction to the concept of uncertainty in engineering, classification of uncertainties.
Introduction to probability - probability space, definitions, axioms, Borel field, product spaces, Bernoulli's theorem,
de Moivre Laplace theorem, Law of large numbers, Conditional probability and Baye's theorem.
Random variables - discrete and continuous, probability distribution and density functions, statistics of random
variables, moment generating functions, characteristic functions, cumulants, functions of random variables,
extension to higher dimensions, Monte Carlo simulations of random variables.
Stochastic processes- definitions, calculus of stochastic processes, definitions of convergence, integration and
differentiation, Fourier transforms, Power spectral density and correlation functions, narrow band and broad band
processes, Monte Carlo simulations of Gaussian and non-Gaussian processes.
Crossings of Gaussian and non-Gaussian processes, translation processes, first passage times, extreme value
distributions, peak distributions, fractional occupation times.
Applications to random vibrations, time variant reliability problems, random fatigue and expected life estimation.
Advanced topics: Karhunen Loeve expansion, polynomial chaos expansions, stochastic Galerkin method,
stochastic collocation,
Text Books:
1. A. Papoulis. (1997). Probability, random variables and stochastic
processes. McGraw-Hill, New York.
2. Y.K. Lin (1967). Probabilistic theory of structural dynamics. McGraw-Hill,
New York.
3. L.D. Lutes, S. Sarkani (2004). Random vibrations: analysis of structural
and mechanical systems, Elsevier, Amsterdam.
Reference Books:
1. N.C. Nigam (1983). Introduction to random vibrations. MIT Press,
Massachusetts.
2. J. Solnes (1997). Stochastic processes and random vibrations: Theory
and practice. John Wiley & Sons, Chichester
3. D Xiu (2010). Numerical methods for stochastic computations. Princeton University Press.

Course No: AM5545
Course Name: Introduction to Multiphase flows
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Multiphase flows involving solid particles, droplets and bubbles are widely encountered in many engineering
disciplines. These range from traditional applications such as energy generation using solid or liquid fuels or
fluidized-bed chemical reactors, to emerging problems such as CO2 capture, biomass gasification and water
filtration. This course will provide students with the theoretical background to formulate and analyze multiphase
flows. A course project gives the opportunity for hands-on experience with computational and/or experimental
approaches to a practical multiphase flow problem. This course is suitable for all students interested in multiphase
flow applications including fluidized beds, colloidal dispersions, sprays and turbulent multiphase flows. It will be
primarily of interest to students in mechanical, chemical, aerospace, civil and environmental engineering, but all
majors are welcome.
• Understand multiphase flow kinematics and dynamics; mass, momentum and energy transfer of single particles,
drops and bubbles in flow. Recognize important nondimensional groups.
• Develop skills in problem formulation and mathematical modeling of multiphase flow problems
• Develop awareness of conservation equations for Lagrangian-Eulerian and Eulerian-Eulerian averaged
descriptions of multiphase flow
• Knowledge of commonly used models and correlations for multiphase flows
• Students will complete a course project using simulation and/or experimental methods to analyze a multiphase
flow problem of their choice and interpret the results.
Course Content:
Introduction to Multiphase flows
An overview of applications of multiphase flows, basic definition of phase, recap of single phase conservation
equations, recap of turbulence, properties of dispersed phase flows, size distribution
Single Particle Motion
Flow around a sphere, unsteady effects, Maxey-Riley equation
Interactions and physics
Colloidal and interfacial physics, particle-fluid Interaction, particle-particle interaction, continuous phase equations
Volume averaging methods for conservation equations
Volume-averaged two-phase equations, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes in multiphase systems
Introduction to numerical models
Eulerian-Eulerian models, Eulerian-Lagrangian models, Particle-Resolved Direct Numerical Simulation (PR-DNS)
introduction, interface tracking and capturing methods.
Experimental methods
Intrusive methods, system measurements, microscopic measurement motivation, optical laser-based methods for
particle velocity, particle sizing and temperature.
Text Books:
1. Crowe, Sommerfeld, and Tsuji, Multiphase Flows with Droplets and Particles, Second edition, CRC Press,
2011
2. Clift, Grace and Weber, Bubbles, Drops and Particles, Dover press, 1978
3. Christopher E. Brennen, Fundamentals of Multiphase Flow, Cambridge University Press, 2005
4. Subramaniam and Balachandar, Modelling approaches and computational methods for turbulent particle-laden
flows Academic Press (Edited collection of articles by top researchers in the field.), 2022

Course No: AM5565
Course Name: Physiological Control Systems
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The primary goals of this course it to provide various techniques employed in control theory, system analysis and
model identification that can be used to understand biomedical systems, specifically the processes involved in
physiological regulation.
The course will mainly focus on: mathematical modeling of dynamic systems, system identification, parameter
estimation, control system design and optimization for physiological systems. The course will provide detailed
application of these topics to model, analyze, optimize and design control systems for various physiological
systems.
The objective of this course is to provide a comprehensive knowledge on these aspects to the M.Tech, MS and
Ph.D. students, primarily to enhance their analysis and employability skills.
Course Content:
Introduction to Physiological Control Systems
Basic control definitions, Fundamental control concepts, Feedback control, Sensors and actuators, Control of
cardiovascular, respiratory and glucoregulatory systems
Elements of Control Systems Engineering
Dynamic system modelling, State space analysis, Linear time invariant systems, Laplace transforms, Time-domain
analysis, Stability analysis, Frequency domain analysis, Discrete systems, Z transforms, Modelling of
glucoregulatory system, Static analysis of physiological systems Simulation studies: Modelling and analysis of
cardiac output, Regulation of ventilation
System Identification and Parameter Estimatio
Nonparametric and parametric estimation methods, correlation functions, Introduction to least squares estimation,
estimation in frequency domain, Input design for estimation, ARX and ARMAX models, Kalman filter, Simulation
studies: Adaptive estimation of pulmonary gas exchange, Parameter estimation for modelling of endogenous
glucose production
Control System Design
Basics of controllers, Proportional, Integral and derivate controllers, Tuning of PID controllers, Introduction to
Model predictive controllers, MPC using data driven models, Introduction to optimal controllers, Dynamic
optimization, Simulation studies: Model Predictive Control Framework for glucose regulation in type I diabetes
mellitus, Simultaneous state estimation and model predictive control in intravenous anaesthesia
Applications and advancements
Modeling, analysis, optimization and control studies for Type I Diabetes Mellitus, Computational modeling and
control mechanisms in respiratory system, Analysis of Cardiovascular system, Modeling, analysis and control
strategies for anesthesia administration, Modeling and control studies for treatment of HBV (Hepatitis B Virus),
Introduction to control using machine learning approaches, Intelligent decision support for lung ventilation using
advanced machine learning techniques

Course No: AM6011
Course Name: Theory of Free Surface Wave motion
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The goal of this course is to make the student familiar to different types of free surface waves and related theories.
The suitability of potential flow based formulation will be reviewed in this course. Later the limitation of potential
theory will be also highlighted. This course will also introduce asymptotic analysis and explain the derivation of
higher order equation of water wave. In later part of the course, computational aspects of free surface wave will be
discussed.
Course Content:
• Airy wave theory: Water wave equation based on potential flow theory, Linearized equation, Dispersion relation
for capillary and gravity waves, Concept of phase and group velocities.
• Second-order wave properties: Wave energy density, Wave action, Wave mass, momentum and energy flux,
Stokes drift, Stationary phase
• Classification of waves: Shallow and deep water waves, Long wave, Nonlinear wave theory and asymptotic
analysis, Shallow water wave equations, Hyperbolic PDEs, KdV and KP models, Deep water wave equations,
Schrodinger equation, Benjamin-Feir instability, Wave interaction and wave mixing
• Wave forms in coastal water: Shoaling, Refraction, Diffraction and Wave breaking.
• Special topics of free surface wave: Kelvin Helmholtz instability and wave generated by wind, Tsunami, Free
surface dynamics in a small tank, Sloshing.
• Wave and current in viscous fluid: Numerical approaches, Volume of Fraction, Wave-structure interaction.
Text Books:
• James Lighthill, Waves in Fluid, Cambridge University Press, 1996.
• Robert G Dean and Robert A Dalrymple, Water Wave Mechanics for Engineers and Scientists, World Scientific
Publishing Co. Pvt. Ltd., 2000.
• Linear Water Waves, N. Kuznetsov, V. Maz’ya and B. Vainberg, Cambridge University Press, 2002.
Reference Books:
• R. S. Johnson, A Modern Introduction to the Mathematical Theory of Water Waves, Cambridge University Press,
1997.
• Lokenath Debnath, Nonlinear Water Waves, Academic Press, INC, 1994.
• Pengzhi Lin, Numerical Modeling of Water Waves, CRC Press, 2008.

Course No: AM6023
Course Name: Geometry & mechanics of materials
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
• Gain insights and develop intuitions as to how the geometry interplays with the material properties to determine
its mechanical response
• Get introduced to the analytical & numerical techniques used to solve non-linear problems in elastic systems
Course Content:
• Revision of bulk elasticity concepts, Classification of materials based on their geometry: filaments, ribbons,
sheets and shells
• Geometric properties of curves in 3D using Serret-Frenet and Darboux frames
• Introduction to the Kirchhoff rod theory, Solution to the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation, Euler’s solution to the

• Instabilities in filaments, Using numerical continuation to identify solution branches and bifurcation points
• Representation of surfaces: first and second fundamental form, Gauss’ Theorema Egregium
• Derivation of Foppl-von Karman plate equations, Lamé problem in thin-sheets and mechanism of wrinkling
• Summary of instabilities in sheets: wrinkles, folds and cusps
• Geometry of origami, designing materials using kirigami and overview of differential growth problems in biological
systems

Course No: AM6024
Course Name: Reduced Models in Dynamical Systems
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course is for students who would like to learn development of reduced order models from large order systems
specially systems with complex geometries modelled in finite elements. At the completion of the course, class
members would have exposure to various model reduction techniques both for FE models and experimental data.
The
course will have primary focus on models for linear dynamical systems. Exposure will be given to models that work
on
weakly nonlinear systems and also data driven reduced models.
Objectives:
? Introduce students to the mathematical development for reduced models in linear as well as weakly nonlinear
system but large ordered systems with and without damping.
? Prepare students to carry out vibration analysis of academic or industrial problems related to large order
systems
? Exposure to data driven models for dynamical systems
Course Content:
Elements of Dynamical Systems (6 hours)
• Review of SDoF, MDoF Systems
• Review of Flexible Body Systems
• Review of Linear Algebra
Exposure to Finite Element Vibration Analysis (6 hours)
• Differential Eigen Value Analysis of Flexible bodies
• FE modelling of Flexible body vibrations, use of commercial software for dynamic analysis
• Modal order reduction for Flexible bodies
Reduced Order Models in Dynamical Systems (18 hours)
• Introduction to RoM: Philosophy and principles of model order reductions, numerical
example, choice of master and slave DoFs. Physical type and modal type condensation, symmetry consideration
• Static/Guyan Condensation: Static problems, dynamic problems, eigen problems,
numerical Issues and demonstrations, generalized Guyan condensation
• Dynamic Condensation: Classical dynamic condensation, modal-type dynamic
condensation, error analysis of Guyan Condensation, iterative methods for dynamic condensation.
• RoM for Damped systems: Static and dynamic condensation for classically and nonclassically
damped systems
• SEREP: model development, numerical examples
• POD: mathematical background, POD in dynamics, other examples, data driven POD
models
Substructuring Techniques (9 hours)
• Concept of Primal and Dual assembly of dynamic models
• Substructuring approaches for linear systems: Substructuring methods with free and fixed
interfaces, Craig Bampton method, interface reduction, constraint handling
• Substructuring approaches for weakly nonlinear systems
• Substructuring approaches in experiments
Introduction to Data driven models (3 hours)
• Introduction to Dynamic mode decomposition
Text Books:
Q. Q. Zu, Model Order Reduction Techniques with Applications in Finite Element Analysis, Springer, 2020.
Reference Books:
A.C. Antoulas: Approximation of Large-Scale Dynamical Systems, SIAM, Philadelphia, 2005.
• M. S. Allen, D. Rixen, M.V. Seijs, P. Tiso, T. Abrahamsson, R. L. Mayes, Substructuring in Engineering

Course No: AM6190
Course Name: Cellular structures and mechanics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The aim of the course is developing an appreciation of the role played by mechanics in governing the response of
living cells, both as a singleton and as a collective. The living cell and its surrounding will be examined from a

relevant processes such as development and pathogenesis. The overarching theme of the course is the exposition
of various techniques of cellular quantification and manipulation, invoking purely physical principles.

intracellular rheology with development and disease progression.

isotropic and entropic networks.
• Surface phenomena and biomembranes: Intermembrane forces, Membrane curvature, Bilayer compression and
bending.
• Modulation of membrane stiffness during development and pathogenesis.
• Bilipid layers as an experimental model: quantification of protein-protein interaction, surface force apparatus,
binding affinity, and avidity.
• Tissue remodelling: cellular forces, extracellular matrix (ECM) and its response to cellular forces.
• Methods for ECM characterization.
• Cell-migration modes and characteristics.

Course No: AM6513
Course Name: Advanced Computational Fluid Dynamics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The primary focus of this course is to introduce advanced numerical techniques for the solution of non-linear
continuum governing flow and transport equations. Emphasis will be placed on different grid generation
techniques, finite volume formulation on unstructured and adaptive grids to analyze complex, coupled (fluid flow
and transport) problems of practical engineering interest. Some modern techniques for simulating turbulent flows
are also focused
Course Content:

difference and finite volume methods in structured orthogonal grids, Incompressible Navier-Stokes equation

collocated schemes.

behavior and control, multi grid methods, Dual time step methods.

analytical and numerical models, Applications.
LES and DNS of Incompressible flows: Introduction, Boundary conditions. DNS: Temporal and Spatial
discretization schemes, LES: Filtering, Sub-grid scale modeling and Sample results.

Course No: AM6515
Course Name: Boundary Layer Stability
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course briefly revisits the concept of a boundary layer. It details the physical concepts behind boundary layer
thickness, boundary layer displacement and momentum thickness and friction drag. It discusses the basic
Navier-Stokes equations and their subsequent non-dimensionalisation to derive the Prandtl’s Boundary Layer
Equations and discusses exact solutions to these equations.
It concentrates primarily on the transition of the laminar boundary layer to turbulence; hence the stability o
Course Content:
The course begins with an introduction to the physical concept of a boundary layer dealing with governing
equations for Newtonian Fluids, stresses and strains on a cubic fluid element, BL Thickness, BL Displacement
Thickness, Momentum & Energy Thickness and Laminar boundary layer on a flat plate at zero incidence and on
an airfoil. It derives Prandtl’s Boundary Layer Equations for laminar boundary layers and introduces the concepts
of Wall Friction and Friction Drag. It discusses exact solutions for Wedge Flows, Flow in Convergent Channel,
Mixing Layer, Moving Plate, Free & Wall Jet. It explains the Asymptotic behaviour of solutions downstream and
Integral Relations of the Boundary Layer. It introduces stability of laminar flows with laminar to turbulent transition.
It discusses Small-perturbation stability, Linearized Stability of Parallel Viscous Flows, Parametric effects in Linear
Stability Theory, Orr-Sommerfeld Equation and Transition to turbulence. It next discusses Equations of Mean
Turbulent Flow, i.e. Continuity, Reynolds Equations, k-Equations in Turbulent Boundary Layers and discusses
Turbulent fluctuations. Finally, this course discusses Averaging and Boundary Layer Equations and Computational
Methods for unsteady turbulent boundary layers.
Text Books:
Boundary Layer Theory, H. Schlichting, K. Gersten, Springer, 2001
Reference Books:
1. An Introduction to Fluid Dynamics, G. K. Batchelor, Cambridge University Press, 2010
2. Viscous Fluid Flow, F. M. White, McGraw Hill, USA, 1974
3. Fluid Mechanics, F. M. White, , McGraw Hill, USA, 1979
4. Fundamentals of Aerodynamics, John D. Anderson, , McGraw Hill, USA, 2007

nature of boundary condition at solid–liquid interfaces, conceptual models of slip. Theories of hydrophobic
surfaces.Water in nanochannels: definitions and models (atomistic models).Static behavior of nano-confined
fluids: density distribution and dipole orientation, hydrogen bonding, contact angle. Dynamic behaviors: diffusion
transport, filling and emptying kinetics. Introduction to multiscale modeling of gas and liquid flows.

Course No: AM6550
Course Name: Advanced Gas Dynamics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course introduces the concepts of the primary differences between an incompressible flow and compressible
flow. It draws the connection between compressible flow and speed of sound, Mach Number and thermodynamics.
It then builds on the governing equations to derive the commonly known equations and tackles both 2D and 3D
problems.
The physical concept of shocks and the resulting changes in the thermodynamic properties of a fluid form a major
part of this course. The course concentrates primarily on the understanding of the physical concepts of
compressible flow and keeps reference to various numerical methods for solving the governing equations to a
minimum.
Course Content:
Introduction:Governing equations of compressible flow.
1 D Flow: Introduction - Normal Shock Relations - Hugoniot Equations.
Oblique Shocks - Supersonic flow over wedges and cones - Interaction of shocks of opposite families -
Intersection of shocks of same family.
3D Shock Waves - Prandtl-Meyer Expansion waves - Shock expansion theory - Crocco's Theorem.
Linearized Flow - Linearized velocity potential equation - Linearized pressure coefficient - Linearized Subsonic flow
- Improved compressibility corrections - Linearized supersonic flow - Critical Mach Number.
Unsteady wave motion - Moving normal shock wave - Reflected shock waves - Incident and reflected expansion
waves - Shock tube relations - Finite compression waves.
Method of Characteristics.
3D flow - Cones at angle of attack - Blunt-nosed bodies at angle of attack.
Text Books:
1. Elements of Gas Dynamics, H. W. Liepmann and A. Roshko
2. Modern Compressible Flow, John D. Anderson, Jr.
Reference Books:
Dynamics and Thermodynamics of Compressible Fluid Flow (volumes I and II), Ascher H. Shapiro

1. Introduction to the course – A review of brain structures (current understanding) – one week
2. The four central dogmas of modern neuroscience
3. Role of structures on behavior (passing of iron rod throughSection the head and its effect on behavior – the
case of Phineas Gage)
4. “The Neuron doctrine” - Works of the father of modern neuroscience, Santiago Ramon Y Cajal (1887)
5. “The Balancing brain” - Works of Robert Barany on the physiology/pathology of vestibular system (1914)
6. “The Synaptic formulation” - Works of the father of modern neurophysiology, Sir Charles Sherrington (1906,
1932)
7. Localization Vs Mass Action – A review of works of Fritsch & Hitzig, Hughlings Jackson and others until Wilder
Penfield - An Alternate point of view (Lashley)
8. The incredible case of patient H.M., and his role in understanding the distinct memory functions of the brain.
(Scoville, Milner, Corkin et al) (1957 to 2008),
9. “The emotional brain” - Neural mechanism of rage (Bard, 1929), Psychic blindness – effect of bilateral temporal
lobectomy (Kluever and Bucy, 1938), Visceral theory of emotion (Papez, 1937)
10. Contributions of Hodgkin & Huxley in explaining functions of neuronal membrane using ionic (electrical)
mechanisms (Hodgkin & Huxley, 1952)
11. The role of neurotransmitters in neural (and neuromuscular) function (HH Dale, 1936) & (Katz, 1968)
12. “The split brain – a tale of two halves” - Pioneering work of Sperry & Gazzaniga (1962) in understanding
hemispheric functions of the brain (Cases of patients W.J., P.S., Vicki).
13. “Mirrors in the brain” - Pioneering works of Rizzolatti and colleagues (1992) to describe the functions of mirror
neuron system (in area F5) of the adult monkey brain in understanding of motor events – possible role (?) of mirror
neurons in imitation, empathy and social coSectionnnectedness – controversial claims.
14. “Colored numbers and pain in the non-existent limb” - The works of VS Ramachandran in understanding
synesthesia and Phantom limbs
15. “Maps in the brain” - Role of grid cells in spatial navigation (Year 2014 Nobel prize winning work of Moser &
Moser; 2004, 2006)
16. “The lost word” (the “last” word): The classic works of Broca (1861,1865) in describing the role of “the site of
faculty of articulated speech”
The classic work of Wernicke in understanding/perceiving speech (1874) – the importance of the superior temporal
gyrus (area 22) in understanding language.
Text Books:
There is no text book for this course. All classic papers (listed above) will be supplied by the faculty, who will
coordinate discussion in class. These papers will form the reading material.
Reference Books:
Leroy, F., A Century of Nobel Prize Recipients. Chemistry, Physics and Medicine, New York: Marcel Dekker, Inc.,
2003
Rapport, R., Nerve Endings. The Discovery of the Synapse, New York: W.W. Norton & Co., 2005
Meyers, M.A., Happy Accidents. Serendipity in Modern Medical Breakthroughs, New York: Arcade Publishing,
2007
Principles of Neural Science, Eric R. Kandel, James H. Schwartz, Thomas M. Jessell, Steven A. Siegelbaum, A.J.
Hudspeth, McGraw-Hill Medical; 5 edition (2012)

Course No: AM7020
Course Name: GIAN151003L04: Modeling Engineering Turbulent Flows
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Number of turbulence modelling techniques and models are available in the literature. This course will bring out
salient features of different techniques and models and demonstrate their applicable capability with illustration.
Concepts behind modelling techniques and models will be introduced with implementation in CFD codes.
Course Content:
Characteristics of turbulent flows - scales; Concept of averaging and governing equations; Zero & one equation
models; Two equation models - k-e and k-? family models, their variants; Low Re models. Wall functions &
boundary conditions.
SA models and their variants; Introduction to LES; Filtered Equations; Subgrid Models; Wall modeling; Hybrid
RANS-LES methods; Applications
Text Books:
D.C.Wilcox, Turbulence modelling for CFD, 2006, DCW industries, USA.
Reference Books:
S.B.Pope, Turbulent Flows, Cambridge University Press, 2000.
H.Tennekes and J.L.Lumley, A first course in Turbulence, MIT Press, 1972.
P.A.Davidson, Turbulence-An introduction for scientists and engineers, Oxford University Press,2004.
S.B.Pope, Turbulent Flows, Cambridge University Press, 2000.
