Course No: HS1141
Course Name: World Literature
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This introductory level course aims to introduce the learners to a wide range of writings produced in different
nations, languages and cultural contexts. While this course cannot claim to cover all literary traditions from all time
periods, it does try to introduce the learners to representative texts that are available in the English language. The
objective of the course is to focus on learning how great writings can intervene and engage with global cultures
while remaining rooted and situated in their specific, local contexts, highlighting the translatability of literary works
across languages and cultures. These discussions need to be seen as ‘entry points’ that would enable the learners
to explore world literatures.
Outcomes:
This course will enable learners to understand cultural and historical contexts, while also familiarising themselves
with diverse literary and philosophical traditions. Learners should be able to appreciate the centrality of
translatability and transculturality to the idea of world literature, and acquaint themselves with literary traditions in
their respective mother tongues.
Course Content:
1. Introduction to World Literature, its emergence as an idea, changing meaning, theoretical frame-works.
2. Different approaches to World Literature – Goethe, Tagore and current debates
3. Literature in translation and its possibilities
4. Oral/performance vs. print cultures in world literatures
5. The predominance of English language in World literature
6. The classics in Western and Eastern civilisations
7. Non-canonical and lesser known literatures
8. African-American literature
9. Asian literatures
10. The role of theory in reading world literatures
11. Contemporary writers and new genres
Text Books:
1. D'haen, Theo. The Routledge Concise History of World Literature. London: Routledge, 2012
2. Lawall, Sarah (Ed). Reading World Literature: Theory, History, Practice. Texas, University of Texas Press, 1994.
3. Damrosch et al (Eds). Longman Anthology of World Literature. Boston: Longman, 2004
4. Lawall, Sarah et al (Eds). The Norton Anthology of World Literature. Boston: Massachusetts, 2003
Reference Books:
1. Morretti, Franco. "Conjectures on World Literature". New Left Review 1 (January-February 2000): 54-68.
2. Shields, Kathleen. "Challenges and Possibilities for World Literature, Global Literature, and Translation."
CLCWeb: Comparative Literature and Culture 15.7 (2013): https://doi.org/10.7771/1481-4374.2381
3. Damrosch, David, and Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak. “Comparative Literature/World Literature: A Discussion with
Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak and David Damrosch.” Comparative Literature Studies, vol. 48, no. 4, 2011, pp.
455–485. JSTOR, www.jstor.org/stable/10.5325/complitstudies.48.4.0455. Accessed 20 July 2021.
4. Apter, Emily. Against World Literature: On the Politics of Untranslatability. London: Verso, 2013.
5. Lawall, Sarah et al. The Norton Anthology of World Literature. Second Edition. Norton, 2002.
6. David, Damrosch. What is World Literature? Oxford: Princeton University Press, 2003.
7. Helgesson, Stefan et al (Eds). Literature and the World. London: Routledge, 2019.
8. Mani, Venkat B. Recoding World Literature. Libraries, Print Culture and Germany’s Pact with Books. New York:
Fordham University Press, 2017.

Course No: HS2011
Course Name: Foundations of Social and Political Thought
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course aims to provide an overview of the foundational texts of modern social and political thought. By
reading selected passages from Machiavelli, Hobbes, Hume, Smith, Marx and Weber, in particular, the course will
attempt to identify the main philosophical threads within contemporary social and political discourse.
Course Content:
Selections from the key writings of 6 major thinkers in the history of modern social and political thought. These are
Machiavelli, Hobbes, Hume, Smith, Marx and Weber. In addition, the course will also consider very briefly the
ideas of Spinoza, Locke, and Rousseau.
The central themes that run through the course are liberty, virtue, state, civil society, empiricism, impressions and
ideas, value, justice, and bureaucracy
Text Books:
Machiavelli, Niccolo (1513) The Prince
---- (1517) Discourses on Livy
Hobbes, Thomas (1651) Leviathan
Hume, David (1690) An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding
Smith, Adam (1759) The Theory of Moral Sentiments
---- (1776) Wealth of Nations
Marx, Karl (1845) – The German Ideology
----(1844) Philosophical and Economic Manuscripts
---- (1867) Capital
Weber, Max (1905) – The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
All books are available electronically through http://ebooks.adelaide.edu.au/ as well as other sites.
Reference Books:
Political Theory

Course No: HS2012
Course Name: International Relations: Theory and Practice
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Objectives: This is a core course for MA students. The course will introduce fundamental concepts in international
relations theory, including realism, liberalism, neo-realism, neo-liberalism, Social Constructivism and Non-Western
Approaches to IR, and their major critiques. The course will also discuss the evolution of the discipline and the
major debates in IR on historical origins, or IR and role of state.
Learning Outcomes: The students will be equipped with a critical understanding of theories of IR with familiarity in
fundamental concepts of IR reflecting contemporary epistemological debates of the discipline. The students will
have a grounding in the role of state as an actor in IR its related critiques, including feminist and post-colonial
perspectives.
Course Content:
The theoretical content would include:
1. concept of state and sovereignty,
2. Realist theory of IR and its critiques
3. Liberal Theory of IR and its critiques
4. The First Great Debate in IR
5. Neoliberalism, Neorealism and their critiques.
6. Social Constructivist theory of IR and its critique
7. Theories of nuclear deterrence and game theory
8. Critical approaches to IR including Feminism and Non-western approaches.
Text Books:
• Jackson, Robert, and Georg Sorensen, Introduction to International Relations, Theories and Approaches, Third
Edition, Oxford University Press, 2006
• Mansbach, Richard, and Kirsten Rafferty, Introduction to Global Politics, Routledge, 2008
Reference Books:
• Burchill, Scott, Andrew Linklater, Richard Devetak, and Jack Donnelly. Theories of International Relations:
Fourth Edition, Palgrave Macmillan 2009.
• Lake, David A. "The state and international relations." In Christian Reus-Smit and Duncan Snidal (eds) Oxford
Handbook of International Relations: London: Oxford University Press, 2008.
• Carr, Edward Hallett, and Michael Cox. The twenty years' crisis, 1919-1939: an introduction to the study of
international relations. London: Macmillan, 1946.
• Morgenthau, Hans Joachim, Kenneth W. Thompson, and W. David Clinton. "Politics among nations: The
struggle for power and peace." McGraw Hill, 1985
• Schelling, Thomas C. The Strategy of Conflict: Harvard university press, 1980.
• Waltz, Kenneth N. Theory of international politics. Waveland Press, 2010.
• Keohane, Robert O. After hegemony. Princeton university Press, 2005.
• Wendt, Alexander. Social theory of international politics: Cambridge University Press, 1999.
• Shilliam, Robbie (ed) International relations and non-Western thought: Imperialism, colonialism and
investigations of global modernity. Routledge, 2010.
• Sankaran Krishna, On the pitfalls of geo-cultural pluralism in IR, International Politics Reviews, July 2021.

 9 
Course No: HS2014
Course Name: Environment and Society
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course aims to explore the interactions between the natural environment and human societies through an
interdisciplinary lens. It aims to explore how the relationship between the environment and society is a product of
socio-cultural, economic, and political processes drawing on various eminent thinkers in the field of environment
including Carson, Meadows, Gandhi, Scumacher, Forsyth and Hintz.
Course Content:
The course will examine the following issues, from a theoretical perspective and will use case studies, to discuss
and debate environmental implications of development. The issues will include, relations between society and the
environment, the evolution of environmental thinking, evaluation of environmental problems, especially those
relating to development, environmental decision making – principal and theories and the socio-political and
economic structures that determine the exploitation of natural resources. The theoretical perspectives will draw on
traditions and disciplines related to political ecology, ecological anthropology, environmental sociology,
environmental history, and environmental economics. The case-studies would focus on particular environmental
issues and a range of actions and responses to these environmental issues – for example, anthropogenic global
change; common property resource management; approaches to pollution management; conservation and
biodiversity; agriculture and deforestation; population and environment; climate change and development;
ecological footprint analysis; and fundamental differences in the environmental movements in the North and the
South. The discourse on sustainability will be an integral part of the discussions in most case-studies. It is
intended that students develop a sound understanding of and an interdisciplinary perspective on the relationship
between environment and society.
Text Books:
Forsyth, Tim. 2003. Critical Political Ecology: The Politics of Environmental Science. London: Routledge.
Hintz, John and Sarah More, 2010. Environment and Society: A Critical Introduction. UK: Wiley-Blackwell
Reference Books:
Gadgil, Madhav and Ramachandra Guha, 1993. This Fissured Land: An Ecological History of India. University of
California Press.
Meadows, Donnella, Jørgen Randers, and Dennis Meadows, 2004. Limits to Growth: The 30-Year Update,
Chelsea Green Publishing Company and Earthscan
Taylor, Paul W. 1986. Respect for Nature: A Theory of Environmental Ethics. Princeton Univ. Press
IPCC, 2007. Climate Change 2007: Synthesis Report of Working Groups I, II and III to the Fourth Assessment
Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, Cambridge University Press.

Course No: HS2015
Course Name: Culture and Society
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course offers an introduction to the foundational relationship between culture and society, by examining
anthropological approaches to the study of culture. The course will help address the following questions: What is
the culture concept? How and when did it gain primacy in anthropology, sociology and cultural studies? What are
the critiques of the culture concept? How does one perform cultural analysis?
Course Content:
- The Culture Concept: History and Provenance
- Vocabulary and Keywords
- The Cultural Turn
- Writing Culture
- Performing cultural analysis
- Contemporary applications of the culture concept
- Critiques
Text Books:
Rapport, Nigel, and Joanna Overing. 2000. Social and cultural anthropology: the key concepts. London:
Routledge. http://site.ebrary.com/id/10054224.
Williams, Raymond. 1985. Keywords : A Vocabulary of Culture and Society. New York :Oxford University Press.
Reference Books:
Geertz, Clifford. 1973. The Interpretation of Cultures. New York: Basic Books (2000)
Bourdieu, P. 1984. Distinction: A Social Critique of the Judgment of Taste. London: Routledge.
Hebdige, D. (1979). Subculture: The Meaning of Style (pp. 121-131). Gelder, K. (ed.). (2005). The Subcultures
reader. London and N.Y.: Routledge.
Nash, Kate. “The 'Cultural Turn' in Social Theory: Towards a Theory of Cultural Politics.” Sociology, vol. 35, no. 1,
2001, pp. 77–92. JSTOR, www.jstor.org/stable/42856250.
Bonnell, Victoria E.. Beyond the cultural turn: new directions in the study of society and culture. Berkeley, Calif. :
University of California Press, c1999. http://hdl.handle.net/2027/heb.04780.0001.001.

Course No: HS2025
Course Name: Logic and Critical Thinking
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Why do we need Critical - logical and Creative Thinking? Are these special skills only a chosen few possess and
not available to the multitude? This course attempts to explode this myth. Most, if not all, possess and apply
critical and logical thinking every living second but intuitively. Logic and Critical Thinking HS 1070 introduces the
students to the foundations of Logical Thinking and Reasoning. The objective of the course is to tease out an
understanding of the art of questioning assumptions, reasons, validity claims and conclusions, a la Socratic
method. The students will also be introduced to Indian Logic, specifically, the Nyaya and the Buddhist Logic.
Course Content:
1. Introduction to Logic and Critical Thinking
2. The structure of various forms of arguments: Propositions, Sentences, Arguments
3. Deduction, Induction, Validity, Probability
4. Informal fallacies
5. Different kinds of fallacies in arguments
6. Distinguishing valid forms of arguments from invalid forms
7. Syllogistic structure of deductive arguments: Categorical Propositions, Venn Diagrams, Aristotelian and
Boolean Square of Opposition
8. Arguments in Ordinary Language, Translating Categorical Propositions, Enthymemes and Sorites
9. Disjunctive and Hypothetical Syllogisms and Dilemma
10. Indian Logic: Nyaya, Jaina and Buddhist Logic
11. Modern mathematical and Symbolic logic
12. Quantification rules and logical relations
Text Books:
1. Copi, Irving, M., and Carl Cohen, 2004. Essentials of Logic, New Jersey: Prentice Hall.
2. Govier, Trudy, 2019. A Practical Study of Argument, Enhanced 7th ed., Boston: Wadsworth.
Reference Books:
1. Black, Beth (ed.), 2012. An A to Z of Critical Thinking, London: Continuum International Publishing Group.
2. Damer, T.E., 2005. Attacking Faulty Reasoning, 5th ed., Belmont: Wadsworth.
3. Hooks, Bell, 2010. Teaching Critical Thinking: Practical Wisdom, New York and London: Routledge.
4. Jacquette, Dale, 2000. Symbolic Logic, Belmont: Wadsworth.
5. Johnson, Robert. M., 1999. A Logic Book, 3rd ed., Belmont: Wadsworth.
6. Kahane, Howard and Nancy M. Cavender, 2002. Logic and Contemporary Rhetoric: The Use of Reason in
Everyday Life, 9th Edition, Belmont: Wadsworth.
7. Kuhn, Deanna, 1991. The Skills of Argument, New York: Cambridge University Press.
doi:10.1017/CBO9780511571350
8. Munson, Ronald, 1976. The Way of Words: An Informal Logic, Boston: Houghton Mifflin.
9. Norris, Stephen P. and Robert H. Ennis, 1989. Evaluating Critical Thinking (The Practitioners’ Guide to
Teaching Thinking Series), Pacific Grove, CA: Midwest Publications.
10. Paul, Richard W. and Linda Elder, 2006. The Miniature Guide to Critical Thinking: Concepts and Tools, Dillon
Beach, CA: Foundation for Critical Thinking, 4th edition.

Course No: HS2030
Course Name: Modern Govt & Comparative Constitutions
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
In general there are events in recent past which have further ignited the interests of scholars and students to
freshly look into the various governments and their constitutions. The advantage of studying politics comparatively
across world not only helps to interpret new developments, it also enables one's own country to be seen in a new
light. Additionally, the comparative study of governments enables us to test general hypotheses about politics,
improves our classifications of political processes and gives us some potential for prediction and so on. As active
participants of the governance processes, this course empowers students to understand the structure, process
and outcome of state and government.
Course Content:
Module-1
Fundamental Ideas: Politics, Government, Governance, State
History of Government
Origin of state: Theories of State, Social Contract - Hobbes, Lock, Rousseau, Hegel and so on
Module-2:
Dominant Concepts: Sovereignty, Citizen, Rights, Liberty, Equality, Justice
Module-3
Comparative Constitutions: Constitution of United Kingdom, Constitution of USA, Constitution of Canada, and
Constitution of India
Text Books:
1. Hague, Rod and Harrop, Martin (2004), Comparative Government and Politics: An Introduction, 6th Edition,
Palgrave Macmillan: New York
2. Heywood Andrew (2004), Political Theory: An Introduction, Palgrave Macmillan: New York.
3. Bhargava, Rajeev and Acharya, Ashok, (ed.) (2008), Political Theory: An Introduction, Pearson Longman:
Noida
4. Hoffman, John (2007), A Glossary of Political Theory, Edinburgh University Press Ltd: Edinburgh.
5. Poguntke, Thomas and Webb, Paul (ed.) (2005), The Presidentialisation of Politics: A Comparative Study of
Modern Democracies: OUP: London
6. Appadorai, A (1944), The Substance of Politics, OUP: London
7. N. H. Brasher, N.H., (1977), Studies in British Government, Macmillan Press: London

Course No: HS2080
Course Name: Korean II
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Korean II is a further study of the Korean language and some aspects of Korean culture and daily life as the
second half of the elementary Korean language course. It features the integrated development of language skills in
listening, speaking, reading, and writing. To ensure maximum exposure to the new language, classes are
conducted as much as possible in Korean. Multimedia will be used dynamically to enhance language
teaching/learning and cultural awareness through task-based practice. Students are encouraged to have
autonomy and participation as active language learners.
This course intends to help students to perform at the level of the CEFR Basic User A1 and the level of the TOPIK
Level I or above.
The Level I student will be able to:
• Carry out basic conversations related to daily survival skills such as self-introduction, purchasing, ordering food,
etc., and understand the contents related to very personal and familiar subjects such as himself/herself, family,
hobby, weather, and the like.
• Create simple sentences using a basic vocabulary of approximately 800 words and understand basic grammar.
• Understand and compose simple and useful sentences related to everyday life.
Outcomes
At the end of Korean II, students should be able to:
• Understand and use sentences/frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance;
• Communicate in routine tasks requiring a direct exchange of information on familiar and routine matters;
• Ask and respond to questions about the topics and functions covered in class;
• Carry out the given tasks (speaking and writing) individually, in pairs, and/or in groups;
• Read the passage or paragraphs related to the topics in the text;
• Make good use of media sources related to learning items and share them with others;
• Demonstrate an awareness and understanding of some aspects of Korean culture.
Course Content:
- Communicative functions and topics
• Topics: Family, the time, body, health, traffic, etc.
• Functions: Introducing family members, making an appointment, etc.
- Grammar: Honorific language forms, verb forms, connecting clauses, etc.

????(Hello.), ????? ? ???(Please take me to Seoul station.), etc.
- Culture Notes: Home remedies for a cold, Korean age, Public transportation, etc.

Course No: HS2090
Course Name: An Introduction to Detective Fiction
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course aims to understand the generic ontology and ideological
underpinnings of detective fiction through select stories. The major ideas that this course intends to
discuss in the class include the concepts of justices, human right and ethics of retribution; the strong
interconnection between the form of detective stories and the veracity of truth portrayed in these
stories, and the problematics concerning the depiction of the society where the crime occurs. The
following are the major objectives of this course.
1) To introduce students to the generic specialties of detective fiction.
2) To familiarize students with the scientific temper and analytical skills involved in the genre.
3) To discuss the social issues portrayed through detective fiction.
4) To understand the ideological undercurrents fashioning the subjectivity of the sleuth and his
perception of the nature of crime and the society where crime occurs.
5) To introduce students to the formal changes that the genre had undergone.
Course Content:
Detective fiction, which is a sub-genre of crime fiction, is one of the most popular
genres in literature. Though the origin of detective fiction is a contentious topic, there is a general
consensus among literary critics that it was in the late 19 th and 20 th centuries that it developed into a
recognizable literary genre. The traditional elements underpinning a detective story include (1) a
perfect crime, (2) the wrongly accused suspect who is going to be incriminated on the basis of
circumstantial evidence and (3) a detective who is endowed with greater powers of observation.
Though detective fiction is deeply conservative in its formulaic conventions, it is highly radical in its
diversity, the portrayal of the world in which the story is set and the disposition of the sleuths
towards the society that s/he lives in and deals with. Detective stories, which usually operate on the
principle that superficially convincing evidence is often misleading, believe in reinventing the truth
concerning a crime through systematic observation and deduction. In other words, scientific temper
and logical deduction are often considered the sine qua non of a detective story. It is also important
that the methodology and the observations of a sleuth should be convincing to the on-lookers. In
short, the success of detective fiction oftentimes lies in the sleuth presenting his method of solving
the conundrum convincingly to the reader. The generic singularities defining the ontology of a
detective story also play a vital role in presenting the views endorsed by the detective as correct and
objective. Therefore, it is important to see these stories from a critical vantage point. This course
intends to problematize a slew of ideas pertaining to the art of detection such as the idea of justice,
ethics, human rights and the power of this genre in indoctrinating the readers certain ideological
positions indirectly, yet convincingly. Though the course begins with canonical writes in this genre,
it eventually shifts its focus to the Indian writers of detective fiction.
Text Books:
“The Murder in the Rue Morgue” — Edgar Allan Poe
“The Adventures of the Speckled Band”— Sir Arthur Conan Doyle
“The Adventure of the Solitary Cyclist”— Sir Arthur Conan Doyle
“The Tuesday Night Club” —Agatha Christie
“Danger in Darjeeling” — Satyajit Ray
“The Royal Bengal Mystery” — Satyajit Ray
“The Inquisitor” — Sharadindu Bandyopadhyay
“The Venom of Tarantula” — Sharadindu Bandyopadhyay
“The Grandest Wedding in Town” —Vithal Rajan
“The Visitor” —Vithal Rajan
“The Mark of Art” — Madhulika Liddle
“A Face in the Crowd” —Kalpana Swaminathan
“The Sixth Pandava” — Kalpana Swaminathan
Enola Holmes— Directed by Harry Bradbeer
“The King of the Verdant Island” — Sunil Gangopadhyay
Reference Books:
Keep, Christopher, and Don Randall “.Addiction, Empire, and Narrative in Arthur Conan Doyle's the Sign of the
Four.” Novel: A Forum on Fiction, vol. 32, no. 2, 1999, pp. 207-221.
Grossman, Jonathan H. The Art of Alibi: English Law Courts and the Novel. Johns Hopkins UP, 2002.
Knight, Stephen. Crime Fiction Since 1800: Detection, Death, Diversity. 2nd ed. New York: Palgrave Macmillan,
2010.
Priestman, Martin, ed. The Cambridge Companion to Crime Fiction. Cambridge UP, 2003.
Scaggs, John. Crime Fiction: The New Critical Idiom. Routledge, 2005.
Watson, Kate. Women Writing Crime Fiction, 1860-1880: Fourteen American, British, and Australian Authors.
McFarland, 2012.

Course No: HS2130
Course Name: Contemporary German Philosophy
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course introduces some basic ideas discussed by several German philosophers from the 19th century to the
present day. After a brief survey of European philosophy, it examines the historical background of German
philosophy. It demonstrates how philosophers after 1850 have responded to the cardinal questions of philosophy.
After discussing the fundamental ideas of Marxism, it focuses on Nietzsche’s works with a particular focus on his
ideas of overman, will to power and rejection of moral traditions of the west. This will be followed by an
examination of the phenomenological tradition where the idea of presuppositionless philosophy is examined and
the philosophies of Husserl, Heidegger and Gadamer are analysed. The course concludes with an examination of
the debate between Gadamer and Habermas on the question of enlightenment and the importance of tradition.
Outcomes:
This course will familiarize the students with the philosophical theories of some important contemporary German
thinkers. This will help students to conceptually situate and understand important theoretical issues and problems
that shape the nature of contemporary debates taking place in the social, political and cultural realms.
Course Content:
• Historical Background to Contemporary German Philosophy
• Contemporary German Philosophy (after 1850)
• Marxism and the interpretation of history and the role of the proletarians.
• The problem of alienation
• Nietzsche’s radical criticism of morality and religion
• Will to power
• The Concept of overman
• Phenomenology: Husserl and the idea of phenomenological reduction
• Transcendental phenomenology and transcendental subject
• Heidegger’s idea of Being and dasein
• Gadamer’s hermeneutics
• Linguisticality of human understanding
• Criticism of enlightenment philosophy
• Habermas and unfinished project of modernity.
Text Books:
1. Bowie, Andrew. 2003. Introduction to German Philosophy: From Kant to Habermas. Cambridge: Polity Press.
2. Gorner, Paul. 2000. Twentieth-Century German Philosophy. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
Reference Books:
1. Gadamer, Hans-Georg. 2004. Truth and Method. Translated by Joel Weinsheimer, Donald G Marshall. United
Kingdom: Continuum.
2. Habermas, Jürgen. 1987. The Philosophical Discourse of Modernity. MIT Press.
3. Heidegger, Martin. 1996. Being and Time. A Translation of "Sein und Zeit". Translated by Joan Stambaugh. 7th
ed. Albany, New York: SUNY Press.
4. Husserl, Edmund. 1970. The Crisis of the European Sciences and Transcendental Phenomenology. Evanston:
Northwestern University Press.
5. Nietzsche, F. 2010. Beyond Good & Evil: Prelude to a Philosophy of the Future. United Kingdom: Knopf
Doubleday Publishing Group.
6. Spiegelberg, Herbert. 1983. The Phenomenological Movement: A Historical Introduction. 3rd ed. The Hague:
Martinus Nijhoff.

Course No: HS2150
Course Name: Indian Literature
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course will draw upon a broad spectrum of texts in translation, largely from the Indian subcontinent. The
objective of the course is to “decolonize” our understanding of literature, to look beyond the western literary canon
for an understanding of literature, literary cultures and ways of living. Issues of caste, gender, nation, language
and translation are central to this course
Outcomes: Students will arrive at an understanding of how the idea of “India” has been simultaneously constructed
and challenged through close readings and discussions on a range of literary texts from the Indian subcontinent.
They will also develop a grounding in the literary traditions and movements in India and the ways in which they are
interconnected.
Course Content:
- Medieval and early modern literatures from the Indian sub-continent
- Nationalism, reform movements and literatures from pre-independence India
- The construction of the Indian nation state and post-independence literatures.
- Caste, gender and Indian literatures
- The role of translation and the translated text
Text Books:
Compendium of texts including, but not limited to, works such as the following:
Fiction:
Imayam’s Pethavan (translated from the Tamil) OR Perumal Murugan’s Seasons of the Palm
Autobiography:
Bama’s Karukku (translated from the Tamil)
Kumud Pawde, “The Story of my Sanskrit” (translated from the Marathi)
Drama:
Vijay Tendulkar’s Silence! The Court is in Session (translated from the Marathi)
Short Stories:
AK Ramanujan, “Annayya’s Anthropology” (translated from the Kannada)
“A Flowering Tree” (Kannada folktale transcribed and translated by AK Ramanujan)

Course No: HS2200
Course Name: Introduction to Indian Philosophy
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course is a survey of Indian philosophical thought from the Vedas and Upanishads, orthodox schools known
as six darsanas and heterodox schools such as Carvaka, Buddhism and Jainism to more recent philosophers such
as Swami Vivekananda, Tilak, Gandhi, Aurobindo, Iqbal, et al. The emphasis would be to relate the textual to the
contextual, historical, cultural and social understanding.
Outcomes:
Students will be exposed to various concepts in Indian philosophical thought from the Vedic age, Upanishads,
Carvaka, Jainism, Buddhism, Nyaya, Vaisesika, Sankhya, Yoga, Mimamsa and Vedanta, later Buddhism, and
contemporary Indian thought. The traditional academic distinction between metaphysics, epistemology, ethics and
aesthetics will also be discussed. Students would gain a panoramic view of Indian philosophical thought over three
millennia.
Course Content:
1. Introduction, Pre-Upanishadic Thought
2. The Upanishads
3. Early Post-Vedic Period, General Tendencies
4. The Bhagawad Gita
5. Early Buddhism
6. Jainism
7. The age of systems, Preliminary, Materialism
8. Later Buddhistic Schools
9. Nyaya-Vaiseshika
10. Sankhya-Yoga
11. Purva-Mimamsa
12. Vedanta – Advaita
13. Vedanta – Vishistadvaita, dvaita – Bhakti movement, Sufi
14. Contemporary Indian Philosophers – Swami Vivekananda, Sri Aurobindo, Bala Gangadhar Tilak, Gandhi,
Iqbal and others

Course No: HS3011
Course Name: The Rise of the Novel
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course will trace the rise of the novel, placing the genre within the socio-political and cultural contexts of
colonization and industrialization in England of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. It will also explore the
diverse histories of the novel in the non-western world, providing an overview of various theories of the novel and
its many forms. Students will be trained to close-read and locate novels ranging from Don Quixote and Robinson
Crusoe to early novels published in the non-western world.
Outcomes: It is hoped that students will develop an understanding of the rise of the novel in terms of its formal
innovations and socio-political contexts. Through close readings of the texts and discussions, students will be
exposed to a variety of issues such as the fictional construction of race, gender, nationality, caste and class. The
course will train students to map the ways in which the western novel has been shaped and the ways in which it
has been re-written elsewhere in the world.
Course Content:
- History of the form: Is the novel an altogether new literary form? How does it differ from the prose fiction of the
past? How do we understand conflicting theories and claims about what constitutes the “first” novel? How do we
understand the genre in relation to diverse literary histories such as, for instance, that of the Indian sub-continent?
Feminist and anti-imperialist accounts of the development of the novel, how the novel as a genre silenced and
excluded both woman and people of colour.
- The rise of the English novel: The realist novel and the criterion of truth to individual experience as opposed to
works inspired by legend and history; Formal realism in the works of Defoe, Richardson, Fielding and others.
- Theories of the novel: The novel’s nineteenth century associations with privacy, individuality, domesticity, and the
feminine, its association with interiority as subjectivity, of character as personality and selfhood, and of plot as the
progressive development of the integral individual, the invention and significance of “free indirect discourse,” and
the doctrine of realism as formulated by the early theory of the novel.
Text Books:
Readings of excerpts from the following novels (available as e-texts on Project Gutenberg and other sites):
Murasaki Shikibu, The Tale of Genji (early 11th Century – exact year unknown)
Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote (1605)
John Bunyan, The Pilgrim’s Progress (1678)
Aphra Ben, Oroonoko (1688)
Daniel Defoe, Robinson Crusoe (1719); Moll Flanders (1722)
Samuel Richardson, Pamela (1740); Clarissa (1748)
Henry Fielding, The History of Tom Jones, A Foundling (1749)
Laurence Sterne, The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman (1759)
Jane Austen, Pride and Prejudice (1813)
William Makepeace Thackeray, Vanity Fair (1847)
Charlotte Bronte, Jane Eyre (1847)
Baba Padamji, Yamuna Paryatan (1857) - Marathi novel
George Eliot, The Mill on the Floss (1860)
Charles Dickens, Great Expectations (1860)
Chatterjee, Bankim Chandra. Rajmohan’s Wife (1864)
Thomas Hardy, Tess of the d’Uurbervilles (1891)
Joseph Conrad, Heart of Darkness (1899)
Reference Books:
Pamuk, Orhan. The Naïve and the Sentimental Novelist. New Delhi: Penguin, 2011
McKeon, Michael ed. Theory of the Novel: A Historical Approach. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins UP, 2000.
Auerbach, Eric. Mimesis: The Representation of Reality in Western Literature. Princeton: Princeton University
Press, 2003
Watt, Ian. The Rise of the Novel: Studies in Defoe, Richardson and Fielding. Berkeley: University of California

This course provides an introductory understanding to cities and urbanization. It focuses on a basic and all-round

Course No: HS3014
Course Name: Statistics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
To provide the students with conceptual understanding of modern statistical tools, starting from descriptive
statistical measures, alternative charts and diagrams, etc. to report qualitative and quantitative data, we would like
to discuss various tools and methods of modern inferential statistics to draw inference about a large population on
the basis of the counterpart characteristics of a sample alone!
Outcomes:
On successful completion of the course, a student would be able to represent information in concise manner,
through uses of various tables, charts, diagrams and descriptive statistical properties of it. The would also be able
to draw effective prediction about unknown characteristic(s) of a population, scientifically analyzing a sample
drawn from it!
Course Content:
1. Collection of Data: Classification and Tabulation
Meaning of Statistics—Variables vs. Attributes—Primary vs. Secondary Data—Population vs. Sample—Some
other useful terms and concepts.
2. Charts and Diagrams
Objects of Diagrammatic Representations—Different types of Charts and Diagrams.
3. Useful Mathematical Devices and Frequency Distributions
Logarithmic transformation—AP and GP series—Different types of Polynomial operations—Permutation and
Combination—Summation notation—Interpolation.
4. Measures of Central Tendency
Mean, Median, Mode, Quartiles, Deciles, Percentiles etc.—Concepts, Formulae and their Calculations.
5. Measures of Dispersions
Alternative absolute and relative measures of dispersions—Lorenz curve—Gini.
6. Moments, Skewness and Kurtosis
7. Some discussion on Correlation and Regression
8. Index Numbers
9. Theory of Probability
10. Random Variable and Theoretical Distributions: Binomial, Poisson and Normal
11. Sampling Theory
12. Estimation and Test of Significance/Hypothesis Testing
13. Some Discussion on Time Series (If Time Permits)
Text Books:

Reference Books:

Course No: HS3018
Course Name: Global Politics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course will introduce global politics as a domain that is systemically organized around the concepts of state,
anarchy and sovereignty, which in turn are derived from international relations theory. The course will take a

critical theory and decolonial theory. The course will discuss the evolution of the discipline and contextualize major
epistemological debates in global politics.

• The state as an actor in the international system
Disciplinary positions in IR theories of realism, liberalism, international political economy and social constructivism.
• The Great Debates in international relations
• Anarchy (realist, liberal, constructivist, critical, decolonial positions)
• Sovereignty (realist, liberal, constructivist, critical, decolonial positions)
• Global institutions (realist, liberal, constructivist, critical, decolonial positions)
Case studies will focus on the following themes by drawing on contemporary global challenges
• Disaggregated sovereignty
• New social movements
• Cosmopolitanism
• Global justice

Course No: HS3019
Course Name: Language and Society
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course introduces the fundamental concepts that link language and society and deals with the interplay of
language with social factors (both internal and external) such as class, gender, ethnicity, and age, including how
language varies and changes. To build understanding about the complex relationship between language and
society, this course will introduce nuances of language learning (acquisition) and structure (sounds, words, and
sentences). The use of language in society (performance) as multilinguality and the notion of language as
linguistic competence would be clearer with the content that this course offers. The close parallels between
variation and the use of two or more languages (multilingualism) will be drawn, including discussion of language
attitudes, language planning, and language contact (code-switching/mixing of languages). Communication is the
function of language and not the definition becomes clearer with nuanced study of language and its applications.
This course explores the relation of language to national and individual identity and the degree to which a society’s
culture may manifest itself in its language and influence the world view of its speakers. Are all languages equal?
What does it mean to speak a dialect of a language? Exploring answers to these simple-looking questions, this
course helps us see how our being is predicated on language as the medium of construction and decimation of
knowledge.
Course Content:
•Fundamental Concepts in the study of language and society; Language as a System; Design Features; Language
and Culture; Language and Gender; Language and Identity
•Language Acquisition and Learning, Innateness Hypothesis, Linguistic Competence, Critical Period Hypothesis,
Communicative Competence; Mother tongue vs. first, second, and foreign language
•Language (Sounds, words, sentences, and discourse)
•Multilingual speech communities; Languages and dialects; National languages and language planning; Diglossia;
Linguistic minorities, Code-switching and Code-mixing (translanguaging)
•The Eighth Schedule and Official Language(s) of India; and Linguistic Diversity of India; English in Multilingualism
India
•Language and Variations and sociolinguistic theories (Labov-Martha Vinyad, Social Stratification of English in
New York City)
•Language ‘choice’, language loss and endangerment, language maintenance, language and globalization
•Language and communication; social networks, the ethnography of communication, style and register, speech
functions and politeness, cross-cultural communication and pragmatics, accommodation theory, discourse
analysis, language and the media.
Text Books:
Trudgill, Peter (2000). Sociolinguistics: An introduction to language and society. London: Penguin.
Wardhaugh, Roland (2006). An introduction to sociolinguistics. Massachusetts: Blackwell Publishing.
Reference Books:
Dube, S.C. (2018). Indian Society. New Delhi: National Book Trust.
Foster, E.M. (1924). A passage to India. New York: Harcourt Brace
Khubchandani, L. M. (1997). Language policy and education in the Indian subcontinent. In Encyclopedia of
language and education, pp. 179-187. Dordrecht: Springer.
Pandharipande, R. (2002). Minority matters: issues in minority languages in India. International Journal of
Multicultural Societies, 4(2), 213-234.

Course No: HS3021
Course Name: Macroeconomics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The purpose of this course is to enhance students’ understanding of macroeconomic issues and problems. The
course will help students to analyse questions such as, what is economic growth and how to achieve it, why is
there unemployment, why are there short-run fluctuations in the economy, what causes inflation and business
cycles. Upon completion of this course, students will be in a position to analyse issues of policy relevance and
relate specific issues to theory.
Course Content:
Introduction- Measurement of Macroeconomic Variables - Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply - The
Income-Expenditure Model - The Fixed-Price AD-AS Model - The Output Multiplier - The Monetarist

Course No: HS3024
Course Name: Research Methods and Programme Evaluation
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course aims to develop students' knowledge and understanding of methodology question in the humanities
and social sciences. Theoretical and methodological debates in selected disciplinary areas will be discussed in
order to motivate students to pursue a critical approach to research. The imperative for ethical research practices
will be presented. The course helps students recognize and reflect on the strengths and limitations of various
research methodologies, determining the link between theory and practice, critically evaluating research, and
addressing ethical and practical dilemmas. In this course, students will learn, step-by-step, how to design and
implement quantitative and qualitative methods, including case studies, in-depth interviews, focus group
discussions, participant observation, and textual and media analysis. The course includes lessons on how to deal
with and analyze data, as well as how to write up and present findings.
Outcomes:
The course will make students understand the research process that includes, at a minimum, selecting appropriate
conceptual/theoretical framework, identifying and reviewing select literature, framing research questions, choosing
appropriate research methods, and synthesizing the observations/finding to develop a set of coherent arguments.
In addition to developing a set of transferable workplace skills, it is expected that the students will gain the
knowledge and ability to do original research.
Course Content:
1. Introduction to social science research
2. What is the methodology question in social science research?
3. Discussion on the history of disciplines in social science and the question of critical disciplinary approach
4. Discussion on interdisciplinary, multi-disciplinary & transdisciplinary research
5. Overview of select academic disciplines/sub-disciplines and a discussion on why such mapping is necessary.
6. Mapping of select disciplines – Economics; History; English Studies; Development Studies, etc. – to discuss
how the direction of inquiry has changed overtime and subsequently the research methods.
7. Research methods - Quantitative Vs. qualitative methods & mixed methods
8. Quantitative research methods and secondary data sets
9. Survey method I – Basic concepts in quantitative research & Sampling techniques
10. Survey method II – Developing research questions; Preparing a questionnaire
11. Survey method III – A discussion on data analysis with select examples
12. Qualitative research methods and data gathering process
13. Ethnography/Auto-ethnography
14. Textual and discourse analysis
15. Focus group discussions (FGDs)
16. Vignettes, case studies, and participant observation
17. Project evaluation and monitoring
18. Research ethics – ethics committees, anti-plagiarism guidelines, formal acknowledgments, data privacy, and
confidentiality, etc.
Text Books:
1. Byman, Alan. (2012). Social Research Methods. Oxford University Press.

Course No: HS3026
Course Name: Twentieth Century Fiction
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course captures major strands of 20th century fiction, taking into account the genre’s multiple literary forms.
The course shall introduce to the learners fictional samples from around the globe written between 1901 and 1999
through close readings and classroom discussions around themes carefully chosen from varied sources, including
the prescribed textbooks. A survey course of this kind is intended to give students vivid impressions concerning
lived realities unique to 20th century and celebrate the art of storytelling.
Outcomes:
The course is a training in the anatomy of fiction. Students are introduced to major 20th century fiction writers and
their unique contributions. Students completing this course should be able to develop an understanding of the art
of storytelling.
Course Content:
1. Introduction – What is fiction? What are the major forms of fiction? Some major 20th century themes
2. How to read a novel? – Discussion of J.M Coetzee’s novel Disgrace
3. Young adult fiction (YA) – Young adulthood, adolescence, and the problem of growing up; short stories from
Ernest Hemingway and Catherine Mansfield
4. The stream of consciousness technique – Introduction to James Joyce, a close reading of a story by Virginia
Woolf
5. Point of view and postmodernism – Interior monologue; the idea of repetition; postmodernism and gender
politics
6. Magic realism – Postcolonial fiction; surrealism, realism, and magical realism; short story by Gabriel Garcia
Marquez
7. Flash fiction – Fiction and artificial intelligence; fiction and the ephemera; fiction and the rhizome; film and
fiction; problems of translation; intermediality
8. Students’ fiction – Appreciation of fictional pieces by student members
Text Books:
1. Lodge, David. The art of fiction. London: Secker and Warburg (1992).
2. Michael J Hoffman and Patrick D Murphy (Eds). Essentials of the Theory of Fiction. Duke University Press,
2005.
Reference Books:
1. Keen, Suzanne. Empathy and the Novel. Ukraine, Oxford University Press, 2007.
2. Warnes, Christopher. Magical Realism and the Postcolonial Novel: Between Faith and Irreverence. Springer,
2009.
3. Booth, Wayne C. The Rhetoric of Fiction. London: Penguin, 1991. Print.
4. Critique: Studies in Contemporary Fiction: https://www.tandfonline.com/toc/vcrt20/current

Course No: HS3029
Course Name: Principles and Parameters of Natural Language
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course offers a view of human language as a rule governed system. It will show how language is learnt and
how structure of language functions in human mind. It introduces components of linguistics theory in generative
framework. It deals with how languages are similar to and different from one another.
Outcomes:
This course introduces computation of language in human mind. It helps us understand the theory of language and
the development of principles and parameters. This course will build foundation in understanding abstract
mechanism underlying structure of language.
Course Content:
• Introduction to language and linguistics as a scientific domain of systematic investigation into language at the
levels of sounds, words, and sentences
• What is language?
• Language and Languages
• Languages in India (Language, Dialect and Variety)
• Principles and Parameters
• Generative Foundations of Language Acquisition
• Biological Foundation of Language
• Language Acquisition Device
• Universal Grammar
• Order of Words in Sentence (Subject-Object-Verb)
• X-bar Theory (Specifiers, Head, Complements (Arguments), Adjuncts)
• Command, C-Command, and M-Command, Government
• Theta-Theory, Theta Role Assignment
• Case Theory (Abstract, Inherent, and Morphological Case, Exceptional Case Marking, Nominative-Accusative
vs. Ergative-Absolutive patterns)
• Raising Movement
• A and A Bar Movements
• Passives and Questions
• Binding Principles
Text Books:
• Haegeman, L. Introduction to Government and Binding Theory, Oxford: Wiley-Blackwell, 1994
• Culicover, P. Principles and Parameters: An Introduction to Syntactic Theory, Oxford: Oxford University Press,
1997
Reference Books:
• Culicover, P. Simpler Syntax, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2005
• Chomsky, Noam. Aspects of the theory of syntax. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1965

Course No: HS3033
Course Name: Philosophy in Literature and Films
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The objective of this course is to examine how certain central philosophical themes and problems find expression
in creative art, particularly in world literature and world cinema. After introducing certain important philosophical
problems and concepts, a few representative artistic texts—novels, short stories, poetry and films—are examined.
It examines how effectively philosophical issues are represented through literature and films and the process
through which this is done and the problems involved.
Outcomes:
The students will learn some fundamental philosophical ideas and approaches to human problems through the
analysis of various selected texts from literature and films. They will learn to appreciate films and literature from
the perspective of philosophical thinking. The students will read sections from world literature and watch selected
films that have philosophical significance.
Course Content:
• Philosophical thinking
• Philosophy and art
• Aesthetics – both Western and Indian
• Philosophical themes to be discussed: death, power, personal identity, free will, meaning of life, God, ethics and
morals, question of evil, freedom and human existence, hedonism, existentialism, feminism etc.
• Philosophy and classical art and literature – Greek and Indian
• Modernity and its problems in literature and films
• Industrialization – technology and man
• Crisis of modernity – fragmentation etc.
• Ethical crisis represented in literature and films
• Existentialism in literature and films
• Postmodern art, literature and films.

Course No: HS3060
Course Name: Social History of Medicine in Colonial India
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
To enable the students understand the social and cultural dimensions of the colonial public health and medical
policies; and of the encounter between diverse medical traditions during the British colonial rule in India
Course Content:
i. Western Ideas of Indian Environment – Medical Topography – Environmental Determinism, Tropical Paradigm –
Shifts in the discourses on race, climate and diseases
ii. From Military/White personnel’s’ health to ‘Native’ and Public Health – Challenge of Epidemics: Cholera, Small
Pox, Plague, Malaria; Public Health Measures, Compliances and Resistances
iii. Emergence of the local western medical profession – changing roles assigned to Indians in the public health
system, entry of Indians into the army and the provincial and central medical services, medical colleges; avenues
for private practice and employment in non-state sectors.
iv. Social Response to Techniques and Technologies – local reactions to new technologies like X-rays and
techniques like drug testing
v. Colonial Medicine and Gender – Zenana Missions, Lock Hospitals, Scientific Midwifery, Women doctors,
Women’s Medical Institutions.
vi. (Colonial) State contribution Vs Public Philanthropy - Setting up of Funds, dispensaries, hospitals and colleges
on private initiative, the role of Princely States.
vii. Encounter with indigenous systems (like Ayurveda, Unani and Siddha) – ‘accommodation’, marginalization,
revivalist movements, hybridization; implications for subsequent medical pluralism.
Text Books:
• Arnold, David, Colonizing the Body: State Medicine and Epidemic Disease in Nineteenth-Century India, Univ. of
California Press, Berkeley and Los Angeles, 1993.
• Kumar, Deepak and Raj Sekhar Basu. Medical Encounters in British India, Oxford University Press, New Delhi,
2013.
• Pati, Biswamoy and Mark Harrison (eds.), The Social History of Health and Medicine in Colonial India,
Routledge, London & New York, 2009.
Reference Books:
• Arnold, David (ed.), Imperial Medicine and Indigenous Societies, Manchester University Press, Manchester,
1988.
• Arnold, David (ed.), Warm Climates and Western Medicine: The Emergence of Tropical Medicine, 1500-1900,

Course Name: Short Story Classics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course introduces students to a selection of short stories by major practitioners of the genre across nations
and time periods. It familiarises students with literary terms, trends, and narrative structure in terms of the short
story genre. The course illustrates influential artistic, historical, and cultural contexts to select short stories from
across the globe. It offers a special Victorian Short Story module, which introduces students to the form and its
thematic concerns through the works of great writers such as Charles Dickens, Rudyard Kipling, Oscar Wilde,
Edgar Allan Poe, and others.
Outcomes:

narrative strategies that create the maximum impact on the reader. Students will learn to perform interpretations of
stories in light of cultural and historical contexts of world short stories, including the Indian short fiction. They will
understand the process of close reading and its importance for understanding themes. Students will learn to
compare and contrast in terms of analytic categories across stories from different countries and time periods.

• Performing close reading of texts
• Dynamics between Narratives and Narrators
• Exploring themes of tradition, modernity, and power
• Domesticity, identity, and the public sphere
• Relation between Texts and Contexts
• Definitions of the term “classic”
• Explorations of the nature of the global/world short story.

Course No: HS3100
Course Name: Economic Network Analysis
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The purpose of this course is to develop an understanding of the network of relations which meditation interactions
between economic agents. The
course is divided into two parts. The first part explores types of networks (like random and scale-free networks)
and techniques used to characterize
networks (like "degree distribution", "centrality", "clustering", "assortativity"). This part of the course will develop
mathematical descriptions of network
measures and implement computer algorithms to implement these measures. The second part of the course
explores recent literature on the role of
production networks (firm to firm buyer-seller network) and financial networks (bank-firm or bank-bank network) in
generating various economic
phenomena. This part of the course will develop theoretical models of economic interactions on fixed networks and
models of network formation.
Course Content:
1. Why model economic networks?
2.Types of networks
2a.Random graphs
2b.Scale-free networks
2c.Balanced networks
2d. Small world networks
3.Statistical measures of networks
3a.Degree distribution
3b.Centrality
3c.Assortativity
3d.Clustering
4.Simple models of network formation
4a.Random graphs: ErdosRenyi algorithm
4b.Scale-free networks: Barabasi Albert algorithm
5.Production networks (firm to firm buyer-seller networks)
5a.Empirical regularities
5b.Microeconomic Applications
5c.Macroeconomic Applications
5d.Monetary dynamics on production networks
6.Financial networks
6a.Empirical regularities
6b.Cascading of risk
7.Economic games of network formation
7a. Nash strategy in forming network links
7b. Formation of network with cost minimization
Text Books:
"Social and Economic Networks" by Matthew Jackson. Princeton University Press. 2008
"Economic Networks" by David Knoke. Polity Press. 2012
Reference Books:
"Networks, Crowds, and Markets: Reasoning About a Highly Connected World" by David Easley and Jon
Kleinberg. Cambridge University Press. 2010
"Networks: An Introduction" by M E J Newman. Oxford University Press. 2010.
"Network Science" by Albert-LászlóBarabási. Cambridge University Press. 2015.

Course No: HS3230
Course Name: History of English Language & Literature
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This is a foundational course that covers a wide arc of literary history from the Old English Period to the
mid-twentieth century and helps students understand the historical, social and political changes that have played
important roles in the shaping of English literature. The course also helps students familiarize themselves with the
origin and evolution of the English language and identify the various language families it originates from. The main
focus of the course is, however, to place major writers in a chronological order and also classify major literary
genres via texts that have been contextualized within specific literary periods. The student will be introduced to
literary forms, terms and theories through the texts taken up for analysis.
Outcomes:
Through this course, students will be able to demonstrate knowledge of the history, culture and literature of the
English language, as well as identify the salient features of literary texts from a broad range of English literary
periods.
Course Content:
1. The origin and development of the English Language
2. English Literature Before Chaucer (500-1340)
3. The Age of Chaucer (1340-1400)
4. From Chaucer to Tottel’s Miscellany (1400-1557)
5. Beginnings of English Drama to 1561
6. The Age of Shakespeare (1558-1625): Non-Dramatic Verse, Drama, Prose
7. The Age of Milton (1625-1660): Milton?, Other Poets and Prose Writers
8. The Age of Dryden (1660-1700): Verse, Prose and Drama
9. The Age of Pope (1700-1745): Verse?, Prose and Drama
10. The Age of Johnson (1745-1798): General Prose, The Novel, Verse
11. The Age of Wordsworth (1798-1832): Poetry, General Prose The Novel?
12. The Age of Tennyson (1832-1887): Verse, General Prose, Novel
13. The Age of Hardy (1887-1928) : Verse, Drama, Novel
14. The Twentieth Century: The rise of Modernism and Postmodernism, Representative Movements and Writers .
Text Books:
Carter, Ronald and John McRae. The Routledge History of Literature in English. London: Routledge, 2017.
Hudson, William Henry. An Outline History of English Literature. New Delhi: Rupa, 2015.
Wood, Frederick T. An Outline History of the English Language. New Delhi: Trinity, 2015.
Reference Books:
Blamires, Henry. A Short History of English Literature. London: Routledge, 2003.
Compton-Rickett, Arthur. A History of English Literature. New Delhi: USB Publishers, 2012.
Daiches, David. A Critical History of English Literature in Two Volumes. London: Mandarin, 1994.

Legouis, Emile and Louis Cazamian. History of English Literature. Delhi: Macmillan India Ltd, 2017.

Course No: HS3250
Course Name: Chaucer, Milton and the Bible
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course is aimed at introducing students to some of the major literary texts that are foundational to the English
literary landscape, enabling them to place these texts in their appropriate historical and linguistic contexts. The
course will introduce students to the works of Geoffrey Chaucer, the deservedly famous author from medieval
England who had an exceptionally good sense of humour. Most of the coursework regarding Chaucer will focus on
his magnum opus, the Canterbury Tales, an ambitious collection of tales culled from different places and genres.
As far as the poetry of John Milton is concerned, the course will focus not just on the texts themselves, but also on
the various contexts that are relevant to Milton’s oeuvre, from the tumultuous political and religious period in which
he lived to the literary network with which his texts interact. The course will also take a close look at Paradise Lost,
Milton’s great epic in the classical tradition. The Bible will be studied as a foundational text of the Western
civilization and also as the key to unlock Milton’s Paradise Lost. The objective of this exercise is not doctrinal
certainty, but biblical literacy and an acquaintance with biblical resources that have enriched humanity’s worldwide
heritage in the past.
Outcomes:
Through this course, students will read closely and understand Middle and Early Modern English, from Chaucer’s
rhyming couplets to Milton’s blank verse. They will demonstrate knowledge of the style, structure and content of
the assigned literary texts, from Chaucer to Milton. They will identify the unique qualities of the authors studied in
order to compare and contrast their works, situating them within their respective historical contexts. They will also
appreciate the pervasive and perennial influence of the Bible upon English literature.
Course Content:
• Prologue to the Canterbury Tales
• Paradise Lost and Other Poems – Selections
• Social, Intellectual and Historical Contexts of Chaucer and Milton
• The Bible – Select Passages from the book of Genesis, the Parables and The Book of Job
Text Books:
1. Geoffrey Chaucer, The Riverside Chaucer, ed. Fred Robinson, Oxford University Press, 1998.
2. Carroll, Robert P, and Stephen Prickett. The Bible: Authorized King James Version. Oxford: Oxford University
Press, 1997.
3. Chaucer, Geoffrey, and Larry D. Benson. The Riverside Chaucer. Boston, Mass: Houghton Mifflin Co, 1987.
4. Milton, John, 1608-1674. Paradise Lost. New York: Penguin Books, 2000.
Reference Books:
1. Danielson, Dennis. Ed. The Cambridge Companion to Milton. Cambridge: Cambridge UP, 1999.
2. Rossignol, Rosalyn.A Critical Companion to Chaucer: A Literary Reference to His Life and Work. New York:
Facts on File, 2006.
3. Boitani, Piero and Jill Mann. Eds, The Cambridge Companion to Chaucer. Cambridge: Cambridge UP, 2003.
4. Bradford, Richard. The Complete Critical Guide to John Milton. London: Routledge, 2001.
5. Kermode, Frank and Robert Alter, The Literary Guide to the Bible. Harvard UP, 1987.

Course No: HS3280
Course Name: Introduction to Cultural Anthropology
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The goal of cultural anthropology is to understand how people in different places produce cultural, economic, and
symbolic systems that regulate their lives. During this class we will learn about the cultural practices of people
around the world, in order to broaden our understanding of how culture structures and patterns the lives of
different groups, and to gain a better understanding of ourselves. We will begin by looking closely at the concept of
culture as the central theme in anthropology, and how culture patterns human behaviour. We will also look at the
historical development of social and economic systems, the role of language in culture, and various systems of
political power.
Course Content:
Modules
1. What is culture? – In this, we will cover the basic understanding of culture as a set of theoretical lenses.
2. Comparative cultures: In this set of sessions, we look at the ways in which cultures might radically differ from
each other
3. Anthropology and Culture: In this module, we examine the discipline of anthropology and its relationship to
understanding society and culture
4. Kinship, power, structure, and language: This set of sessions introduces the students to the primary theories of
cultural anthropology.
5. Ethnographic research methods: The last set of sessions will involve introducing the students to the research
methods of cultural anthropology
Text Books:
1. McCurdy, David W., Dianna Shandy, and James Spradley, eds. 2016. Conformity and Conflict: Readings in
Cultural Anthropology. New York: Longman. 15th EDITION
Reference Books:
1. Clastres, Pierre. Chronicle of Guayaki Indians. New York: Zone Books, 1998.
2. Muegler, Eric. The Age of Wild Ghosts. Berkeley: University of California Press, 2001.
3. Shostak, Marjorie. Nisa: The Life and Words of a !Kung Woman. New York: Vintage Books, 1981.
4. Stack, Carol. All Our Kin. New York: Basic Books, 1997.
5. Taussig, Michael. Shamanism, Colonialism, and the Wild man: A Study in Terror and Healing. Chicago: The
University of Chicago Press, 1986.
6. Willis, Paul. Learning to Labor: How Working Class Kids Get Working Class Jobs. New York: Columbia
University Press, 1977.

Course No: HS4006
Course Name: Science and Technology in the 20th Century
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
In the Age of Extremes that was the 20th century, the world, and with it the natural sciences, had gone through
fundamental ideological, technological and political transformations. We will discuss the nature of science and
technology and the complex relationship between the two, and critically examine the interaction between science,
technology and society. We will discuss paradigmatic changes in the sciences in the 20th century such as the
emergence and rise of quantum mechanics, theory of relativity and genetics, and the technological changes that
came with computing, media technologies, and warfare.
Learning outcomes:
The students will learn about the development of science and technology in the 20th century and how it related to
other developments in society. They will learn how to understand science and technology as historical processes.
The course will enable students to understand and reflect on the development of science and technology in its
epistemological, cultural and political context in the last 150 years.
Course Content:
• 2nd industrial revolution: chemical industry, electrification, railways
• Science, technology, colonialism and decolonization
• Science and engineering education
• From classical to modern physics
• Science & tech, WWI and WWII
• Technologies of mass media
• Industrial research
• The Atomic Age, science in the Cold War, Big Science
• History of computing and the Digital Age
• Aeronautics and space science
• Molecular biology and genetics
• Environmental science and environmental awareness
Text Books:

Reference Books:

Publishers, 1997.
Rhodes, Richard. The Making of the Atomic Bomb. New York: Simon and Schuster, 1986.
Kragh, Helge. Quantum Generations: A History of Physics in the Twentieth Century. New York: Princeton
University Press, 1999.

Course No: HS4007
Course Name: Computational Economics and Public Policy
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Given the emergence of digital economy, the complex nature of public policy making processes, and importance of
assessing alternate policy options, it has become essential for students (from diverse disciplines) to be able to
synthesize economic and computational perspectives in specific public policy domains.
Objectives:
This course will enable students to (a) explore the interface between economic thinking and computational thinking
and (b) illustrate the importance of synthesizing economic and computational perspectives in the design,
implementation and assessment of public policy.
Remark: This course does not aim to impart computational skills (such as c++) and statistical skills
Course Content:
1. Understanding the Economy (evolutionary, complexity and adaptive nature of economy) - 2. Agent Based
Economy and Social Systems – 3. Goals of public policy –- 4. Elements of computational Thinking –
5. Algorithmic game theory (both co-operative and non-cooperative) – 6. Auctions – 7. Matching algorithms -
8.Markets for information – 9. Formation of trust and reputation – 10. Computational social choice: (preference
aggregation (voting), judgment aggregation, manipulative actions) – 11. Fair division: single divisible resource
("cake-cutting") and multiple indivisible and un-shareable resources ("multi-agent resource allocation")
Issues that arise in specific domains will be covered:
Health care;
Finance: asset and option pricing, digital currencies;
Environment: management of renewable and non-renewable resources;
Government and regulation: price controls, income redistribution;
Students will be encouraged to build simulation models (using pre-packaged tools) to explore solutions to
problems in these (and other) domains
Text Books:
1. G. Venkatesh and Madhavan Mukund, Introduction to Computational Thinking : a primer for programmers and
data scientists (Mylspot Education, 2021)
2. Thomas Mayer, Invitation to Economics: understanding argument and policy (Wiley Blackwell,, 2009)
3. Kurian C.T. Economics of Real Life: A new exposition, (Academic Foundation, 2020)
4. Paul Carney, Understanding Public Policy: Theories and Issues, (Red Globe Press, 2020)
5. Avinash Dixit: Microeconomics: a short Introduction (OUP, 2014)
Reference Books:
1. David F Batten, Discovering Artificial Economics (Westview Press, 2000)
2. Avinash Dixit, The Making of Economic Policy (MIT press, 1996)
3. Deborah Stone, Policy Paradox: The art of political decision making (Norton and Company, 2012)
Besides, the course material will be drawn from diverse sources (including, published journal articles, policy
documents, case studies (legal and other sources).

Course No: HS4010
Course Name: Indian Fiction in English
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course intends to provide a comprehensive understanding of fiction written in English in India since its
emergence in the 19th century, and introduce the learners to the literary ground covered in major literary histories,
anthologies and critical discussions from the 1960s onwards. Apart from a chronological survey, the course will
focus on the historical and literary origins of the genre, its political and economic underpinnings, the debates and
controversies within the field and the crisis in contemporary literary studies. The objective of the course is also to
expose the students to questions of nation, secularism, caste, gender, region and identity inherent in the writings.
To enable a more nuanced engagement, selected novels will be read and analysed within current critical
frameworks such as postcolonialism, feminism and historiography studies. New trends in writing and publishing
are also discussed in order to give a perspective of the genre in the present century.
Outcomes:
At the end of the course the students will acquire a comprehensive understanding of the literary traditions and
critical methods prevalent in Indian fiction in English. In addition to familiarity with selected texts, the students will
also be able to develop research aptitude to close-read texts and map them to various frameworks and
approaches.
Course Content:
1. Introducing the category ‘Indian writing in English’.
2. Historically situating ‘fiction’ in the history of Indian writing in English
3. The rise of the novel and an Indian critical tradition
4. Colonial modernity and Indian fiction
5. Gandhian fiction and the 1930s
6. Women writers and post-Independence decades
7. Caste in Indian English fiction
8. Partition novels
9. Writings from the Northeast
10. 1980s and Post-Rushdie generation
11. New writings in the contemporary; graphic novel and digital fiction

Course Name: Built Environment and Society

Course No: HS4013
Course Name: Gender and Development
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The syllabus of this course covers both the conceptual and analytical frameworks in the domain of gender and
development, and interrogates development through a gendered lens. As this course follows the Feminist Theory

practice. This course throughout emphasizes the cross-sectionality of gender as a cross-cutting theme.

the analytical skills required to locate gender issues within development practices; c) give students a better
understanding of intersectionality as an analytical approach in the social sciences; and d) give them practical
experience analyzing gender-related data sets.

2. Feminist Theory in the domain of Gender and Development

7. Empowerment as a theoretical construct and a practical strategy
8. Gender and sexuality studies
9. Men & masculinity studies
10. Women's organizations in the changing world
11. Locating gender as a cross-cutting theme and examining its intersectional character
12. Frameworks and strategies for mainstreaming gender
13. Various statistical measures of women's progress and empowerment
14. Workshops on gender budgeting and analysis of gender related secondary data sets

Course No: HS4014
Course Name: State and Development
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The aim of this course is to introduce core concepts in the political economy of development, examining the role of
state as the primary agent for social and economic change.
Course Content:
Theories of the state: Miliband-Poulantzas debate, the regulatory state, the capitalist state, the developmental
state. State planning The role of institutions and institutional change in development. Reform and political change
in the context of new international political economy and resource wars.
Case studies will include the rise and collapse of East Asian tigers in the 20th century, the Japanese post-war
economic miracle, India and China’s economic development, the Soviet Union and its aftermath, 20th century
mercantilism in Africa and West Asia in the context of natural resource exploitation; the roles of the state in
development of Brazil and Argentina in the early 20th century; the political economy of oil in the Middle East in the
early to mid-20th century, resource wars in Africa in the late 20th, early 21st century.
Text Books:
1. Pranab Bardhan (2004) Scarcity, Conflicts, and Cooperation: Essays in the Political and Institutional Economics
of Development. MIT Press.

Princeton University Press.

Course No: HS4100
Course Name: German III
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The overall objective of this course is to acquire good knowledge of the German language, corresponding to the
B1 proficiency level of the European Common Framework of Reference for Languages. This level includes
elementary appreciation of simple literary texts in German language and an acquaintance with the history of
Germany since the Enlightenment.
Outcomes:
On successful completion of the course, learners should be able to understand the main points of clear standard
input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.; deal with most situations likely to
arise while travelling in an area where the language is spoken; produce simple connected text on topics that are
familiar or of personal interest; and describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions and briefly
give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans.
Course Content:
• Advanced German sentence structure including all subordinate and coordinate clauses / compound sentences;
subjunctive; passive voice; complete adjective and substantive declension including gerunds and adjectives as
nouns; all tenses, cases and prepositions
• Intermediate written and spoken communication skills covering standard situations encountered in the context of
higher education / professional work / independent travel and residence in German speaking countries.
• Basic outline of German history from the 19th to the 21st century; simple literary texts in German such as poems
and short stories.
Text Books:

Course content:

Public Policy instruments
Managing common resources

Course No: HS4350
Course Name: Contemporary Issues in Development
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
From the post-World War II era to the present, we will examine key concepts and historical developments that
have shaped the notion of Development. The course examines Development as a practice and Developmentalism
as a discourse. This course explicitly situates these debates in the Indian context.
Outcomes: This course will a) provide an overview of development discourse; b) allow students to examine and
evaluate select contemporary development debates and issues in the context of India.
Course Content:
• A brief introduction to the subject of Development and Development Studies as an academic subfield
• Post-world war II era and the crystallization of the idea of Development
• The historical context within which Development in India has been framed - the colonial history and its impact on
the development process
• Bretton Woods institutions, changing economic order and the geo-politics
• Development theories - Modernization theory, Dependency theory, World Systems theory and theories of
Globalization
• Various critiques of Development and the idea of Post-development
• Gender critique of Development
• Environmental critique of Development and the concept of Sustainable Development
• Role of State, Civil society, and other actors in the domain of Development
• Centralized vs. decentralized governance - 73rd and 74th constitutional amendments and the PRIs.
• Contemporary approaches and measures of Development - the role of economic growth in Development and the
significance of social sectors; Human Development to well-being; changing approaches to understanding poverty
from quantitative to qualitative dimensions.
• Social movements, participation, and citizenship questions in the context of Development.
Text Books:
1. Chandra, B. (1999). Essays on Colonialism, New Delhi: Orient Longman.
2. Corbridge, S. (1995). Development studies: a reader. London: Edward Arnold.
3. Pieterse Nederveen, J. (2001). Development Theory Deconstructions/Reconstructions, London: Sage
Publications.
Reference Books:
1. Corbridge, S. (2007). "The (im)possibility of development studies." Economy and Society 36(2): 179-211.
2. Corbridge, S., M. Srivastava and R. Veron (2005) Seeing the State: Governance and Governmentality in India.
Cambridge: Cambridge University Press
3. Dyson, T., ‘Growing Regional Variation: Demographic Change and its Implications’ in Jeffery, Roger and Heath,
Anthony (2010), eds., Diversity and Change in Modern India. Economic, Social and Political Approaches (Oxford:
Oxford University Press).
4. Leftwich, A. (2000). States of development: On the primacy of politics in development, Cambridge: Polity Press.
5. Molyneux, M. and S. Razavi.(2002). Gender justice, development, and rights, Oxford: Oxford University Press.
6. Myrdal, G. (1974). "What is development?" Journal of Economic Issues, 8(4): 729-736.
