Course No: HS4381
Course Name: Meaning, Truth, and Language
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course seeks to answers the central questions of analytic philosophy; what is meaning, what is it for a word or
expression to be meaningful, and how do we understand speaker’s utterances. The term 'meaning' is explained in
various ways, such as; meaning as use, meaning is determined of its truth-conditions, meaning is picture of a
thought, etc. All these issues are treated separately by philosophers like; Frege, Wittgenstein, Logical Positivists,
Bhartrihari, Bhatta and Prabhakara Schools of Mimamsa. The course will discuss these philosophers’ ideas,
arguments and thoughts pertaining to meaning and language in the course curriculum.
Outcomes:
After successful completion of the course, students will be able to distinguish the semantic from the syntactic
structure of language. They will be able to elucidate the notion of meaning in a linguistic system and relate the
concept of meaning with theories of truth.
Course Content:
• Frege’s sense and reference
• Wittgenstein’s picture theory of meaning
• Logical Positivists theory of verifiability of meaning
• Nyaya theories of meaning
• Late Wittgenstein’s use theory of meaning
• Davidson’s convention-T
• Tarski’s T-schema
• Quine’s theories of meaning
• Indian theories of meaning.
Text Books:
Sethy, S.S. (2016). Meaning and Language, New Delhi: D.K.Print World
Lycan, W.G. (2008) Philosophy of Language: A Contemporary Introduction, New York: Routledge.
Matilal, B.K. and Lalshaw, J. (Eds.)(1984). Analytical Philosophy in Contemporary Perspective: Exploratory Essays
in Current Theories and Classical Indian Theories of Meaning and Reference, London: Springer.
Soames, S. (2012) Philosophy of Language, UK: Princeton University Press.
Reference Books:
Ammerman, R.R. (1965) (Eds.) Classics of Analytic Philosophy, New York: McGraw-Hill Publication.
Chaturvedi, M. (2009) Bhartrhari: Language, Thought, and Reality, New Delhi: Motilal Banarasidass Publication.
Davidson, D. (2001) Inquiries into Truth, and Interpretation, New York: Oxford University Press. 4.
Raja, K.K. (1969) Indian Theories of Meaning, Madras: Theosophical Publishing House.

Course No: HS4570
Course Name: Gandhian Thought
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Gandhi experimented all his life with variegated ideas concerning ethics, politics, economy, law, health, ecology,
spirituality and society. One can say that his life-long quest was to arrive at a path that would be a confluence of a
moral individual, an ethical society and a principled polity. The aim of this course is to explore various aspects of
Gandhi's life and the stream of thought inspired by his ideas. In many ways, Gandhi himself was an idea and his
life an experiment, to paraphrases his autobiography, The Story of my Experiments with Truth. This course would
examine the influence of Gandhian ideas on a wide variety of topics that continue to wield tremendous influence
during contemporary epoch such as self-governance, decentralization, rural development, cooperative movement,
education, women's rights, social inequality, religious amity, environmental sustainability, inclusive economic
growth, multiculturalism, conflict resolution, health and hygiene, to name a few. Students would be exposed to a
critical approach to Gandhian ideas and a more holistic perspective on Gandhi based on which they can evaluate
his contribution.
Outcomes:
In this course, alongside the seminal writings of Gandhi, many works on Gandhi that explore his social, political,
economic, cultural, religious and spiritual writings will also be discussed. Gandhi’s socio-political experiments in
Africa, his impact of African and post-colonial freedom struggle, contribution to legal ethics, social construction
program, women’s empowerment, powerful debates with Ambedkar, similarities with Abraham Lincoln, problems
with modernity and technology, attempts to unite India in mind and spirit and impact on ecological movements in
India and around the world will be studied as well. Students would also learn how Gandhian thought impacted law,
policy and polity through case studies.
Course Content:
1. Gandhi in South Africa
2. India in the post-independence years
3. Gandhian economics - J.C. Kumarappa
4. Psychoanalyzing Gandhi's search for truth - Erik Erikson
5. Gandhi and the partition of India
6. Gandhi on Law and Justice
7. Hind Swaraj
8. Tilak and Gandhi on The Gita
9. Gandhi on Ecology
10. Construction program
11. Panchayati Raj - Village self-governance, decentralization, rural development and strengthening local
economy
12. Gandhi-Ambedkar debates - Constituent Assembly Debates - Drafting of the Constitution of India
13. Gandhi's impact on freedom movements in Africa and other parts of the world
14. Gandhi and Rev. Martin Luther King Jr, Rev. James Lawson - Civil Rights Movement in the US
15. Gandhi and deep ecology
16. Gandhi and conflict resolution
17. Gandhi today
Text Books:

Course No: HS4574
Course Name: Health, Environment and Human Wellbeing
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The objective of the course is to initiate a philosophical examination of the issues related to the prevailing ideas of
health and human wellbeing by relating these fundamental concepts with other ideas we have about humankind. It
examines how human health, wellbeing and environment are represented in our modern discourses (various
discourses like science, technology, literature, other art forms etc) and tries to problemalise the various
assumptions lying under them. It also examines the basic ethical, aesthetic and other evaluations with regard to
human health and wellbeing and also environment. It critically examines the evolution of modern medicine and the
moral frameworks developed in order to ensure ethical practice. Finally, it explores the possibilities of developing a
broad and more holistic ecosophical perspective from where these fundamental concepts can be approached,
evaluated and understood.
Course Content:
Conceptions of human wellbeing, health and man’s relationship with nature; Anthropocentric and
non-anthropocentric perspectives; Our relation with nature and our conceptions with regard to its uses and our
ideas about our relationship with it; Fundamental concepts in human health and disease; Modernity and the
changing ideas of wellbeing; Science and reason Vs. religion and spirituality; Conceptions of knowledge and
progress; Changing conceptions of moral considerability; Modern medicine and ethics; Fundamentals of ethical
decision-making- different ethical approaches; The traditional ethical frameworks like virtue ethics, utilitarianism,
deontology and the principalist approach; The environmental crisis and the crisis facing humanity; the possibilities
of an ecosophy; Value of traditional wisdom; Politics of health and environment; Case discussions and screening
documentary films dealing with issues related to environment, health and human wellbeing.
Text Books:
1. David R. Keller .(2010).Environmental ethics: The Big Questions. Wiley-Blackwell.
2. Beauchamp, Tom L. and Childress, James F, Principles of Biomedical Ethics. New York and Oxford, Oxford
University Press. 1994.

Course No: HS4580
Course Name: Sanskrit for Yoga
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course is intended to introduce the students to the basic philosophy of Yoga as detailed in some classical
Sanskrit texts. In the process it will also expose the students to the basics of Sanskrit Grammar as well as
important technical terms in Yoga, enough to get you started on some primary Yoga texts. The main objective of
this course is thus to make the language of the yoga texts transparent.
Given that Yoga is a multi-billion-dollar business today, and the fact of its open endorsement in scientific circles, its
importance in preventive as well as curative aspects of health is indubitable. From another angle, Yoga is a true
representative of India since Indic religions viz. Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism freely deploy concepts
and techniques of Yoga. Thus, Yoga is a synonym of Indic heritage.
A reclamation of this heritage also involves an understanding of the original texts on Yoga, rather than via their
translations. All texts of importance are in Sanskrit, and the standard of Sanskrit in many of the currently used
texts is not very exacting. Yet many of our teachers and students of Yoga are unfortunately not well-versed in it.
The course will address that gap in institutional learning.
Course Content:
Common Yoga vocabulary
Declension of Nouns – Ajanta-sadhara?a, Halanta-sadhara?a, Sarvanama, Sa?khya-vacaka and a few vise?a
sabda-s; Karaka and non-Karaka relations.
Conjugation of Verbs – Sakarmaka, Akarmaka, the Three Vacya-s, Lakara-s, and Upasarga-s, ?ijanta-s
Sandhi – Ac and Hal Sandhi-s, Visarga Sandhi, Internal Sandhi
Samasa – Tatpuru?a, Karmadharaya, Dvigu, Bahuvrihi, Dvandva, Avyayibhava
Passages for Translation
Text Books:
1. Swami Digambaraji (1998) Hatha-pradipika. Lonavala : Kaivalyadhama.

Course No: HS4790
Course Name: Gothic, Sensation and Newgate Novels
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
• The course aims to introduce students of literature to the distinctive features of the gothic, sensation and
Newgate fiction, immensely popular literary sub-genres from the late eighteenth and nineteenth century.
• The course deconstructs the narrative ingredients of these subgenres such as the supernatural (assumed and
real), financial and property fraud, criminal confessions, sexual intrigue, murder, madness, fake identities, bigamy,
blackmail, and other insidious human behaviour that are beyond the pale of respectable middle-class domesticity
in the context of the social, cultural and historical upheavals that were shaking up the social order of the
eighteenth and nineteenth century.
• The course will also encourage students to explore the different thematic configurations of the gothic such as the
“female gothic” and “the imperial gothic” to understand the cultural and historical anxieties reflected and refracted
in such narrative consciousness of the period.
• The course will also expose students to the complications in the gender dynamics embedded within these
narratives of terror, and trace the literary and historical conditions that led to the construction of complex female
characters across these subgenres.
• Students will also significantly tease out the rationale behind the choice, and dysfunctional nature, of the
different kinds of story setting that are often times used to define and identify novels as belonging to a particular
subgenre.
Course Content:
• The course discusses the origins, rise and defining traits of the gothic, sensation and Newgate novel in the
eighteenth and nineteenth-century English fiction.
• It explores the distinctions and parallels in terms of their plot trajectories and narrative elements involved in the
shaping of these popular subgenres, whose continuing influence can be observed even in contemporary
bestsellers such as Paula Hawkins’ The Girl on the Train (2015).
• The course juxtaposes the Newgate novel with the Gothic and Sensation fiction in order to map the coexistence
and implications of the various narratives of crime, terror and horror that caught the imagination of the reading
public of the eighteenth and nineteenth century.
• The course covers a wide range of eighteenth and nineteenth century novelists who were practitioners of these
subgenres such as Horace Walpole, Ann Radcliffe, Mathew Lewis, Bram Stoker, Mary Shelley, Henry James,
Harrison Ainsworth, Wilkie Collins, Charles Dickens, Charlotte Brontë, Ellen Wood, Thomas Hardy, Mary Braddon,
J. Sheridan Le Fanu, Rhoda Broughton, and Charles Reade.

Course No: HS4820
Course Name: Fashion in Literature and Cinema
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course explores the ways in which clothes 'perform' in a wide range of texts. It will aim at examining the
interconnected worlds of fashion as well as literary and cinematic texts, providing perspectives from socio-cultural,
historical and theoretical readings of fashion. Covering a range of genres and periods, this course will analyze how
dress communicates, and engages in meanings across different cultures and contexts.
Outcomes:
Students will be familiarized with the various trends, concepts and theories in world fashion and their impact on
cinema and literature. They will be acquainted with the synergy between socio-cultural and historical movements
that shape our appreciation of these visual mediums.
Course Content:
• Fashion and its historical context: This will trace the evolution of fashion down the ages, and particularly
consider fashion trends in literature, as reflected in the works of Thomas Carlyle, Marcel Proust and Oscar Wilde.
• Fashion as a system of signs: This concerns the semiotics and codes of fashion, and the way in which clothes
articulate meanings.
• Fashion and icons: This will focus on iconic figures in literature and cinema ranging from Marie Antoinette and
Beau Brummell to Bret Ashley in Hemingway’s The Sun Also Rises, Nicole Driver in F Scot Fitzgerald’s Tender is
the Night, and Woody Allen’s Annie Hall; also, how certain stars gain recognition as fashion icons.
• Fashion and adaptation: The way in which fashion is foregrounded when texts are adapted from page to screen,
for examples in the cases of Breakfast at Tiffany’s, A Single Man, Clueless, The Great Gatsby, Anna Karenina,
and Nicholas Sparks’ The Notebook.
• Fashion and gender: Fashion and clothing are intertwined with each other in creating a gendered-structure of
society. Fashion generates and alters identity based on the gender-based relations in a society, for example in
Virginia Woolf’s Orlando.
• Fashion and globalization: This considers how fashion engages in dialogue with globalization.
Text Books:
1. Barnard, Malcolm (ed.). Fashion Theory: A Reader. NY: Routledge, 2007.
2. Bruzzi, Stella & Pamela Church Gibson (eds). Fashion Cultures: Theories, Explorations and Analysis. NY:
Routledge, 2000.
3. Church Gibson, Pamela. Fashion and Celebrity Culture. NY: Berg, 2012.

Course No: HS4870
Course Name: Climate Economics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Climate change is one of the most significant challenges humanity as a whole has ever faced. It is a truly global
collective action problem, whose social costs will be massive, widespread, unpredictable, and inequitably
distributed. This course undertakes the challenge of climate change from an economics perspective. This course
will use the lens of economics to clarify the costs and benefits of climate change; understand the challenges of
climate change mitigation, and understand the theoretical and empirical impacts of climate policies. This course
will begin by reviewing some foundational economic concepts and studying the effects of climate change.
The objectives of the course are to understand,
1. how the costs and benefits of mitigation are measured and how to simulate them in a numerical model;
2. the economics of climate change and policies;
3. the current landscape of domestic and international policy planning and implementation related to climate
change.
Learning outcomes
1. Articulate key issues relating to climate change;
2. Explain how economics can offer public policies aimed at mitigating the effects of climate change;
3. Undertake independent research in the area of the economics of climate change mitigation.
Course Content:
Part-A: Understanding climate economics
1. Externalities and public goods: An introduction
2. The science of climate change
a. Process
b. Projections
3. Emissions scenarios and options for emission reduction
a. Sources of greenhouse gas emissions
b. Trends and scenarios of future emissions
c. Options for emission reduction
d. Beyond the Kaya identity
4. Abatement costs
a. The cost of emission reduction
b. Negative emissions
c. Negative abatement costs
Part-B: Policy instruments
5. Policy instruments for emission reduction
a. The justification for a public policy
b. Direct, market-based instruments
c. Second-best regulations
6. Impact of climate change
a. Total economic impacts
b. Impact and development
c. Marginal economic impact
7. Climate and development
a. Exponential growth
b. Poverty trap
c. Natural disasters
Part-C: International cooperation
8. Adaptation policy and optimal climate policy
a. Adaptation versus mitigation
b. Adaptation and development
9 .International environmental agreements
a. Cooperative and non-cooperative abatement
b. Free-riding
c. International climate policies
Text Books:
Tol, Richard SJ. Climate Economics: Economic Analysis of Climate, Climate Change and Climate Policy. 2nd ed.
Cheltenham, UK: Edward Elgar. 2019.
Reference Books:
1. Kolstad, C. D., Intermediate Environmental Economics, Oxford University Press. 2011
2. Stern, Nicholas, and Nicholas Herbert Stern. The economics of climate change: the Stern review. Cambridge
University Press, 2007
3. Published research papers on "Climate Change and Economics"

Course No: HS5000
Course Name: Engineering Ethics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course has three major objectives: 1) to help engineers recognize moral problems when these arise in their
professional work; 2) to provide information concerning the context of engineering, including its history and
sociology, likely to be useful in designing or evaluating potential solutions to such problems; and 3) to offer a
framework for analyzing such problems, designing potential solutions, and making choices among them that are,
all things considered, reasonably defensible.
Course Content:
Course Contents:
This course is concerned with understanding engineering ethics as a reasonable practice; it is an attempt to
provide rational, convincing, and practical answers to such questions as the following:
i. What special moral responsibilities, if any, do engineers have?
ii. What does it mean to claim that engineering is a profession?
iii. What is the moral status of codes of engineering ethics?
iv. What do engineers owe to their employers? The public?
v. What are the moral responsibilities of engineering societies?
vi. Do answers to questions like these changes as engineers move from one country to another or from bench to
executive office?
vii. How should a practicing engineer make engineering decisions?
Course Syllabus
Engineering and professionalism, Ethical theories, NIEE code of ethics, NSPE code of ethics, IEEE code of ethics,
and Engineering Council of India code of ethics, Two models of professionalism, Responsibility in engineering,
Design standards, Ethics design, Framing the problem, Resolving problems, The social and ethical value
dimensions of technology, Compute technology: Privacy and social policy, Trust and reliability, Risk and liability in
engineering, The engineer’s approach to risk, Limitations in detecting failure modes, Engineers in organizations,
Engineers and the environment, International engineering professionalism, Engineering in the global context,
Some case studies.
Text Books:
Harris, C.E, Pritchard, M.S., Rabins, M.J., James, R.W., Englehardt, E. (5th Ed.) (2014). Engineering ethics:
Concepts and cases. USA: Wadsworth Cengage Publication.
Reference Books:
Sethy, S.S. (Ed.) (2015). Contemporary ethical issues in engineering. USA: IGI Global Publication.
Rachels, J. (6th Ed.) (2010). The elements of morality. USA: McGraw-Hill Publication.
Edwards, A. M. (2000). Writing to learn. USA: McGraw-Hill Publication.
Journals: Science and Engineering Ethics, Journal of Engineering Education, European Journal of Engineering
Education.

Course No: HS5003
Course Name: Environmental Economics and Policy
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course aims to introduce students to the fundamental principles of environmental economics, explore the
relationship between economic activities and environmental outcomes, and examine various policy instruments
used
to address environmental problems.
Course Content:
Unit 1: Economic Perspectives on Environmental Sustainability
• Scope and significance of environmental economics
• Paradigms of Sustainable Development - Economic growth and environmental sustainability, Environmental
Kuznets Curve (EKC) Hypothesis, Sustainable Development Indicators, Environmental Accounting and Green
GDP.
• Renewable vs. non-renewable resources: Management of Renewable Resources- Maximum Sustainable Yield,
economics of energy; Management of Non-renewable Resources -Hotelling Rule, Solow- Hartwich approach,
El Serafy Approach
• The economics of climate change: Mitigation and adaptation strategies
Unit 2: Environmental Goods, Externalities and Market Failure
• Public Goods, Private Goods, Common-Pool Resources and Tragedy of the Commons, and Common Property
Resources (CPRs), Collective Action.
• Blue economy and marine resources, forests, biodiversity
• Externalities -Concepts and Types
• Internalisation of Externalities: Command-and-control vs. market-based instruments (MBIs)
• Policy Instruments: Pigouvian solution - environmental subsidies and effluent taxes; Coasean Property Rights
Approach - tradable pollution permits, carbon credit mechanism and tradable water rights; Baumol and
Oates’ Least-Cost Approach.
Unit 3: Social Benefit-Cost Analysis and Economic Valuation of Environmental Goods and Services
• Social Cost-benefit analysis (CBA) in environmental decision-making -Controversies over Time Preference
and Social Discount Rate
• Total Economic Value Concept: Use Values and Non-Use Values
• Economic Valuation Techniques: Revealed Preference Methods (Production Function Approach, Hedonic
Pricing Method, Travel Cost Methods, Cost-based methods)
• Economic Valuation Techniques: Stated Preference Methods -Contingent Valuation Method and Choice
Experiments -Addressing Validity and Reliability issues caused by Biases and Errors.
Unit 4: Behavioral Economics and Environmental Policy
• Behavioural and Experimental Approaches to environmental economics
• Bounded Rationality and Environmental Policy: Framing Effect, Endowment Effect, Social Norms, Self-Control
and Hyperbolic Discounting.
• Nudging for environmental sustainability: Applications and case studies
• Policy applications: Green nudges, default options, and behavioral incentives
Unit 5: Environmental Policy in India and Global Perspectives
• Major Environmental Issues in India, India’s environmental damage cost
• Environmental policies and regulatory frameworks in India
• Global Environmental Agreements and India’s commitments
Text Books:
Callan, Scott J and Janet Thomas (2013). Environmental economics and management: Theory, policy, and
applications. Cengage.
• Common, M., & Stagl, S. (2005). Ecological economics: an introduction. Cambridge University Press.
• Keohane, N. O., & Olmstead, S. M. (2016). Markets and the Environment. Island Press.
• Perman, R., Ma, Y., McGilvray, J. & Common, M. (2003). Natural Resource and Environmental Economics.
Pearson Education.
Reference Books:
• Angner, E. (2020). A course in behavioral economics. Bloomsbury Publishing.
• Hanley, N., Shogren, J. F., & White, B. (2007). Environmental economics in theory and practice. Palgrave
Macmillan.
• Kolstad, C. (2011). Intermediate environmental economics: International edition. OUP Catalogue.
• Peer-reviewed journal articles in the field of environmental and ecological economics.

Course Name: Political Economy of 21st Century China
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course provides immersion into understanding of 21st Century China from an integrated political-economy
perspective. Beginning with an introduction to the historical and institutional background to Modern China, the
course would equip student’ understanding of the politics, economics and foreign policy of China. Detailed
assessment of China’s ‘rise’ would be brought down to the present day, thereby explicating major trends in China
that impact contemporary global politics.
Course Content:
Module: Situating China in a global world [Weeks 1, 2, 3]
Understanding the traditional Chinese World Order, introduction to the Cultural Revolution, the pattern and Logic
of China’s Economic reform, role of ‘Plan’ Versus ‘Market’ in China’s Socialist Market Economy, Challenges Facing
the Chinese Economy
Module: China: regionalism and regionalization [Week 4, 5, 6]
Coverage of issue-areas such as China’s Regional Policy in East Asia and its characteristics, the South China Sea
Dispute and China-ASEAN relations, China and the BRICS initiative.
Module: India-China relations [Weeks 7, 8]
Sino-Indian Boundary Dispute: Genesis and developments leading to (and the aftermath of) the 1962 war,
India-China economic relations.
Module: China: major relationships and key issues [Weeks 9, 10, 11]
Concept of “The Responsible Power”, important dyadic relationships such as bilateral ties with the United States,
China’s engagement in Africa, issue-areas such China’s energy security, the Malacca dilemma and responses
Module: Cross-Strait relations [Weeks 12, 13, 14]
Peace and Security Across the Taiwan Strait, Economic interdependence and political divergence across the
Taiwan Strait, legal position of the PRC on the status of Taiwan
Module: China: looking ahead [Week 15, 16]
Interrogating the question - Does China Matter? How does one cope With China's Financial Power its role in world
economy, its fast productivity growth and rising innovation capacity?

Course Name: Contemporary Media Studies
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course is designed to help students build their understanding of the role of mediated communication in
contemporary societies. Students will be made aware of social, cultural and political impact of mediated
communication in globalized times.
Course Content:
Modules
A. Theories of Media
1. Media theories: We will cover the basic understanding of media as a social force and modes through which it
can be analyzed.
2. Analyzing media, power and control: Explicit connections will be made between media production and content
management and forms of power and control in society
B. Visual Culture: We will examine how visual culture can be analyzed in continuity with visual arts while evolving
its own language in the context of modern media.
C. Media Instruments
1. TV & Radio: This module will examine the evolution of television and radio both in terms of the politics of
invention and production as well as the ways in which they distinguish themselves from other media channels.
2. Print media: In this section, we will make explicit the connections between literacy, nationalism, and print
media.
3. Internet and new media: In this module, we track the emergence of new media and internet cultures in relation
to youth, identity, and questions of copyright and distribution
D. Media and cultural globalization: The last module will bring together all of the above concerns within the
umbrella rubric of cultural globalization. Here we tackle questions of homogeneity as well as difference.

This course builds a nuanced understanding of the theoretical elements that comprise the empirical study of
language. This will help develop an advanced foundation for appreciating linguistic theory and exploring the study
of nature and structure of language. The course also helps students to explore the social foundations of language.
Outcomes:
Participants will build foundations for research capabilities in language at an advanced level. The components of
this course enable researchers to develop linguistic insight into any spoken language. It helps develop confidence
in locating research in various fields of language studies.
Course Content:
• Language and Linguistics – philosophy of linguistics; knowledge of language; status of linguistic theories;
competence and performance
• Language and Human Mind – theories of language acquisition; linguistic relativity; relationship between
language and human cognition; mentalese; Language of Thought Hypothesis (LOTH)
• Structure of Language – structure of sounds, words, and sentences; generative phonology (origins, rules and
principles); meaning and formal semantics in generative grammar; formal linguistic theories and crosslinguistic
variation; functional categories and parametric variation; tense, aspect and mood; word order variation;
agreement; negation; voice; copula; nominalization
• Language and Society – language and ethnicity; saving languages; conversation analysis; attitudes and
ideologies; politeness hierarchy and language form; language families in India; India as a linguistic area; the
nature of language variation and language change; language and social power structure and culture
Text Books:

Course No: HS5020
Course Name: Gender and Development
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
-
Course Content:
The course is intended to highlight the gendered dynamics of development and pleads for engaging women as
change agents, and not merely as targets of development projects. Instead of perpetuating an exaggerated
segregation between men and women the course engages some of the fundamental concepts through shifting
theoretical positions and illustrates the same with case studies and success stories of women achievers. It
operates at a macro level addressing issues relating to representation, state, media and other institutions. It also
involves micro level approaches focusing on individual agency in the family. But overall the course offers a new
paradigm that places women at the center of development studies and treats cultural practices at par with the
institution of market economy.
Development studies and masculinist paradigms - Gender perspectives: HDI, GDI, Health, Education, Economy –
Politics of representation – Family, identity and inheritance - The shift in gender issues in development: WID,
WAD, GAD, WCD – Social exclusion and empowerment - Women, democracy and participation – Third World
gender perspectives - Gender and environment – Science and technology – Gender, globalization and
neocolonialism - Resistance to development - Gender and postmodern development – Post-development criticism
– Alternative visions.

Course No: HS5021
Course Name: Conflict and Economic Interdependence
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course focuses on the relationship between economic interdependence and conflict among states, to
understand causes of war and the conditions of peace under the liberal International Relations (IR) framework.
In-depth application of the theoretical framework against significant dyadic case studies (Cross-Strait ties,
India-China, US-China, China-Japan, and security in the Asia Pacific, among others) would comprise an important
part of the course.
Course Content:
Module 1: Introductory texts on causes of war and the conditions of peace; on why neighbors fight; and the
theoretical introduction to economic interdependence and conflict
Module 2: Key Theories in IR on conflict and economic interdependence (including detailed discussion on
structural realism, war in neo-realist theory) and discussion on the World Wars with reference to the
interdependence framework.
Module 3: Critique of lead theories (both Realist and Liberal) and examination of trends such as regionalization
(vis-à-vis conflict resolution)
Module 4: Case study analysis of significant dyads (Cross-Strait ties, India-China, US-China, China-Japan,
Economic Interdependence and Security in the Asia Pacific, chiefly)

Course No: HS5023
Course Name: Performance Traditions of the Mahabharata in Tamil Nadu
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course deals with the performance of Mahabharata as a koothu (music, dance and theatre) festival in
hundreds of villages in Tamil Nadu. The Mahabharata is enacted as a folk traditional theatre and aesthetic text for
the past thousand four hundred years, from the Pallava period. What is striking is as to how the Mahabharata is
seen in these villages; a narrative of a calamitous war between cousins is perceived as an anti-war text. The Epic
is performed annually to foster ‘Samarasam’ or peace and harmony in the festival villages. Each family in the
village contributes money for the festival and total amount spent on these festivals can vary between 35 Lakhs to
100 Lakhs depending on the affluence of the festival village. The festival is unique because it is probably the
longest running, independently funded theatre festival in the world being performed for well over a thousand years.
Conflict resolution also seems to be one core of the festival and in every festival, you can see old resentments
flaring up, conflicts between communities and sometimes conflicts amongst the organisers themselves. A lot of
these conflicts are resolved during the course of the festival itself, while some are deferred to raise their head
again, in the next festival. The course will provide an aesthetic, literary, textual, dramaturgical and sociological
perspective on these villages, the history of the festival from its origins in the Pallava period to the contemporary
times.
Course Content:

Course No: HS5025
Course Name: Linguistic Typology
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course familiarizes students with the similarities and differences between languages that belong to different
families that may or may not share genetic relationships and/ or language contact. It enables them to understand
the nuances of language-typological generalizations of various kinds. It also helps to conceptualize the
fundamentals of linguistic issues from a typological perspective that includes its form, function, meanings, sounds
and historical change.
Outcomes:
The course facilitates the learning of different ways of constructing language samples and acquaints the
participants with sources for obtaining language data. It also prepares them for working on a comparative analysis
of grammars of human languages, which may eventually reveal systematic patterns of variation.
Course Content:
• Linguistics: Some fundamental concepts: Nature of human language; Language and languages; Branches of
linguistics
• Language typology: Form and function: Lexical typology; Morphological typology; Syntactic typology
Phonological typology; Semantic typology; Pragmatic aspect of typology
• Language Universals and linguistic typology: Approaches to language universals; Classifying and explaining
language universals; Typology and universals; Universals in child language; Tracing universals in acquisition of
second language
Text Books:
1. Moravcsik, E. A. (2012). Introducing Language Typology. London: Cambridge University Press.
2. Akmajian, A., Farmer, A. K., Bickmore, L., Demers, R. A., & Harnish, R. M. (2017). Linguistics: An Introduction
to Language and Communication. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.
3. Comrie, B. (1989). Language Universals and Linguistic Typology: Syntax and Morphology. Chicago: University
of Chicago Press.
Reference Books:
1. Chomsky, N. (1975). Reflections on Language. New York: Pantheon Books.
2. Croft, W. (2002). Typology and Universals. Cambridge, Mass: Cambridge University Press.
3. Evans, N. (2010). Semantic Typology. London: Oxford University Press.
4. Givón, T. (1984). Syntax: A Functional-Typological Introduction. Amsterdam: Benjamins.
5. Subbarao, K. V. (2012). South Asian Languages: A Syntactic Typology. London: Cambridge University Press.
6. Dryer, M. 1992. ‘The Greenbergian Word Order Correlations.’ Language 68, 81–138.
7. Kemp, C., Xu, Y., & Regier, T. (2018). 'Semantic typology and efficient communication.’ Annual Review of
Linguistics, 4, 109-128.
8. Lehmann, C. (1986). ‘Grammaticalization and linguistic typology.’ General Linguistics, 26(1), 3.
9. Miestamo, M. (2000). ‘Towards a typology of standard negation.’ Nordic Journal of Linguistics, 23(1), 65-68.

Course No: HS5026
Course Name: Indian Aesthetic Thought
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course introduces the students to the foundations and development of Indian aesthetic theory and explores
the relation between art and beauty. Starting from Bharatamuni’s Natyashastra, the course traverses through the

bring the ancient and the contemporary to conversation.

Course No: HS5029
Course Name: Universal Grammar and Natural Language
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course offers a view of human language as a rule governed system. It shows how language is learnt and how
the structure of language functions in the human mind. The course also introduces components of linguistics
theory in generative framework for developing ideas to examine natural language.
Outcomes:
The course builds capacity in analyzing language using recent developments in syntax with special focus on
nano-syntax, bio-linguistics, syntax-morphology and syntax-semantics interface. It develops familiarity with varied
trends in syntactic theory for language study.
Course Content:
• Language and linguistics as a scientific domain of systematic investigation into sounds, words, and sentences;
Languages in India (Language, Dialect and Variety); Principles and Parameters
• Generative Foundations of Language Acquisition; Biological Foundation of Language; Language Acquisition
Device; Universal Grammar
• X-bar Theory (Specifiers, Head, Complements (Arguments), Adjuncts); Command, C-Command, and
M-Command, Government; Theta-Theory; Case Theory
• Raising; Movement; A and A Bar Movements; Passives and Questions; Binding Principles
• Exploring Nano-syntax; Case system: A nano-syntax perspective; Minimalist Program (theoretical goals,
technical innovation); Bare Phrase Structure
Text Books:

Course No: HS5050
Course Name: Indian Culture
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Objectives:
This course is an introduction to Indian culture, history, philosophy, religion, economy, society, art, architecture, fine
arts, literature, science and technology. The course would be a survey of ancient, medieval, modern and
contemporary India. The orientation of the course is to provide a practical understanding of India's "unity in
diversity" while utilizing textual resources to provide a theoretical framework. Documentaries, films, field visits to
museums, archaeological sites, historical places and music and dance concerts would form an integral part of the
course work to show the linkages with the past and to analyze how relevant the past is to an understanding of
contemporary India.
Outcomes:
Students would gain a nuanced understanding of the complex cultural history of the Indian subcontinent which
possesses mind boggling diversity of religions, regions, languages, ethnicity and socio-economic groups. This
course would also highlight the challenges of negotiating diversity in contemporary India. It would highlight how
Indian democracy serves as the crucible of contestation and dialogue between variegated view points.
Course Content:
1. Ancient India - An overview of Indus Valley Civilization
2. Political economy and society in Ancient India
3. The origins of Art, culture, philosophy and religion in various regions of Ancient India
4. An introduction to early Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism
4. Early Medieval India - The history of three powerful kingdoms - Harshavardhana, Pulakesin-II and
Mahendravarma and Narasimhavarma Pallava
5. Medieval Art and Architecture - Ajanta, Ellora, Mamallapuram, Kailasanatha, Brihadeeswara, Gangaikonda
Cholapuram, Srirangam, Madurai, Chidambaram and Darasuram
6. Indo-Saracenic art and architecture - Taj Mahal, Agra and Delhi Red Forts, Jaipur Hawa Mahal, Bada Imambara
Lucknow - Chikan
7. Sufi Islam, Medieval devotional movements and the origins of Sikhism as a new faith
8. Indian Medicine - Charaka, Susruta and Vagbhatta
9. Science and Technology tradition in India - Bhaskara, Aryabhatta and Brahmagupta
10. Mughal Empire - state and economy
11. India under the British rule - East India Company, 1857 First War of Independence and India under the British
Crown
12. India's Freedom Movement, Round Table Conferences and Partition - Tilak, Gandhi, Nehru, Patel, Ambedkar,
Jinnah, Azad and Prasad
13. India's Constituent Assembly Debates
14. Post-independence India - 1947 to 2021

Course No: HS5060
Course Name: Technology & Sustainable Development
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course starts with an introduction to technology, society and sustainable development from the perspectives of
the history of industrialization and technology, and science and technology studies (STS). We will take a critical
look at discourses of development and sustainability and their relationship with technology. In the second part of
the course we will discuss specific aspects of technology and sustainable development on the basis of case
studies such as energy production and consumption, global warming, agriculture, traffic and transport,
urbanization, water and wastewater management, industrial production and human consumption, pollution and
waste, and limits of natural resources.
Learning Outcomes:
The students will learn about the relationship between science, technology and society, and how technology
affects sustainable development. The students will learn how to argue in class, how to develop their own semester
project, to give an oral presentation and to give comments to the presentations of other students, and how to write
a term paper.
Course Content:
• Introduction to Science and Technology Studies
• The Social Construction of Scientific and Technical Realities
• The Evolution of Large Technological Systems
• Do Artefacts have Politics?
• The Normative Structure of Science
• The Industrial Revolution
• India's Technological Imaginary
• The Club of Rome and the Limits to Growth
• The Brundtland Report
• Deconstructing Development Discourse
• What is Sustainable Technology? Perceptions, Paradoxes and Possibilities
• The United Nations' sustainable development goals of the 2030 Agenda
Text Books:
Sergio Sismondo, An Introduction to Science and Technology Studies. Chichester, West Sussex: Wiley, 2010.
Andrea Cornwall and Deborah Eade, Deconstructing Development Discourse: Buzzwords and Fuzzwords, Oxford:

Course No: HS5061
Course Name: Migration and Development
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The objective of this course is to introduce the fundamental concepts and theories that underpin the study of
migration. The course will examine various migration patterns, with a specific emphasis on internal migration in
India, including labor migration, seasonal migration, and ethnic migration. The course will also delve into the life
and social world of the Indian diaspora community in order to comprehend the intricate interplay between
migration, ethnicity, and culture.
Course Content:
Part I: Theorising Migration: Understanding concepts in migration theory-the culture of migration, international
theories of migration, migration and development; gender and Migration, segmented assimilation; remittances;
ethnic enclaves; urban villages. Part II: Migration Pattern in Contemporary India: migration and colonialism;
rural-urban migration; seasonal migration; female migration; tribal migration; affective labour migration-migration
from Northeast to metropolitan centres; climate change induced migration. Part III: Histories and Trajectories of
Indian Diaspora: Indian indentured migration (Caribbean, Mauritius, Natal and Fiji); Education and international
migration; Skilled migration to developed countries- brain drain, brain gain, its economic implications; care and
female domestic workers abroad. Part IV: Migration, Race and Ethnicity: Conserving ethnic heritage; Polity and
politics in diaspora- Indian diaspora as emerging political force, Indian diaspora in international relations; caste
identity; religious identity; Retention and survival of linguistic heritage; Cinema and music in diaspora; migrants
discrimination, racism and violence
Text Books:

Course No: HS5062
Course Name: An Introduction to Tirukkural
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The objectives of the course are to enable students appreciate the universal values of life from the selected
chapters of the ancient Tamil literary text Tirukkural and help them learn how to live a purposeful and peaceful life
as responsible members of the society, including, government and private organizations.
After doing this course, students will be able to perform their role as responsible members of their family, society,
and professional organizations with a clear understanding of the time-tested ethical principles of individual and
collective wisdom, as propounded by Thiruvalluvar in Tirukkural. They will also learn how to appreciate the value
of effective communication through the couplet form and practice it appropriately in their own lives in any language
that they may use.
Course Content:
The original text of Tirukkural is available in multiple languages but then this course will use the Penguin edition of
P. S. Sundaram’s translation in English. Of the 133 chapters, relevant themes from the first two sections of
Tirukkural will find discussion in class. Some notable themes are the blessing of rain, the strength of virtue,
domestic life, hospitality, gratitude, impartiality, forbearance, social obligation, charity, fame, kindliness,
truthfulness, warth, realization, fate, learning, hearing, wisdom, knowing time, knowing place, compassion, energy,
fortitude, persuasiveness, honest dealing, mind reading, wealth, friendship, nobility, honor, greatness, character,
courtesy, and so on. Discussions will revolve around the individual and social relevance of the couplets as
evidenced from books like Rajaram’s Corporate Wisdom in Tirukkural to help students live their personal and
professional life meaningfully. It will also pay attention to a few specific kurals, which have guided leaders like A P
J Abdul Kalam to find their anchor in life.

Thiruvalluvar. 1990. The Kural. Trans. P. S. Sundaram. New Delhi: Penguin.

Course No: HS5111
Course Name: Semiotics: Theory and Practice
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Objectives: The aim of this course is to introduce students to the principles and practices of semiotics for
understanding and applying them to literary and cultural phenomena with an awareness of interdisciplinary and
multimodal dimensions.
Outcomes: After doing this course, students should be able to analyze literary and cultural texts and explicate the
process of producing and disseminating meaning in society, to examine the patterns of relationships among
socio-economic-political ideological practices, and conduct both quantitative and qualitative study of literary and
cultural texts.
Course Content:
As a scientific study of signs, semiotics considers the universe as its object of study from language, literature,
myth, fashion, theater, film, and sports to social media, marketing and architecture. It is essentially interdisciplinary
which has drawn ideas from various fields like philosophy, linguistics, anthropology, medicine, communication, etc.
With its origin in the Greek philosophers and St Augustine through John Locke, Ferdinand de Saussure and
Charles Sanders Peirce, it has grown into a ubiquitous field of knowledge and also a method of study, though with
diverse perspectives. While this course will substantially deal with Saussurean linguistics and Peircean logic, it will
also consider semiotic concepts form Roman Jakobson, Claude Levi-Strauss, Roland Barthes, Jaques Derrida,
Jacques Lacan, Vladimir Propp, Thomas Sebeok, Yuri Lotman, Umberto Eco, Louis Hjelmslev, and A J Greimas,
so as to gain an in-depth knowledge of the field for application of the gained knowledge to such areas as literature
and visual media.
Course Modules:
Module 1: Origins of semiotics, Plato, Aristotle, St Augustine, John Locke
Module 2: Ferdinand de Saussure and Charles Sanders Peirce
Module 3: Roman Jakobson, Levi-Strauss, Vladimir Propp, Roland Barthes, Derrida, Lacan,
Module 4: Thomas Seboek, Yuri Lotman, Umberto Eco, Louis Hjelmslev, A J Greimas
Module 5: Applications in literature, radio, film, television, social media, fashion, sports
Text Books:
Chandler, D. 2017. Semiotics: The Basics. 3rd ed. London: Routledge.
Ennis, R. E. ed. 1986. Semiotics: An Introductory Reader. London: Hutchinson.
Reference Books:
Bignell, J. 2003. Media Semiotics. Manchester: Manchester University Press.

Hodge, R, and Kress, G. 1988. Social Semiotics. Ithaca: Cornell University Press.

Mouton.

Course No: HS5115
Course Name: Introduction to International Organisations
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
International Organisations (IOs) now govern all areas of world politics – from international peace and security,
nuclear proliferation and human rights to commerce, economic development, public health and environmental
protection. While the study of international relations traditionally puts its primary attention on interactions between
states, the existence of scores of IOs necessitates the study to focus more on their overall role and functioning in
international politics. The course investigates questions of why states create IOs and whether and how they
exercise authority in world politics with what political and legal consequences.
Outcomes:
The students, after the course, would be able to comprehend the historical context of the emergence of major
international and regional organisations and have a better understanding of the important ways in which these
organisations affect international law and politics. Additionally, they will also understand the contemporary issues
and challenges that these organisations face.
Course Content:
• Evolution of International Organisations: Concert of Europe (1815); League of Nation (1919); United Nations
(1945)
• IOs and Dominant theoretical framework of IR: Realism and the problem of state-centric approaches; anarchy;
Balance of Power; security dilemma; Liberal institutional approach to IOs, regime making; mitigation of anarchy
and possibility of cooperation between the states.
• International Organisation in International Law: IO as actor in international law; legal personality; treaty relations;
treaty making power; IOs role in evolution of customary international law
• The UN System and the Changing context of Global Politics: Structure and Functions of UN organs; Specialised
Agencies; UN and the unfolding Global Governance Framework
• Key Regional Organisations: European Union; ASEAN; SAARC; ADB; NDB; Arab League
• India’s foreign policy and IOs: Basic contours of Indian foreign policy; recent transformations; from Look East to
Act East; India’s de-hyphenated policy in West Asia and its consequences; India in the UN

Course No: HS5120
Course Name: School Education in Modern India
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The objective of this course is to gain an overview of School Education as it has emerged in modern India,
especially since the 19th century, as well as an orientation to the competing visions and debates that inform the
discourse on School Education in India.
Taking Dharampal's important survey of the state of education in pre-British India (referred to by Mahatma Gandhi
as ‘the Beautiful Tree’) as the point of departure, this course looks at how the indigenous school education system
was gradually transformed to suit the human resource requirements of the colonial government, and how ‘modern
school education’ opened up avenues of social transformation. It examines the whats and hows of the changes
that have taken place in mainstream school education after 1947, including recommendations of various Education
Commissions as well as national level Education Policies, particularly since the Kothari Commission.
The course also surveys and contrasts theoretical/philosophical positions on the idea of Education and Pedagogy,
particularly relevant to but not limited to the period that it surveys (i.e. the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries) –
Jambhekar-Phule-Tagore-Gandhi-Ambedkar, for example; or Holt-Dewey-Illich-Freire-Aurobindo-Krishnamurti.
This opens up the possibility of comparing and contrasting mainstream school education with contemporaneous
alternative theories and models of schooling in India.
Outcomes:
The serious learner should get an overview of the evolution and status of School Education in India over the past
two centuries; they should get acquainted with the nature of “school” education in pre-colonial times and have
some orientation in the competing visions and debates that inform the discourse on School Education in Modern
India.
Course Content:
• Overview of education in Ancient and Medieval India – Vedic Schools – Buddhism – Decline of the two –
Education under Muslim rulers – Vocation and Education – Language and Literature
• 18th century onwards – role of the East India Company – 19th century – Macaulay – Indian ‘Enlightenment’
thinkers – Missionary education – Vernacular to English medium – Expansion and control of education – Woods
and Hunter – 1900 to 1947
• Educational policies since 1947 – Literacy and Education – Nature and spread of mainstream education –
Contemporary Reality of school education, a critique – Dominant models and Alternatives –
Tagore-Gandhi-Aurobindo-Krishnamurti

1. A Students’ History of Education in India 1800 – 1973/J P Naik & Syed Nurullah. New Delhi, MacMillan India,

Course No: HS5130
Course Name: Ecofiction
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
In addition to developing a foundational knowledge of environmental issues and ecocritical theory, the course will
discuss how:
Ecofiction read in tandem with ecocritical theories will enable a nuanced understanding of the texts taken up for
discussion.
Ecofiction can be theorized as a mode of critical inquiry that celebrates human creative power.
Ecofiction fulfills the need for new conceptual categories to accommodate diverse and hybrid types of modern
storytelling in order to embrace an open-ended vision of the complex nature of our environmental reality.
Course Content:
The course on ecofiction aims to introduce students to contemporary ecofiction that engages with environmental
issues occupying the centre stage in the Anthropocene. Although the concerns of ecofiction have been voiced in
earlier eco-writings, this genre perhaps marks the culmination of self-conscious Anthropocene writing. For
instance, Jim Dwyer’s field comprehensive guide to ecofiction mentions an entire range of ecofiction examples
spanning across time periods ranging from the earliest cave drawings up to the 21st century.
This supergenre became popular with the environmental movements in the 1970s and 80s when disciplines like
ecocriticism sought to forge connections between literature and the physical environment. The term ‘ecofiction’
does not merely function as a subgenre of science fiction, but can be viewed as a super category of all genres that
depicts the troubled environmental and material realities of our times. Ecofiction is truly a capacious and elastic
term and encompasses a variety of hybrid subgenres like ecopunk, ecotopia, biopunk, solarpunk, climate fiction,
Afrofuturismo, environmental weird fiction, postapocalyptic fiction, among others.
For the purposes of this course, the term ‘ecofiction’ will primarily focus on subgenres in which the role of
speculation is vital to the envisioning of the complex systemic processes that inform anthropogenic global
warming like climate change, flooding, resource depletion, impact winter and other eco-crises.These
ecospeculative narratives can either present a dystopic and counterfactual present world, an alternative past or an
imaginative reality about sustainable futures.
Text Books:

Course No: HS5140
Course Name: Transitions and Transformations to Sustainability
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The aim of this course is to introduce learners to the relatively new field of global sustainability transitions studies
around the core question: Is it possible to initiate and perform a conscious, profound shift in the ways we are living
on planet Earth? This course may be seen as an initial step towards generating a group of learners who acquire
transformation knowledge (theory of change) and competencies to develop transformative knowledge (skills that
might lead to actual change).
Course Content:
1. Foundations:
• Ideas and notions of paradigm shifts (e.g. Meadows leverage points theory)
• Critique of science, wicked problems, systems theories
• Anthropocene
• Transformation and transition
2. Transition and transformation theories:
• Multi-level, multi-perspective theory
• Theory of Social Innovation
• Strategic Niche Management
• Doughnut Economics
3. Cultural dimensions and resources for transformation
• Inner transformation theories and approaches (e.g. Theory U, Integral Theory)
• Faith, religion, spirituality
• Worldviews, values, beliefs
4. Place and geography in transitions
• Role of locality and place specific features
5. Transitions studies and the Global South
• Regional and country specific perspectives
• Global North and South
6. Social innovations at the grassroots:
• Global movements
• Local initiatives, global networks
• Examples: Transition Movement, Global Ecovillage Network, Intentional Communities, ECOLISE
7. Indigenous and alternative transition approaches
• Local, small scale, e.g. Buen vivir, Radical Ecological Democracy
• Degrowth, sufficiency
8. Transitions in specific socio-technical systems (mobility, energy, consumption)
• Energy transitions
• Mobility transitions
• Consumption and lifestyles
• Agro-food systems
• Transformative pedagogy and education/learning
9. Urban sustainability transitions
• Urban areas as nodal points of innovation and change
• Transition governance
10. Methods and Methodologies:
• Transdisciplinarity (multi-/cross-/interdisciplinarity)
• Co-creation and co-production of knowledge, citizens science
• Mode 1 – 2 – 3 science
• Awareness based social science research
• Living Labs/Real-World Labs/Transformation Labs

Course No: HS5210
Course Name: Advanced Social and Political Thought
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course aims to provide an overview of major foundational texts of modern social and political thought at a
level suitable for PhD students. Students will have lectures on and will read selected passages from specified
advanced commentary on Machiavelli, Hobbes, Hume, Smith, Marx and Weber, as well as selections from certain
other philosophers; the plan is to identify the main philosophical threads within contemporary social and political
discourse, and the course will require the students to develop their own capacity for critical commentary at PhD
level.
Outcomes:
A grasp of the selected major thinkers’ main arguments, and the capacity to analyse other writings and
contemporary events in the light of that knowledge. The capacity to identify additional pertinent sources of
different kinds and to write critical evaluations of relevant issues and texts, including contemporary sources and
events, at an appropriate level.
Course Content:
Selections from the key writings of seven major thinkers in the history of modern social and political thought.
The course starts with a brief outline of Plato, Aristotle, and Kautilya before moving on to the major thinkers
specified below.
These are Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, Smith, Hume, Marx, and Weber. In addition, the course will also consider
briefly the ideas of Spinoza and Rousseau, and will take account of the Frankfurt School.
The critical themes that run through the course are liberty, virtue, state, civil society, empiricism, values, justice and
bureaucracy, as well as the epistemological backgrounds of and main assumptions in the work of the respective
thinkers.

Course Name: Introduction to Chinese Language-A
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
With China’s economic development and her growing influence on the international stage, Chinese language has
become one of the most studied languages in the world. Governments, private institutions, companies and various
agencies have increased demand for Chinese language professionals to access Chinese sources for a more
accurate and contextual understanding of Chinese society, politics and economy. Introduction to Chinese is an
introductory course to the language. The course will help students relate to the overall context of discussions
relating to China with Language as an important skill-set.
In addition to the above, content-wise the PhD-level course would comprise additional assignments/readings on
society and culture, given to PhD research scholars and evaluated accordingly. Being an introductory language
course - the nature of the basic language training has to remain as in HS4571.
Course Content:
The course will address the problems of pronunciation, character writing and basic morpho-syntactic elements. By
the end of the course, the students should have mastered 300 characters, 700 words, which should allow them to
carry basic conversations regarding aspects of their daily life.1. Phonetics – pronunciation (initials and finals) and
the four tones2. Basic rules for character writing 3. Greetings - basic questions (yes-no, ma) and sentences with
adjectival predicate4. Introducing oneself – verbal predicate and negation5. Looking for people and things –
interrogative pronouns6. Meeting people and family – the verb “to have”, adverbs, numerals (0-100), basic
classifiers, costs7. Birthdays – expressing time8. Shopping – expressing place9. Abilities and desires – modal
verbs10. Living on campus – objects with preposition, perfective le
In addition to the above, the higher level course would comprise additional assignments/readings on society and
culture, given to PhD research scholars and evaluated accordingly. Being an introductory language course - the
nature of the basic language training has to remain as in HS4571. PhD scholars need language credentials as a
vital component for fieldwork and material collection relating to China studies.

Course No: HS5260
Course Name: Literature and the Environment
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course is organized around a basic question: what is environmental literature? The course will explore this
question by examining major trends that have shaped how Anglophone writers have understood and written about
their environments historically, and how those trends continue to influence our feelings towards, and
understandings of, the more-than-human world. More specifically, by using the tools of literary analysis and
literary history the course will introduce texts across British, American and Commonwealth literature (which
represent only a small sampling of the environmental literary canon) to distinguish a set of shared tropes and
shared concerns indicative of environmental literature in general. This course will be of relevance to higher
semester MA students as well as research scholars who are pursuing research in the domain of environmental
humanities.
Course Content:
Readings will be informed by some key works in recent environmental theory and in relevant critical theory and will
be directed towards an understanding of the way in which fiction both reflects and helps to shape attitudes and
awareness in the community. It will also contribute to framing questions about the idea of “nature”.The course will
identify strategies through which poets, dramatists, and fiction and nonfiction writers have addressed
environmental questions through both the form and content of their works. The course will also introduce the
students to global environmental literature, especially the literature of environmental justice. It will focus
particularly on the ways the assigned texts represent the natural world and issues of environmental
sustainability–and the ways that these concepts are inflected by race, class, gender, and geographical location.
Reading includes authors from diverse racial and national locations—Iraq, South Africa, multicultural U.S., India,
Malawi, Nigeria, China, Canada, Guatemala. Our study will focus on the intersection of environmental issues and
various systems of social injustice, especially racism, sexism, and economic inequity. Primary texts include novels
and stories from world literature: Mahasweta Devi The Pterodactyl; Amitav Ghosh, The Hungry Tide; Helena
María Viramontes, Under the Feet of Jesus; Hassan Blasim, The Corpse Exhibition and Other Stories of Iraq; Mo
Yan, “Iron Child”; Rigoberta Menchú, “Death of Her Little Brother in the Finca”; Margaret Atwood, Oryx and Crake;
and Bessie Head, When Rain Clouds Gather.Students will help lead discussion by taking responsibility for certain
portions of each text that we study together, they will practice close reading and comparative analysis, and they
will present their original research in a seminar presentation at the semester’s end.

Course No: HS5501
Course Name: Indian Social Structure and Development
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This is a foundational course that introduces students of Development Studies to the sociological theorizations on
the structure of Indian society. It provides an overview of the sociological understanding of Indian social structure
with a specific focus on its major categories viz caste, tribe and religion and their implication to the development
question. This course also highlights the central role of the state in shaping and negotiating the developmental
experiences of different social categories of Indian population.
Outcomes: Students get exposed to the multiple frameworks, epistemological and methodological orientations and
other intellectual influences that shaped the sociological study of Indian society. They will also appreciate the
centrality of social categories and their significance in the developmental trajectory of Indian society. Students also
get in-depth understanding of the centrality of Indian state in mediating the development experience of these social
categories
Course Content:
UNIT-1: Understanding Indian Society: The debates and trajectories
Colonial influence on studying Indian society; multiple perspectives- structural functional, Marxist, structuralist and
Dalit frameworks of understanding Indian society. An overview on the debates on Indian social structure and social
stratification in India.
UNIT-2: Caste in India
Theoretical debates on caste as a system of stratification; caste and state interventions; changing trajectory of
affirmative action and the caste question; caste and economic development in contemporary India.
UNIT-3: Tribes in India
Sociological and Anthropological framing of the tribal question in India; Tribal development and state; Issues of
autonomy, indigeneity and tribal rights.
Unit-4: Religion in India
India’s religious composition and its implications; Minority rights, state and development questions; Debates on
secularism, citizenship and political transformations.

Course No: HS5502
Course Name: Climate Change, Technology and Sustainable Development
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course starts with an introduction to technology, society and sustainable development from the perspectives of
the history of industrialization and technology, and science and technology studies (STS). We take a critical look at
discourses of development and sustainability and their relationship with technology in the precarious material
context of the Anthropocene. In the second part of the course, we will discuss specific aspects of technology and
sustainable development on the basis of case studies such as energy production and consumption, global
warming, agriculture, traffic and transport, urbanization, water and wastewater management, industrial production
and human consumption, pollution and waste, and limits of natural resources.Outcomes:The students will learn
about the relationship between science, technology and society, and how technology affects sustainable
development in a world facing the very serious threat of climate catastrophe. The students will learn how to argue
in class, how to develop their own semester project, to give an oral presentation and to give comments to the
presentations of other students, and how to write a term paper.

Development Goals

Course No: HS5503
Course Name: Development and Ethics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course aims to highlight the place that ethics occupies in the context of the diverse theories and arguments
with regard to the idea of development. It tries to outline some important ethical challenges facing development in
the contemporary world. It aims to introduce students to some ethical theories in the context of development,
understood broadly as the fundamental societal changes needed toward economic well-being, environmental
prosperity, and social and cultural harmony.
Outcomes:
At the completion of the course students will be able to appreciate the centrality of ethics in development theory
and practice. They are expected to familiarize with the major challenges to development and learn the three broad
frameworks of ethical thought: consequentialism, rights-based deontology, and virtue ethics. They are also
introduced to “New Harms” involving structural injustices associated with environmental or developmental injuries
associated with compound social practices across generations.
Course Content:
1. Contemporary ethical challenges of development.
2. Ethical issues concerning issues such as well-being, freedom, empowerment, human rights, justice, corruption,
poverty alleviation, equity, environmental sustainability etc.
3. Ethical Theories such as Consequentialism, Kant and agent-centric deontological theories, Rawls and
contractualist theories Virtue Ethics etc.

Course No: HS5505
Course Name: Foundations of Social and Political Thought
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course aims to provide an overview of the foundational texts of modern social and political
thought. By reading selected passages from Machiavelli, Hobbes, Hume, Smith, Marx and Weber, in
particular, the course will attempt to identify the main philosophical threads within contemporary social and political
discourse.
Outcomes:
Students will gain familiarity and a deep reading of the primary texts that inform the social sciences as well as
development studies. They will learn the philosophical bases of modern institutions, governance and statehood.
Course Content:
Selections from the key writings of 6 major thinkers in the history of modern social and
political thought. These are Machiavelli, Hobbes, Hume, Smith, Marx and Weber. In addition, the course will also
consider very briefly the ideas of Spinoza, Locke, and Rousseau. The central themes that run through the course
are liberty, virtue, state, civil society, empiricism, impressions and ideas, value, justice, and bureaucracy.

Course No: HS5506
Course Name: Development: Theory and Practice
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Development: Theory and Practice is an introductory course to the Development Studies program. In this course,
we examine how geopolitics and development thinking have changed over time. In addition to discussing major
theories of development, we will evaluate how development practices have evolved over time, particularly in the
neoliberal context. Also, the course seeks to problematize development thinking and practice in the context of the
Global South.
Outcomes: Students will gain a historically grounded location as well as context for the concept of development.
They will learn to apply theories of development within real-world contexts through case-studies and analysis.
Course Content:
• The concept of development: Mapping its origin and evolution since the Second World War. Contextualization of
the idea in the Indian scenario by tracing the colonial history and discussing and establishing significant
continuities.
• Theories of Development: Discussion of mainstream theories of development, including modernization theories
and the economic growth models, along with dependency theory, world systems theory and theories of
globalization. A brief overview of the neoliberal turn in development thinking and practice (and MDGs) will also be
undertaken.
• Key actors in Development: Critical reading of the role of state (categorisations- development state, welfare state
etc.), civil society and global institutions in development. Discussion of civil society, social movements and the
question of citizenship within the development framework.
• Critiques of Development: Reviewing the gender issues in development and environmental critique of
development towards shaping the idea of sustainable development.
• Post development and anti-development as critiques of development.
• Critical development studies as an emergent domain of critical inquiry.
• Contemporary approaches of measuring development: HDI and summarizing shifts in measuring development
and poverty from a quantitative to qualitative perspective.
• Practical component: Gaining hands-on experience in the realms of policy making, policy evaluation and
implementation (major policies in post-independent India) and the role of development planning and institutional
frameworks for the same.

Course No: HS5520
Course Name: Culture and Development
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Objectives:
In normative development thought, culture is either a realm outside the sphere of development or the pre-history of
development that requires a forward march toward a society of consumption and well-being. This approach
defined development theory during development decades (except for a few articulations as in Sen, Boserup
among others) until the impasse in development theory in the 1980s and early 90s. When the United Nations
announced the Decade for Cultural Development from 1988 to 1997, it brought culture to converse with
development practice in an institutional sense. This was a movement away from the earlier modernization (and
also Marxist) theory and linear understandings of economic development, where culture and tradition need to be
repressed for development to work.
The course will introduce the students (preferably of higher semesters) to the way culture mediates our
understanding of development, and make a case for development that is as much a cultural process as is a
material outcome. Against the conventional wisdom that culture is too vernacular a practice to play any meaningful
role in the global process of development, this course is aimed at offsetting that residual status for culture in
development practice.
Learning outcomes:
The course will help students appreciate the multidimensionality of development practice and equip them with
critical vocabulary to see development as deeply embedded in cultural imaginaries. This engagement will help
them see development as a repository of values and as an everyday and iterative practice.
Course Content:
Course Contents:
Culture, the missing concept, in institutional development thought
Discourses around culture and (modernist)-development, narrativization
Power and knowledge, making of development and underdevelopment
Beyond base and super-structure, faith-based development, culture, religion
Politics of location, globalism, nationalism, localism
Cultural globalization, representation, universality and the making of First/Third world
Culturalism and multiple developments, a new social theory and development practice
Text Books:
Susanne Schech & Jane Haggis. Culture and Development: A Critical Introduction. Blackwell: Malden, 2000.
Deborah Eade. Ed. Development and Culture. Oxfam: Oxford, 2002.
Reference Books:
Peter Worsley. The Three Worlds: Culture and World Development. London: Weidenfeld and Nicolson, 1984.
Thierry G. Verhelst. No Life without Roots: Culture and Development. Zed Books: London, 1990.
Vincent Tucker. Ed. Cultural Perspectives on Development. Frank Cass: London, 2002.
Susanne Schech & Jane Haggis. Eds. Development: A Cultural Studies Reader. Blackwell: Malden, 2002.
John Clammer. Culture, Development and Social Theory. Zed Books: London, 2012.
Ben Garner. The Politics of Cultural Development. Routledge: London, 2016.
Sophia Labadi. The Cultural Turn in International Aid. Routledge: London, 2019.
Rhonda Phillips, Mark Brennan & Tingxuan Li. Eds. Culture, Community and Development. Routledge: London,
2020.

Course No: HS5550
Course Name: Research Methodology
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course aims to develop students' knowledge and understanding of methodology question in the social
sciences. Theoretical and methodological debates in selected disciplinary areas will be discussed in order to
motivate students to pursue a critical approach to research. The imperative for ethical research practices will be
presented. The course helps students recognize and reflect on the strengths and limitations of various research
methodologies, determining the link between theory and practice, critically evaluating research, and addressing
ethical and practical dilemmas. In this course, students will learn step-by-step how to design and implement
quantitative and qualitative methods, including case studies, in-depth interviews, focus group discussions,
participant observation, and textual and media analysis. The course includes lessons on how to deal with and
analyze data, as well as how to write up and present findings.
Outcomes:
This course will make students understand the research process that includes, at a minimum, selecting
appropriate conceptual/theoretical framework, identifying and reviewing select literature, framing research
questions, choosing appropriate research methods, and synthesizing the observations/finding to develop a set of
coherent arguments. In addition to developing a set of transferable workplace skills, it is expected that the
students will gain the knowledge and ability to do original research and writing.
Course Content:
1. Introduction to social science research
2. What is the methodology question in social science research?
3. Discussion on the history of disciplines in social science and the question of critical disciplinary approach
4. Discussion on interdisciplinary, multi-disciplinary & transdisciplinary research
5. Overview of select academic disciplines/sub-disciplines and a discussion on why such mapping is necessary.
6. Mapping of select disciplines to discuss how the direction and method of inquiry has changed overtime
7. Research methods - Quantitative Vs. qualitative methods & mixed methods
8. Quantitative research methods and secondary data sets
9. Survey method I – Basic concepts in quantitative research & sampling techniques
10. Survey method II - Developing research questions; Preparing a questionnaire
11. Survey method III – A discussion on data analysis with select examples
12. Qualitative research methods and data gathering process
13. Ethnography/Auto-ethnography
14. Textual and discourse analysis
15. Focus group discussions (FGDs)
16. Vignettes, case studies, and participant observation
17. Project evaluation and monitoring
18. Research ethics – ethics committees, anti-plagiarism guidelines, formal acknowledgments, data privacy, and
confidentiality, etc.
19. Academic writing
