Course No: HS5551
Course Name: Modern World History
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course examines the History of the Modern World from the early modern period to the twentieth century. The
main objective of the course is to examine how new economic, social and cultural ideologies, mass movements,
technology and wars shaped the modern world. The course will also explore various theories associated with the
growth of nationalism and revolutions in the modern world.
Outcomes:
The students will first understand the later medieval crisis in world history and how the world recovered and
witnessed the emergence of new global patterns of exploration and expansion. By examing the specific cases and
theories of such crisis and recovery in the modern world, the students will learn to critically understand various
dimensions of historical development and changes. Second, the students will familiarise themselves with the
ideological, cultural, and economic world of the enlightenment era, which paved the way for the birth of new
political order of nationalism and liberalism. Third, the students will learn about how the American, French and
Industrial revolutions altered the shape of western civilisation and how the old system of balance of power was
strained by economic rivalries and tensions mounted within each nation in the world during the nineteenth century.
Lastly, the students will learn about the growth of authoritarianism in the twentieth-century world and how
international rivalries and pressure exploded into global wars. The concluding section of the course will discuss the
Cold War, Decolonisation, Collapse of the Soviet Union and the World of 2000s.
Course Content:
Module -1 - World System Approach - World System History / World System Theory -
Module -2 - 13th Century World System – Feudalism, Crisis and recovery (1200-1500)
Module -3 – Age of Exploration, Mercantilism and New World Patterns (1500 - 1700)
Module -4 - 18th Century World – Enlightenment and new ideologies
Module -5- Revolutions - Political & Economic Reordering
Module -6– 19th Century World –Nationalism and International Industrialisation
Module -7 – 20th Century World – Crisis, Rivalries and Mass Movements
Module -8 - Post 1945 World – Emergence of New World and clash of civilization
Text Books:
Norman Lowe, Mastering the World History (London, 1997)
Meenaxi Phukan, Rise of the Modern West (Delhi, 2012).
William J.Duiker, The Essential World History (Boston, 2011)
Robert Tignor (Ed), Worlds Together and Worlds Apart (London, 2011).
Edward McNall Burns, World Civilizations (London, 1991).
Eric Hobsbawn, The Age of Revolution (London, 1962).
Reference Books:
C.A.Bayly, The Birth of the Modern World, 1780-1914 (New York, 2004).
Gizachew Tiruneh,’ Social Revolutions’, Sage Open, 2014, pp.1-12.
Steven M. Beaudoin,’ Current Debates in the Study of the Industrial Revolution’, OAH Magazine of History, Vol.15,
No.1, pp.7-21.
Samuel Huntington, Clash of Civilizations and the Remaking of the World Order (New York, 1996).
Francis Fukuyama, End of History and the Last Man (New York, 1992).

Course No: HS5552
Course Name: The Making of Modern India
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course introduces the history of the making of modern India. The course covers the period from the end of
Mughal period, through the history of British rule, the struggle for independence and the partition and
independence of India in 1947. The course will mainly revolve around the themes like disintegration of Mughal
Empire, colonial theories of governance and conquest of knowledge and most importantly the encounter between
the colonised and the colonisers, bringing upon the themes like socio-economic reforms and early resistance. The
last part of the course will examine the development of nationalism and emergence of Gandhi as an architect of
Indian independence.

Course No: HS5553
Course Name: Perspectives on Health and Biomedical Ethics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The aim of this course is to introduce students to ethical issues in health care after discussing the different
perspectives on the concept of health presented in different medical and philosophical traditions. It examines some
basic ethical frameworks and explores how they can help us in effectively negotiating with some contemporary
questions in medical ethics. It tries to understand how the present-day technological context in medicine is
generating complex moral dilemmas and how is it altering our basic understanding about human life, health,
well-being, and death. The course will also address the larger social organization of medicine and examines how
fundamental ethical challenges stem from it.
Outcomes:
Students are expected to learn the different conceptions and philosophies of health and will be able to identify
some important ethical issues in medicine and healthcare. This course will familiarize the students with some
prominent ethical frameworks that practitioners can employ in resolving dilemmas and they will be able to identify
rational justifications for ethical decisions.
Course Content:
• Health and healing in different traditions.
• Medicine and health: historical analysis
• Health, Medicine and Medical morality in different healing traditions such as Hippocrates, Indian, Chinese, Arabic
etc.
• From medical morality of ancient medicine to medical ethics of modern medicine.
• Different ethical frameworks such as virtue ethics, deontologism, utilitarianism, social contract theories etc., and
challenges to ethical decision-making process such as subjectivism, nihilism, egoism etc.
• Modern medicine and its unique features
• Development of modern bioethics.
• Analysis of different historical incidents that led to the development of contemporary bioethics such as the
Tuskegee Syphilis Study, Willowbrook experiments, NASI experiments, Nuremberg trials and the formation of the
codes of bioethics etc.
• Healthcare technologies and biomedical ethics.
• Sociology of health and the social organization of medicine.
• The future of bioethics.

Course Name: Gender in Indian Society
Course Type:
Theory
Description:

The evolution of patriarchy through human history – from hunter-gatherer to agricultural society to modern

Understanding occupational segregation in contemporary times and the characteristics of feminized work
Measuring and defining gender (in)/equalities in contemporary India
The emergence of dowry as a pan-Indian phenomenon and outcome of capitalist modernity
Understanding declining child sex ratios – from ‘son preference’ to ‘daughter aversion’
Indian women’s participation in social movements for land rights, protection of natural resources and struggles for

Young women’s feminisms in contemporary India

Theory

In the contemporary society, law controls, influences and affects all forms of everyday life. For every action that an

Course No: HS5557
Course Name: China in Contemporary Global Politics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
China, as a rising power is of intrinsic relevance and tremendous interest to political scientists, economists,
technologists, media and foreign and defence policy establishments and analysts. The success of China as a
major economic power, under a controlled political system has thrown up an alternative to the dominant US led
free market system grounded on neo-classical liberal premises. China’s initiatives in economic planning, energy
security, human rights, high technology international cooperation and its arrival at the high table of global politics
have a fundamental impact on our current and future international order.
This course will offer a condensed study of Chinese political structure and China’s foreign policy as a global
power. The course will familiarize the students with the historical context of Chinese political and economic
transformation since the Opium Wars and go on to discuss China’s primary domestic and foreign policy concerns
today. This will include:
• China’s focus on Taiwan, Tibet, Xinjiang, HK as ‘domestic’ issues of urgent concern with foreign policy
implications. The broader context of these discussions will include China’s ethnic minority policies, internet
regulation and demographic changes.
• China’s external foreign policy environment that includes territorial disputes in South China Sea, India and Japan.
The broader context of each of these discussions will cover China’s relations with the US, Russia, its neighbours
as well as Chinese defence modernization.
• The CCP and the Chinese State: Institutional Structure and State-Party dynamics.
Outcomes: Familiarity with Chinese domestic politics and its foreign policy linkages. Students are expected to do a
daily survey of Chinese media sources in English/translation and develop an understanding of what are primary
concerns of the Chinese state and people.

Historical Introduction to China
• China in the traditional world order: The Sinocentric order.
• China: the century of humiliation: Opium Wars to collapse of Qing Dynasty in 1911.
• China in Revolution: 1911-1949.
Major Issues in Chinese Foreign policy & their domestic linkages
• Territorial Disputes: Taiwan, South China Sea, East China Sea, India-China boundary dispute
• Energy Security-Sea lanes of communication, global energy competition and China
• Domestic Stability: Xinjiang, Tibet, Taiwan, HK: Foreign policy and internal politics
• Internet in China: Censorship, Global Governance of the Internet and Cyber-Sovereignty
• Chinese military modernization and the EU Arms Embargo on China
• China & the Covid-19 Pandemic

Course Name: Human Rights and Justice
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course will explore the evolution, institutionalization and practice of human rights and justice in international
law and politics. Understanding the philosophical basis of the concepts of human rights and justice is essential to
this objective. There will be an examination of the universality of human rights in theory and practice. Conceptual
understanding of the Human rights will be followed by the institutionalization and practice of human rights in
international system. The relationship between State sovereignty and universality of human rights will be debated.
The course will take up specific case studies to illustrate the use of humanitarian intervention as a foreign policy
tool. This will be followed by a discussion on future direction of the concept and practice of human rights. The
concept of human rights thus discussed will be critically examined from the perspective of the concept of justice as
related to development.
Outcomes: Understanding of the origins, institutionalization and implementation of current regime of Human
Rights.
Course Content:
Theories of Social Contract and Human Rights
Where do they derive from? What is their philosophical basis? Who are the philosophers credited with the
foundation of natural rights and what is their project? Are Human Rights grounded in natural rights? What are the
contending positions on the foundation of human rights?
Are Human Rights Universal or Culturally Relative?
Do we need a Universal Declaration of Human Rights? Are Human Rights universal? The debate between
universal and culturally contextual human rights. Postmodernist positions on human rights.
Human Rights in the Contemporary International System.
Documents:
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The accompanying covenants on Civil & Political and Economic,
Social & Cultural Rights.
Geneva Conventions
International Humanitarian Law
Implementing Human Rights in International practice
Structure of the UN and its bodies involved in protection of human rights.
What is the relationship between State sovereignty and international protection of human rights. Case studies in
human rights as a bargaining chip in international politics.
Humanitarian Intervention
Debate between humanitarian intervention and State sovereignty. Humanitarian Intervention as a foreign policy
practice. The Kosovo Case. Relationship between preemptive war and protection of human rights. Post 9/11 US
Security Strategy.
International Criminal Court: Origin, Institutionalization and operation.
Concept of Justice. Theoretical Foundations. Utilitarianism. Rawls Theory of Justice. Justice as the foundation for
human rights. Right to Development and democracy. Right to Development using the Singur Land Movement as
case study.

Course No: HS5561
Course Name: Introduction to Cultural Anthropology
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The goal of cultural anthropology is to understand how people in different places produce
cultural, economic, and symbolic systems that regulate their lives. During this class we will learn about the cultural
practices of people around the world, in order to broaden our understanding of how culture
structures and patterns the lives of different groups, and to gain a better understanding of ourselves. We will begin
by looking closely at the concept of culture as the central theme in anthropology, and how culture patterns human
behaviour. We will also look at the historical development of social and economic systems, the role of language in
culture, and various systems of political power.
Course Content:
Modules
1. What is culture? – In this, we will cover the basic understanding of culture as a
set of theoretical lenses.
2. Comparative cultures: In this set of sessions, we look at the ways in which cultures
might radically differ from each other
3. Anthropology and Culture: In this module, we examine the discipline of anthropology and its relationship to
understanding society and culture
4. Kinship, power, structure, and language: This set of sessions introduces the students to the primary theories of
cultural anthropology.
5. Ethnographic research methods: The last set of sessions will involve introducing the students to the research
methods of cultural anthropology

Course No: HS5570
Course Name: Governing AI
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course is an introduction to the challenges of Governing what is likely to be the most transformative of all
technologies to date, the AI. The underlying assumption is that governing the decentralized crypto-AI fusion world
that is emerging, is everyone’s - at least every higher educated person’s - responsibility. We therefore take a
‘humanities’ approach - implying a multi-faceted, nevertheless integrated, framework that incorporates views from
the Economics, History, International Relations, Jurisprudence & Legal, Literature, Mythology, Philosophy, Politics,
Religion and other Social Science academic traditions.
Course Content:
1. AI - the optimistic, realistic and pessimistic outlooks and their rationale.
2. The associated literature on AI ‘risk’, ‘safety’ & ‘alignment’.
3. The likely exponential growth of unpredictable social media issues of misinformation and disinformation - in the

Course No: HS5601
Course Name: Historicizing Literature
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course fundamentally aims to situate literature in a historical context and explores the dynamic and
complementary relationship between history and literature, historicity and textuality. Through a reading of
representative texts, the course will critically demonstrate how historical conditions, narratives, and documentation
affect or amplify the readings and locations of literature and vice versa. Examining the continuities, departures,
and interactions between the two categories, the course introduces the learners to contemporary theories and
concepts that are informing, altering, and challenging the definitions and forms of history and literature.
Accordingly, literature will also be examined as a site of historical recovery, countering erasure, forgetting, and
disappearance. The course, thus, will equip the students to draw on contemporary theoretical engagements that
foreground and unpack the intersection between history and literature. At the end of the course the learners will be
able to critically, chronologically, philosophically, and culturally engage with the diverse modes of interactions that
these two categories have had particularly in the last few decades.
Course Content:
New historicism and cultural materialism
Textuality and historicity – ‘return to history’ movement in literary criticism
Representations of history and power in literary works
Narratives and counternarratives of the Empire
Narrativising gender and race
History, culture, and literature
The narrative turn in historiography
Narratives of trauma, silence, and survival
Remembered histories and memory-narratives
Literature and events
Literature as history, Literature and history, literature in history
Digital storytelling and historical narratives
Text Books:
LaCapra, Dominick. History, Literature, Critical Theory. Cornell University, 2013.
Spargo, Tamsin. Reading the Past, Literature and History. Macmillan Education UK, 2000.
White, Hayden. The Content of the Form: Narrative discourse and Historical Representation. Johns Hopkins
University Press, 1987.

Bruhn, Mark J., and Donald R. Wehrs, ed. Cognition, Literature, and History. Routledge, 2014.

Course No: HS5602
Course Name: The Arc of the Renaissance
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course aims at understanding the Renaissance or the revival of classical learning in Europe over a period of
five centuries which brought about unprecedented changes in the worldview of thinkers from the feudalistic and
monarchic systems to that of individualistic and democratic systems in religion, philosophy, education, arts, and
other areas of life. It will discuss the role of logic and observation which were used to study nature, society, and
self for the welfare of humanity as a whole. Further, it will examine the innovative processes of exploration and
discovery as well as the development of vernacular languages and literatures to their fullest potential, leading to
the flowering of literature in the Elizabethan period in England. While the course will focus on the origin and spread
of the Renaissance in different parts of Europe, it will primarily analyze seminal texts that constitute the English
Renaissance literature with the hindsight of contemporary critical insights into the Renaissance.
Course Content:
• Origin and the spread of the Renaissance in Europe
• Realistic representation of English society in tales
• The significance of rhetorical paradox
• Ideal love and the sonnet sequence
• Allegory of love and the state in epic form
• Critique of the Renaissance ideal in dramatic art form
• Assertion of individualism and the rise of capitalism
• Contemporary perspectives on the Renaissance

Course No: HS5603
Course Name: The Novel and Change
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course seeks to critically map the discourse of change in the literary genre of the novel in significant works
across historical periods and geographical locales. The course therefore embeds the novel firmly within the social
relations, economics, cultures and politics from which it emerged to reflect and construct/reconstruct responses
towards concerns affecting individual liberty and fulfilment, and thereby influencing change in society. The course
enquires into the literary figuration of change and its negotiation of attitudes towards a range of issues such as
race, gender, class, colonialism and other systems of inequity. The course will offer a representative selection for
analysis a selection of novels that adopt various methods to engage with the discourse of change.
Students will understand the major perspectives, approaches, and arguments that underpin the novel of change,
and perceive that novel writing itself is a form of social practice.

Course No: HS5605
Course Name: LANGUAGE AND SOCIETY
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Objectives: This course introduces the fundamental concepts that link language and society, and it deals with the
interrelationship of language with social factors (both internal and external) such as class, gender, ethnicity, and
age, including how language varies and changes. It underlines the complex relationship between language and
society; introduces nuances of language learning (acquisition) and structure (sounds, words, and sentences); and
explores the relation of language to national and individual identity and the degree to which a society’s culture may
manifest itself in its language and influence the world view of its speakers. The close parallels between variation
and the use of two or more languages (multilingualism) will be drawn, including discussion of language attitudes,
language planning, and language contact (code-switching/mixing of languages).
Outcomes: This course provides an opportunity to observe language in its social context. This course provides
tools to look deeper into both language and society with the help of the mechanism of speech as well as the
process of learning. It will enable participants to see how language shapes the way we conceive the world around
us in communication.
Course Content:
Course Contents:
Fundamental Concepts in the study of language and society: Language (Sounds, words, sentences, and
discourse); Language as a System; Design Features; Language and Culture; Language and Gender; Language
and Identity
Multilingual speech communities: Languages and dialects; National languages and language planning; Diglossia;
Linguistic minorities, Code-switching and Code-mixing (translanguaging)
Language(s) of India: Linguistic Diversity of India; The Eighth Schedule and Official language(s); English in
Multilingualism India; Language ‘choice’, language loss and endangerment; language maintenance
Language and Variations: Sociolinguistic theories of language variation (Labov-Martha Vinyad, Social Stratification
of English in New York City); language and globalization
Language and communication: Social networks; Ethnography of communication; style and register; speech
functions and politeness; cross-cultural communication and pragmatics; accommodation theory; discourse
analysis; language and the media.
Text Books:
Downes, William. Language and Society. Cambridge University Press, 1998.
Montgomery, Martin. An Introduction to Language and Society. Routledge, 2008.
Trudgill, Peter (2000). Sociolinguistics: An Introduction to Language and Society. Penguin, 2000.
Reference Books:
Dube, Shyama Charan. Indian Society. National Book Trust India, 1992.

Romaine, Suzanne. Language in Society: An Introduction to Sociolinguistics. Oxford University Press, 2000.

Thomas, Linda, and Shan Wareing. Language, Society and Power: An Introduction. Routledge, 2004.
Wardhaugh, Ronalde. An Introduction to Sociolinguistics. Blackwell Publishers, 1999.

Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The rich legacy of Romanticism has contributed a wealth of ideas about nature and the powers of imagination,

Course No: HS5607
Course Name: Victorian Realism
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course offers a critical introduction to the notion of realism that is manifest in the literary works of the major
writers of the Victorian period in Great Britain. It explores the contested discourse of realism in literature produced
by culturally diverse figures of the period. Embedding the literature in the rapidly changing socio-cultural systems
wrought about by radical material and social shifts such as industrialization, social mobility, colonization, and
empire, the course teases out the tendencies, and implications of the denotation and connotation of narrative
realism such as omniscient narration, vernacular markers, the panoramic, and the microscopic that mark the
literary genres of the time.
The student will understand the various approaches and understandings of the term literary realism, as well as the
links between the ordinary, the middle class, the new woman, the metropolis, and the form of the realist literary
narrative.
Course Content:
Contemporary Life and Fiction
Journalism, Publishing Market, and the Realist Text
Plotting and characterizing Realism
Representation, revelation, and suspense
Social Realism and Narration
Victorian Feminism and New Woman Realism.
Domestic and Gothic Realism
Anti-Realist Elements in Realist Literature.
“Aesthetic Racism”: Realism and its critiques
Neo-Victorianism and Realism

Course Name: 20th Century Modernisms
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course explores the idea of the ‘modern’ through select texts between 1900 and 1950. It will help cultivate
among students a sense of literary and artistic appreciation and the ability to critically evaluate a wide range of
texts from the first half of the 20th century. Students will be directed to recognize the tensions between specific
texts and the artists’ imagination. They will be able to identify the ‘modern’ in literature and art and locate it in the
social, historical and material temper of the 20th century. The course will introduce the participants to writers from
Samuel Beckett to Bertolt Brecht; Joseph Conrad to D. H. Lawrence; James Joyce to Virginia Woolf; Ezra Pound
to W. B. Yeats; August Strindberg to T.S. Eliot; William Faulkner to Ernest Hemingway; Marcel Proust to Franz
Kafka; Hart Crane to e.e. cummings; Sigmund Freud to Gertrude Stein; and Jean Cocteau to Jackson Pollock.
Students will be familiarized with the major transformations in Western artistic, literary and intellectual
developments of the 20th century. They will learn appreciating the language, style and aesthetics of the key artists
of this period.
Course Content:

Avant-garde

Formalism, Futurism, Naturalism, Rationalization and Enchantment, Stream of consciousness, Imagism, Vorticism
• Modernism and Cities in Fiction: Berlin, Vienna, Prague, St. Petersburg, London, Chicago and New York
• Modernism and Literature: Key writers and texts
• Modernism and its Afterlife: Crises of values, The Anxiety of Influence, The Literature of Exhaustion,
Postmodernism

Course No: HS5612
Course Name: Contexts, Politics, and Ideas: An Introduction to Ideologies
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
a)To provide an understanding of the ways political actions and events are informed by ideas of the state, of
political membership, and of human action.
(b).To equip the students with the knowledge to evaluate political events and developments in the light of the
ideologies covered, and to evaluate the ideologies in application to political or other appropriate events.
Course Content:
2.Course Content: Eleven major ideologies, grouped into four modules, roughly by historical period and
progression of the ideas concerned. Each ideology will be set in brief historical context; the main ideas it
expresses will be supported with examples. Each ideology will be evaluated with examples from current South
Asian and international political issues, using appropriate academic papers and books.
Module 1: Fascism, Conservatism, and Liberalism. The rise of modern fascism since the mid-19th century. How
conservatism expresses respect for the past without becoming fascist, but then faces the challenge of liberal ideas
of democracy, rights, and the market.
Module 2: Marx and Marxism, Anarchism, and Feminism. Marx’s main ideas, and some of the problems Marxist
movements face in practice. Non-violent anarchism as starting from a similar point to Marxism but as reaching
very different conclusions. Feminism: a challenge which cuts across other ideologies to ensure that women’s
position and participation have their rightful place in ideologies and in political life.
Module 3: Ecologism, Postmodernism and Poststructuralism. The kinds of challenges the global environmental
condition poses to previous ideologies and patterns of production and consumption; possible responses including
different economic and political systems. Postmodernism and Poststructuralism covers the challenges posed by
the failures of previous ideologies as well as the possibility that the very idea of systematic ideologies needs to be
abandoned.
Module 4: Theocracy and Fundamentalism, Technocracy and Managerialism, Republicanism and Citizenship. In
the first case, an attempt is made to take over the democratic space by claiming a form of unquestionable religious
authority. In the second case the respective claims are to technocratic and managerialist knowledge as political
authority. The concluding topic examines the adaptation of Athenian theories of republican democracy and
citizenship for today’s times. The idea of citizenship as informed judgment has been vigorously debated in political
theory over the last 25 years or so, and has also featured in significant Indian writings over the period.
Text Books:
Heywood, A. 2012. Political Ideologies: an Introduction, 5th ed. Houndmills: Palgrave Macmillan.
Srivastava, S. 2012. An Introduction to Political Ideologies. New York: Pearson
Reference Books:
Bellamy, R. 2000. Rethinking Liberalism. London: Pinter.

Economic and Political Weekly 45 (9): 46–53.

Course No: HS5613
Course Name: Modern Indian Drama
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The objectives of the course are to familiarize students with representative modern Indian plays in the
Post-Independent period with a focus on experimental plays, including absurd drama and epic theatre, translated
into English and also originally written in English; to appreciate the perspectives of women playwrights on the
challenges facing Indian society; and to understand the socio-economic processes that have contributed to the
making of modern Indian drama.
Outcomes:
After doing the course, students will be able to understand the need for Indian drama reflecting Indian concerns
after the Indian Independence, to analyse the elements of drama, including theme, plot, characterization, setting,
spectacle, technical devices, and to write reviews of dramatic texts and theatrical performances. They will also be
able to understand how different people behave in various situations because of the conscious and unconscious
pressures that operate on and within them through the analysis of characters and motives, as presented by the
playwrights.

Course No: HS5614
Course Name: Media Culture and Society
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course is designed to help students build their understanding of the role of mediated communication in
contemporary societies. Students will be made aware of social, cultural and political impact of mediated
communication in globalized times.
Course Content:
Modules
A. Theories of Media
1. Media theories: We will cover the basic understanding of media as a social force and modes through which it
can be analyzed.
2. Analyzing media, power and control: Explicit connections will be made between media production and content
management and forms of power and control in society
B. Visual Culture: We will examine how visual culture can be analyzed in continuity with visual arts while evolving
its own language in the context of modern media.
C. Media Instruments
1. TV & Radio: This module will examine the evolution of television and radio both in terms of the politics of
invention and production as well as the ways in which they distinguish themselves from other media channels.
2. Print media: In this section, we will make explicit the connections between literacy, nationalism, and print
media.
3. Internet and new media: In this module, we track the emergence of new media and internet cultures in relation
to youth, identity, and questions of copyright and distribution
D. Media and cultural globalization: The last module will bring together all of the above concerns within the
umbrella rubric of cultural globalization. Here we tackle questions of homogeneity as well as difference.

Course No: HS5615
Course Name: Poverty and Inequality
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course offers an interdisciplinary exploration of poverty and development, emphasising the reasons why
some countries succeed in reducing poverty and fostering development while others do not. A key focus is the
political economy of development, examining both theoretical and practical perspectives on poverty and
development. The course delves into the political and economic motivations that influence governments' efforts
toward development and poverty reduction, with a particular emphasis on global South. Additionally, the course
explores the connection between poverty and various factors, including inequality, urbanization, population growth,
violence, and democracy.
Course Content:
• Gain an understanding of development and its various forms
• Critically assess the distinctions between poverty reduction and development
• Analyse the interconnections between poverty, inequality, and economic growth
• Evaluate the relationship between poverty and factors such as violence, health, democratisation, urbanisation,
and demographics
Thematic topics:
o Evolution of conceptual notions on poverty
o Capabilities and human development
o Poverty and famines
o Population and development
o Poverty and health
o Poverty, inequality and growth
o Urbanisation and urban bias
o Poverty and violence
o Poverty and democracy
o Aid, SDGs and poverty reduction
o Poverty Measurement

Course No: HS5640
Course Name: Advanced Linguistics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course offers a view of human language as a rule governed system. It deals with how language is learnt and
how human mind deals with the underling structure of language. This course introduces components of linguistics
theory in generative framework. To understand advanced ideas in linguistic theory for appreciating language at the
level of sounds (Phonetics/Phonology), words (Morphology), sentences (Syntax), and cognition and use of
language (Sociolinguistics/Pragmatics).
Course Content:
Acquisition
How do we learn first language? A theoretical Overview; Competence and performance (Form vs. Function); How
language is constitutive of being human?; Critical period hypothesis;
Phonetics/Phonology/Morphology
IPA (International Phonetic Association) Chart; Acoustics and Articulatory Phonetics; Phonology and Assimilation;
Natural Class and Distinctive Features of Sounds; Superasegmental Features; Phonotactic Constraints in Word
Formation;
Sociolinguistics
Homogeneous and heterogeneous perspectives on language (Fluidity of language); Theoretical understanding of
language families and linguistic area; What is the nature of language variation and language change?
Cognition and Culture
How does multilingualism correlate with scholastic achievement, cognitive flexibility and social tolerance?
Syntax
Order of Words in Sentence (Subject-Object-Verb); What makes a sentence?; X-bar Theory (Specifiers vs.
Complements, Arguments vs. Adjuncts); Theta-Theory; Theta Role Assignment; Case Theory (Abstract, Inherent,
and Morphological Case, Exceptional Case Marking, Nominative-Accusative vs. Ergative-Absolutive patterns);
Raising Movement (A-Movement); Movement in Passives; A-bar-Movement (Wh-Movement, Constraints on A-bar
Movements; Binding Theory (Conditions A, B, and C, Role of Structural Relationships such as C-command,
Locality, Binding Domains); Constraints on Movement

Course No: HS5651
Course Name: American Literature & Culture
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course aims to understand the United States through the landmarks of its literature and popular culture. It
endeavors to inculcate in students an appreciation of canonical American writers and texts, along with the literary
history and culture of the United States. It attempts to foster an understanding of the development of various
forms, themes and theoretical underpinnings in select works of American literature and its iconic artists. Students
will learn to appreciate and engage with seminal texts of American literature and culture. They will become
familiar with the intersections between American literature and important historical, socio-cultural and theoretical
developments.
Course Content:
• American Transcendentalism: Emerson and Thoreau, German and British influence, Contemporary relevance
• American Romanticism: American idealism, Humanitarianism, Individualism, Democratic ideals, the Dark
Romantics
• American Literary Realism and Naturalism: Epistemology, Social realism, Detachment, Objectivity
• Ethnic writings and American literature: Race, gender, society, cultural shifts, Jewish writings, the Harlem
Renaissance, Asian-American writings
• American Modernism: Artistic movements, literary genres-novel, drama, poetry, cities and spaces, the ‘Modern’
hero, the Lost Generation, the Jazz Age
• American Postmodernism: Irony, self-referentiality, pastiche, hyper-reality, Abstract Expressionism, pop artists
• American Counterculture and Music : Beat aesthetics, the Civil Rights movement, Feminist writings, the
authentic ‘self’, the road trip novels, Woodstock, rock music, the Vietnam War and responses to the war
• Cult TV shows: Sitcoms, soap operas, ‘prestige’ dramas, remakes, themes, ideology, performance, stardom, TV
shows post- The Sopranos
• Globalization and the American popular culture: The global reach of American popular culture, MTV and beyond
, pulp fiction, the bestsellers, the post-America world
Text Books:

Course No: HS5652
Course Name: Language, Cognition and Computation
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course fosters a broad and integrated approach to understand the cognitive and computational study of
language. Some of the questions that the course explores are ‘How do children learn and develop language?’,
‘Why and how does human mind compute language?’, ‘How does technology drive language evolution?’, and
‘How do humans understand a word, a sentence, or a series of conversation?’. Taking insights from a diverse
group of linguistic disciplines, this interdisciplinary course bridges the gap between structure of language, its social
foundations on one hand and natural language processing and cognitive modelling on the other.
The course will help the students build foundations for research capabilities in the areas related to language,
cognition, and computation at an advanced level. And the interdisciplinary nature of the course will also facilitate
them develop the ability to integrate concepts and ideas related to human brain and language faculty into a
broader logical framework of analysis.
Course Content:
The landscape of Linguistics: Miracles of Human language; Knowledge of language; Expressive power of linguistic
theories; Competence-Performance distinction (Form vs. Function)
Structure of Language: Structure of sounds, words, and sentences; acquisition of pragmatic, cultural and/or
communicative competence in a language; Formal linguistic theories and crosslinguistic variation; Functional
categories and parametric variation; Pragmatic and cultural components in speaking and interaction
Language and Cognition: Formal mechanisms of Language and ‘Human’ mind; Theories of language acquisition;
Linguistic relativity; Mentalese; Language of Thought Hypothesis (LOTH); Cognition with (or without) language;
Language perception, memory, and Consciousness; Neural mechanisms of cognitive processing
Language and Computation: Understanding computability; Theories of Language & Computation; Differences
between Human and Machine Learning; Fundamentals of NLP & AI; Computational principles of syntax; Language
Learning vs. Deep learning; Analysing data (words, sentences and meaning); Experiments in Linguistics

Course No: HS5653
Course Name: Literatures of the Anthropocene
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The Anthropocene- a term coined by Eugene Stormer in the 1980s and popularized by Paul Crutzen in the 2000s
refers to a new geological epoch in which human actions have irreparably affected the planet. The questions that
this course will engage with are: How do we define nature in the Anthropocene? How can ecocriticism find new
ways of responding to this planetary tragedy which poses both a conceptual and representational challenge? The
course offers accessible discussions of prominent ecocritical theories to emphasize notions of interconnection and
entanglement (with a focus on new materialism, environmental justice and postcolonialism) and a wide spectrum
of the literatures of Anthropocene literature that have strong ethical and political implications.
The course will introduce the student to environmentally oriented narratives from the West as well as Global South
Anthropocene narratives.
Course Content:
Anthropocene Contexts:
The Anthropocene: Questions of definition
The Anthropocene as a new planetary condition
The Anthropocene in literary and cultural studies
The Anthropocene: Human and non-human entanglements
The Anthropocene and Ecocriticism
Ecocriticism Contexts and Positions:
‘Waves’ of Ecocriticism and their characteristics
Affective Ecocriticism, Postcolonial Ecocriticism, Material Ecocriticism, Environmental Justice Ecocriticism,
Ecofeminism, Deep Ecology, Zoocriticism, Phytocriticism
Anthropocene Genres:
The Eco-graphic novel, Petrofiction, Eco-speculation, Climate fiction, Solarpunk, the Eco-gothic, Extractivist
narratives, Anthropocene Life Writings, Eco-Fear Narratives, Hydrofiction narratives, Nuclear narratives,
Solastalgia narratives, Prospect poetry

Course No: HS5654
Course Name: Literature, Technology and Medicine
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course aims to introduce students to specialized and advanced interpretative and investigative frameworks to
engage with literary and cultural structures that have informed the understanding of contemporary notions and
practices of technology and medicine. With a multidisciplinary perspective this course critically engages with the
binaries between literature and technology, literature and medicine, and foregrounds the discursive connections
between and across disciplinary boundaries. The course locates literature as a site of narrative, history, and
performance while also connecting it to relevant technological and medical vectors that have played major roles in
determining its form, reception, and circulation at diverse historical periods. Drawing on a range of philosophical
theories on the body and the mind this course provides multiple entry points for the learner to pursue a more
advanced understanding of the rich scholarship on medical and technological discourses while also identifying
historically pertinent literary and cultural narratives. The learning outcome of this course will enable
multidisciplinary possibilities and will facilitate dialogues between and across various interfaces of literature,
technology, and medicine.
Course Content:
The integration of humanities with technological and medical discourses
The mediation of technology in human-human and human-machine interactions
Technoscience, Medical aesthetics
Knowledge systems and cultures of medicine
History and narratives of epidemics
Narrative medicine
Narrative and illness
Medicine, media, and technology
Narrativity and Interactivity
Medicine as performance
Narratives of technological progress in medicine
Technology and human body

Theory
Description:
This course will focus on standard theories, practices, and conventions in editing and publishing with the aim of
presenting one’s work in scholarly academic circles as well for a general educated audience. The learners,
through practice sessions, will be trained in the discipline of professional and academic writing, drawing on
relevant scholarship. The classroom training includes experiential learning through the methods of close reading,
re-reading, collaborative work, extensive peer review and discussion. The practice-based sessions will have a
strong emphasis on grammar, technical aspects of editing, and a thorough understanding of ethical, theoretical,
and practical considerations. In the process, the learners will also be trained in techniques such as attention to
style, register, and correctness. At the end of the course the students will be familiar with latest professional
development resources and databases that assist in the process of editing. The learning outcome of the course
will include developing the skills and practical knowledge required in editing and publishing in literary studies
through hands-on experience. The course will also enable students to pursue careers in professional editing and
publishing and will include suitable engagements with industry-oriented learning.
Course Content:
Introduction to history of editing and publishing, introduction to print culture
Standard requirements and expectations in different domains/disciplines
The editorial triangle – Writer, editor, reader
Developing criteria for evaluation - Communicating to the intended audience
Digital tools and their impact
Developing editorial skills - Checking and avoiding/prevent Plagiarism - Editing for tone, editing for space, editing
for correctness - Proof Reading – difference between copyediting and proofreading - The importance of fact
checking
Condensation and rewriting, identifying jargons/unfamiliar words and expressions, careless abbreviations
Grammatical and structural aspects of editing - language, style, spelling, punctuation, authenticity, reference,
paragraph breaks, headings, sub heads
Developing a manuscript – types, purpose, relevance. Preparing an Index The meaning and scope of Royalty.
Trends and opportunities in publishing

Course Name: Indian Writing in English
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of writings produced in English in India since 19th
century and will introduce the learners to the literary ground covered in major literary histories, anthologies, and
critical discussions. The course will engage with representative works from genres such as fiction, drama, poetry,
prose and will suitably include categories such as travel writing, diasporic writing, women writing, and nation
writing. The course will cover the historical and literary origins and trajectory of this body of writing. Given the
context of IWE’s emergence and growth, this course will also highlight the interactions between English and other
Indian languages and related debates. The course, through a detailed historiographical reading, will foreground the
global attention and critical acclaim that Indian Writing in English has received in the last few decades. The
learners will also be familiarized with discourses related to literary market conditions, global trends in publishing,
and the politics of canon formation. The course will thus provide a thorough historiographical and critical
foundation to Indian Writing in English and will train the learners to read specific works within current critical
frameworks such as postcolonialism, feminism, memory studies, modernity studies.

Indian drama Post-Independence
Women writers from the 19th century onwards
Writings by the Indian diaspora
Nation building and (re)writing of history
English vs. Bhasha writing debates
Indian English writing, readership, and criticism
The city in Indian writing in English
Writings from the margins, the categories of gender, caste, and region
Post-1980s global recognition and narratives of cosmopolitanism
Indian graphic novel

Course No: HS5657
Course Name: Fashion Studies: Literature, Cinema & Society
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Objectives: The course explores the ways in which fashion 'performs' in a wide range of texts. It will examine the
interconnected worlds of fashion, literature, cinema and society, and provide perspectives from socio-cultural,
historical and theoretical readings of fashion. Covering a range of genres and periods, this course will analyze how
dress communicates and engages in meanings across different social groups, cultures and contexts. The course
aims to help students learn how fashion dictates and bends rules in society. They will also become familiar with
key figures, texts, icons, imagery and concepts in this domain. Tangible outcomes would be that students will
become familiar with various trends in world fashion and their impact on cinema, literature and society. They will
understand the socio-cultural and historical contexts of clothes, and different perspectives on fashion and style.
They will be able to discuss, analyze and write about fashion traditions, practices and trends.
Course Content:
• Fashion and its historical context: This section will trace the evolution of fashion down the ages — from the
courts of the Tudors (Henry VIII, Elizabeth I), the Restoration Age, the Georgian Age, the Victorian era, the
Edwardian Age— and consider the fashion trends represented in literature of these periods.
• Fashion Theory: Fashion as a system of signs, the semiotics and codes of fashion, and the way in which clothes
and accessories articulate meanings of race, class, gender and social hierarchies.
• Fashion and icons: This segment will focus on iconic figures in literature, cinema and society; also, how certain
stars gain recognition as fashion icons.
• Fashion and the Costume Drama: Costumes and representation of history and historical events on screen
• Fashion and adaptation: The ways in which fashion is foregrounded when texts are adapted from page to
screen.
• Fashion, gender and performativity: How fashion and clothing are intertwined in creating a gendered-structure
of society; and how fashion generates and alters identity based on gender-based relations in a society.
• Fashion and fashion designers: Films, TV shows, documentaries about fashion designers
• Fashion and popular culture: Iconic TV shows that shaped popular views on fashion and style; Music videos,
MTV; fashion and rock stars.
• Fashion and society: How fashion engages in dialogue with society; counterculture and fashion; gothic; grunge
aesthetics; street fashion; fashion in Bollywood; altered landscapes; sustainable fashion.
• The Spectacle of fashion: Great fashion houses and trends; modes of production; global brands; fashion at
award functions; film festivals; the red carpet look ; fashion magazines; fashion in times of social media.

Course No: HS5658
Course Name: Literature and Rhetoric
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
In the present time of mass media and communication, rhetoric (oral, written, visual and nonverbal) has a power
over humans more than ever before. The course introduces the students to the study of persuasion in both written
and spoken word and helps them understand ways of encoding and decoding. Starting with ancient rhetoricians
through Middle Ages and early modern period, the course traverses the realms of contemporary theory and places
rhetoric in a cross-cultural context. Beginning with primary rhetoric of persuasion in civic life, the course moves to
secondary rhetoric in discourse, literature and art forms.
It seeks to decode the ideological and political fingerprints of literature as well as everyday cultural practices that
includes an engagement with omissions and silences. It will train students to make sense of meanings by
analysing texts and the context in which they are produced and consumed. It is also aimed at appreciating the
function of rhetoric in our cultural lives and equipping the students with the tools to understand the social function
of rhetoric.
Course Content:
Introduction to Rhetoric: State, democracy, education, religion and law
Greek rhetoric: Homer, Plato, Sophists, Aristotle
Roman rhetoric: Cicero, Demetrius, Longinus, polemicists
Rhetoric and their diffusion in Middle Ages
Renaissance and neoclassical rhetoric
Rhetorical methods: Study and Practice
Rhetoric, art and aesthetics
Rhetoric and literary criticism
Rhetoric and discourse analysis
Rhetoric and contemporary critical theory
Indian rhetoric: reason, omniscience and authority, audience
Nyaya and Pramana

Theory
Description:
This course aims to present an interdisciplinary inquiry into human body, embodiment, and literature, examining

Course No: HS5661
Course Name: Literature and Social Justice
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course will explore the ideal of social justice as ‘represented’ in contemporary literature in order to understand
the persistent call for social justice around the world. It will trace the development of justice from a theocentric
framework to a human-centered as well as an earth-centered concept of social justice and examine the noble
ideals of democracy, equality, liberty, fraternity, fairness, virtue, tolerance, etc., which continue to face challenges
from time to time for various reasons, including business. It will examine select literary texts, including novels, from
different socio-economic and political contexts, focusing on race, gender, class, region, etc., so as to gain a
broader understanding of social systems and processes that continue to impede the achievement of social justice
for all sections of the society. The course will combine various aspects of race, gender, class, region, the earth,
etc., under the umbrella of social justice with the underpinning of comparative literature, intersectionality and the
ethical turn in critical studies.
Course Content:
• Theories of justice and social justice
• Racial oppression
• Gender sensitivity
• Colonial hierarchies
• Postcolonial subversions and assertions
• Environmental justice
• Dystopian visions
• The impact of globalization on developing societies

Course No: HS5679
Course Name: Tarka Sangraha - Fundamentals of Indian Logic
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Tarka Shastra, also known as nyaya-vaisheshika system, is the most essential science of logical reasoning in
ancient
India that probes the nature of valid knowledge and the means to obtain valid knowledge. Tarka Shastra contains a
detailed exposition on inductive and deductive reasoning. While the vyakarana (grammar) helps in the precision of
language, Tarka helps in the preciseness of thought. Therefore, it is considered as the gateway to studying all
other
Indian shastras. It is also deemed as a very powerful tool of dialectics that helps to build sound logical reasoning
through a systematic classification and analysis of the nature. In this course, the students will be introduced to the
foundational principles of Tarka Shastra through readings from the fundamental treatise called ‘Tarka Sangraha’
composed by Annambhatta in the seventh century. The course assumes no prerequisites. Ability to read and write
Devanagari is a must. Prior knowledge of Sanskrit is a plus.
Course Content:
1. Seven categories namely substance, quality, etc
2. Classification of dravya (substances)
3. Classification of Gunas (qualities)
4. Knowledge and its nature (jñana?)
5. Means/evidence of obtaining valid knowledge (prama?a?)
6. pratyaksaprama?a? (Direct observation evidence), anumanaprama?a? (inferential evidence), sabdaprama?a?
(evidence of verbal testimony), upamanaprama?a? (evidence of comparison)
7. Exposition of the remaining gunas (quality) and categories.
Text Books:
No prescribed textbook. All the materials will be made available in the class.
Reference Books:
https://ia600306.us.archive.org/22/items/Complete_Works_of_Jibananda_Vidyasagara/Tarkasangraha_English_Tr
ans
lation_-_Jivananda_Vidyasagara_1872.pdf
https://sanskritdocuments.org/scannedbooks/ebooks/Tarka-SangrahaReprint.pdf

Theory

Course No: HS5702
Course Name: Macroeconomics 1
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
In this course, the functioning of the aggregate economy is analyzed starting from basic aggregate data
measurement and concepts. The course moves to the classical macro equilibrium for an open economy. This
course takes both a short and a long-term view of the economy, and aims to help students analyze how modern
macroeconomics can shed light on facts such as business cycles, economic growth, unemployment and money.
Outcomes: With an exposure to performance evaluation measures, methods and their applications using real life
data points, students will have a fair level of confidence to apply these knowledge to their own field of
study/research.
Course Content:
1. Measuring Key Macroeconomic Variables: Various Concepts and Measurements of Aggregate Income –
Income, Expenditure and the Circular Flow – Rules for Computing GDP – Real vs. Nominal GDP – Measuring the
Cost of Living (consumer and whole sale price indices) – Measuring the Unemployment Rate – Unemployment,
GDP and the Okun’s Law.
2. Theories of Consumption: The Classical Views on Consumption – The Psychological Law of Consumption –
Kuznets’s Consumption Puzzle – Fisher’s Inter-temporal Choice Model – Permanent Income Hypothesis – Life
Cycle Hypothesis
3. Theories of Investment: The Neoclassical Theory of Investment – Capital Theory and Theory of the Firm –
Finance and the Cost of Capital – The Accelerator Theory of Investment – The Stock Market and Tobin’s Q –
Inflation and Investment – Policies affecting Investment.
4. IS-LM model (closed economy): The Neoclassical and Keynesian macroeconomic models-The interaction of
real and monetary models-the Neoclassical and Keynesian version of IS-LM model-fiscal and monetary analysis in

Course No: HS5703
Course Name: Statistical Inference
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course is intended to provide an in-depth understanding of the quantitative tools available with us for
analyzing any statistical data points. Presuming that the students already have knowledge of basic descriptive
statistics tools, we will confine ourselves only to discussion on statistical inferences in this course. Clear
demonstration of theoretical concepts along with real life examples will substantiate the understanding of the
students in the subject matter.
Outcomes:
Students will have exposure to the foundational statistical measures using which they can analyze any statistical
data to extract the hidden important information out of it. They can also successfully draw statistical
predictions/inferences using scientific methods. They can do so, of course, including in their own research/project
dissertations.
Course Content:
(a) Theory of Probability: Elements of probability theory: classical and axiomatic definitions of probability, standard
theorems, conditional probability, independence, Bayes’ theorem; discrete random variables—hypergeometric,
binomial, negative binomial, and Poisson distributions; continuous random variables—normal, uniform, and
gamma distributions; moment generating function and characteristic function; bivariate distribution, marginal
probabilities, correlation; bivariate normal distribution and its properties; convergence on probability space,
Chebysev’s inequality, law of large numbers and central limit theorem.
(b) Estimation: Standard sampling distributions: t and F distributions and their properties. Estimation of
parameters: basic concepts—parameter and statistics, estimator and estimate, sampling distribution, sampling
variance and mean squared error, properties of an estimator—unbiasedness, consistency, efficiency, sufficiency;
Cramer-Rao inequality, point and interval estimations.
(c) Testing of hypotheses: Type I and II errors, level, size and power of a test, testing hypotheses about the mean
and the variance of a normal population.
(d) Classical linear regression model: Assumptions, ordinary least squares (OLS) and maximum likelihood
methods of estimation, properties of OLS and ML estimators, tests of significance of the parameters, and ANOVA.
Text Books:
1. An Introductory to Probability Theory and Mathematical Statistics, V.K. Rohatgi, 1976.
2. Introduction to Statistical Theory, P.G. Hoel, S.C. Port and C.J. Stone, 1971.
5. Introduction to Theory of Statistics, A.M. Mood, F.A. Graybill and D.C. Boes, 2017.
6. Statistical Inference, G. Casella and R.L. Berger, 2002
Reference Books:
1. Any Probability Statistics/Inferential Statistics Book by Paul G. Hoel or Paul G. Hoel along with some other
co-author(s), Any Edition.

Course Name: Mathematical Economics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course covers a wide range of mathematical methods in applied economics. Specifically, it aims to provide the
basics of mathematical methods and the range of mathematical techniques that used to explain various applied

makers make decision.
4. They can able to demonstrate most of the theories in economics precisely and strategically.

Course Content:

Concept of a function; Limits, continuity and differentiability of a real valued function; Convex and concave
functions, Differentiation- Partial and total; Interpretation of partial derivatives. Optimization with single and
multivariable functions- Unconstrained and constrained optimization in simple economic problems.
Integration-simple and Definite, Applications to Economic variables

difference equations; Differential Equations, The lagged Keynesian Macroeconomic models.

and simplex method; Concept of duality and statement of duality theorems; Formulation of the Dual and its
interpretation.
Module 5
Game Theory: an introduction. Dominated and Dominant Strategies: The Prisoner‘s Dilemma, mixed strategy
Nash Equilibrium; Saddle point solution; Simple applications to economics.

Course No: HS5706
Course Name: Microeconomics 2
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course is intended to provide an in-depth understanding of the behavior of economic agents, however, more
advanced level topics of Microeconomics. Exposure of how the price and quantities of an entire economy is
determined will also be given to the students using fundamental concepts of general equilibrium analysis. Other
relatively modern topics of Microeconomic theories will also be discussed.
Outcomes: Students will be knowledgeable enough on the advanced and modern Microeconomics theoretical
concepts catered with the topics—as detailed below in the course content. It will equip them to understand the real
life economic phenomena more rigorously and will be confident enough to engage upon even theoretical further
advanced learning and research in Microeconomics, in particular and various other economics domain, in general.
Course Content:
(a) Introduction – partial equilibrium vis-à-vis general equilibrium approach. Exposition of basic concepts. An
elementary general equilibrium model – the Robinson Crusoe economy. Pure exchange economy – the Edgeworth
Boxes, Pareto optimality, contract curve, core, Walras Law, Walras equilibrium. First and second fundamental
theorem of welfare economics (graphical exposition).
(b) A more elaborate exposition of the exchange economy: commodities, agents, preferences, utility functions,
prices, demand and excess demand functions and their properties. Formal definition of allocation, Pareto optimal
allocation, individually rational Pareto optimal allocation, coalition, and core. Walras equilibrium, its relation with
core. Formal proof of first fundamental theorem. Gross substitutability. Price adjustment process. Brower’s fixed
point theorem. Existence of Walras equilibrium and Uzawa equivalence theorem. Social welfare maximization and
its relation with Pareto optimality. General conditions for uniqueness, and discussion of stability – Tatonnement
process. General equilibrium over time – Arrow Debreu scarcity (introduction only). Re-switching and reverse
capital deepening.
(c) Decision-making under uncertainty: lotteries, measures of risk, stochastic dominance. Measures of risk -
Domar-Musgrave index, Roy’s safety index, Mean-Variance, Semi variance. Mini-max regret. Lotteries, preference
relation over lotteries, N-M expected utility theory – basic axiom and representation theorem; violations of EU
theory. Subjective probabilities. Risk aversion – Jensen’s inequality, Acceptance set and risk aversion, various
measures of risk aversion (Arrow-Pratt measure of absolute risk aversion, relative risk aversion), certainty
equivalent and risk premium, Arrow-Pratt approximation of risk premium, Pratt’s theorem, DARA, CARA, IARA,
DRRA, IRRA, CRRA classes of utility functions and their comparative static properties; Applications to various
settings and comparative static results. Stochastic dominance criterion of ordering risky prospects, and
equivalence between expected utility criterion and stochastic dominance criterion.
(d) Introduction to information asymmetries. The elements of the problem. Types of Asymmetric information
problems – moral hazard, adverse selection, signalling. Static Moral Hazard: Full information Benchmark, Hidden
action in a Two action-Two outcome model as well as in a simple Continuous action and continuous outcome case,
Solution through First order approach and its validity, Value of information and characteristics of the Optimal
contract
Adverse selection and Signalling: Akerlof's Model of Lemons, Brief exposure to Mechanism Design and Revelation
Principle, Intuition behind Spence-Mirrlees Single Crossing Condition. Signalling in the Spence's Model of
Education, the notions of Pooling and Separating Equilibria.
(e) Public good and externality: Efficient provision of a discrete public good and its private provision; Voting for it;
Efficient provision of a continuous public good and its private provisioning; Voting; Lindahl allocations; Demand
revealing mechanisms and that with a continuous good; Production Externality and solution for it; Pigovian taxes,
missing markets, and property rights; Efficiency conditions in the presence of externalities.
Text Books:
1. Microeconomic Theory, A. Mas-Colell, M. Whinston and J. Green, Oxford University Press, 2011.
2. Microeconomic Analysis, H. R. Varian, W. W. Norton and Company, 1992.
3. Advanced Microeconomic Theory, G. Jehle and P. Reny, Prentice Hall, 2011.
Reference Books:
A Course in Microeconomic Theory—David Kreps, Princeton University Press, 1990.

Course No: HS5709
Course Name: Indian Economy
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course aims to understand the concepts and measurements of economic development. It provides a
theoretically informed comparative empirical perspective of Indian economic development. It will offer an analytical
understanding of the evolution of economic policies and their impact on economic development. It will also provide
an in-depth analysis of the emerging issues of the Indian economy.
Course outcomes: Through this course, students will be able to comprehend economic development concepts and
measurement issues. They will also have a broad theoretical understanding to analyze the Indian economic
issues. By the end of the course, the students will have an in-depth understanding of the economic database and
be equipped to evaluate changing economic policies.
Course Content:
Topic 1: The concepts and measurement of economic development- Concepts and dimensions of growth and
development; Trade-off among different dimensions of economic development (Lewis model, Lewis-Fei-Ranis
model, Kuznets hypothesis); Overview of the theoretical framework for economic development (Rostow’s stages of
growth, Vicious circle theory, Balanced vs. Unbalanced growth, and Prebisch-Singer hypothesis).
Topic 2: India and the World economy- Indian economy from a historical perspective. British ‘Drain’ on India;
Economic structure during Moghul and British era; Comparative economic performance of India.
Topic 3: Indian economy at Independence- Structural feature of underdevelopment; Early planning (First plan:
1951-1956, Second plan: 1956-1961) and economic development in the agriculture and industrial sectors.

1966-1969, Fourth plan: 1969-1974, Fifth plan: 1974-1978, Rolling plan: 1978-1980) and performances of major
sectors.

1980-1985, Seventh plan: 1985-1990, Annual plan: 1990-1992) and economic performances in the first decade of
economic liberalization, 1991-2000 (Eight plan: 1992-1997, Ninth plan: 1997-2002); Second-generation reforms
and India economic development, 2001-2010 (Tenth plan: 2002-2007, Eleventh plan: 2007-2012); Third-generation
reforms and economic development, 2011-2022 (Twelfth plan: 2012-2017).
Topic 6: Emerging issues of the Indian economy- Unsustainability of growth; Increasing trade balance; Spiraling
prices of essential commodities; Technological change and labor displacement; Informalization and defeminization
of labor employment; Poverty and inequality; and Issues on environmental sustainability.

Course No: HS5756
Course Name: Behavioural Economics and Finance
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Over the past several decades, the field of finance has developed a successful paradigm based on the notions
that investors and managers were generally rational and the prices of securities were generally “efficient.”
However, the recent development in behavioral and experimental economics has shown this paradigm to be
insufficient to describe various features of actual financial markets and firms’ and investors’ behaviour. In this
course, we will use insights from behavioural economics and psychology as well as other social sciences and
more realistic economic settings to guide and develop alternative theories of financial market behaviour and firm
decision-making, while relying on the analytical and quantitative methods common to finance.
After successful completion of the course, students will be able to understand how the insights of behavioural
finance complement the traditional paradigm of finance based on rational choice and expected utility theory. It will
also help them understand investors' trading patterns, the often-anomalous behaviour of asset prices, and
distortions in firm outcomes.
Course Content:
Module I : CONVENTIONAL FINANCE, PROSPECT THEORY, AND MARKET EFFICIENCY
• Foundations of Finance I: Expected Utility Theory
• Foundations of Finance I: Asset Pricing, Market Efficiency, and Agency Relationships
• Prospect Theory, Framing, and Mental Accounting
• Challenges to Market Efficiency
Module II: BEHAVIORAL SCIENCE FOUNDATIONS
• Heuristics and Biases
• Overconfidence
• Emotional Foundations
Module III: INVESTOR BEHAVIOR
• Implications of Heuristics and Biases for Financial Decision-Making
• Implications of Overconfidence for Financial Decision-Making
• Individual Investors and the Force of Emotion
Module IV: SOCIAL FORCES
• Social Forces: Selfishness or Altruism?
• Social Forces at Work: The Collapse of an American Corporation
Module V: MARKET OUTCOMES
• Behavioural Explanations for Anomalies
• Do Behavioural Factors Explain Stock Market Puzzles?
Module VI: CORPORATE FINANCE
• Rational Managers and Irrational Investors
• Behavioural Corporate Finance and Managerial Decision-Making
Module VIII: MONEY MANAGEMENT
• Behavioural Investing
• Neurofinance and the Trader's Brain
Text Books:
1. Behavioural Finance: Psychology, decision-making and markets by Lucy Ackert & Richard Deaves
2. Behavioral Finance: Insights into Irrational Minds and Markets, by Montier
Reference Books:
1. Psychology-based Models of Asset Prices and Trading Volume, by N. Barberis, in
Bernheim, D., DellaVigna, S., Laibson, D. (Eds.), Handbook of Behavioral Economics,
North Holland, Amsterdam, October 2018.
2. Behavioral Corporate Finance: The Life Cycle of a CEO Career, by M. Guenzel and U.
Malmendier, in Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Economics and Finance, September
2020.
3. Behavioral Corporate Finance, by U. Malmendier, in Bernheim, D., DellaVigna, S.,
Laibson,D. (Eds.), Handbook of Behavioral Economics, North Holland, Amsterdam,
October 2018.

Course No: HS5757
Course Name: Corporate Social Responsibility: Integrating Business, Environment, and the Society
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
In the process of doing business and making profit, corporations do impact the environment and society adversely.
Therefore, corporations’ role as wealth creator only is no longer sustainable. In this course, we will examine the
evolution history of the corporations from wealth creator to being socially responsible. We will also analyse the
drivers that motivate corporations to being socially responsible. Next, we will discuss about the implications of
socially responsible investment on cost of capital. At the end, we will discuss the impact of corporate social
responsibility on firms’ economic and financial performance.
Outcomes:
After successful completion of the course, students will be able to understand and demonstrate the intrinsic
interdependence between Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), Corporate Governance (CG), sustainability and
firm performance. As would be managers in corporations or responsible citizens, students will be able to inform
and lead their organizations for sustainable business practices.

• Mandatory CSR law and CSR spending

• Measurements of cost debt and equity capital

Module IV: Corporate social responsibility and firm performance
• Measurements of economic and financial performance of firms
• Impact of CSR on firm performance
• Impact of CSR spending on ESG scores of firms

Course No: HS5760
Course Name: Climate Economics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Climate change is one of the most significant challenges humanity as a whole has ever faced. It is a truly global
collective action problem, whose social costs will be massive, widespread, unpredictable, and inequitably
distributed. This course undertakes the challenge of climate change from an economics perspective. This course
will use the lens of economics to clarify the costs and benefits of climate change; understand the challenges of
climate change mitigation, and understand the theoretical and empirical impacts of climate policies. This course
will begin by reviewing some foundational economic concepts and studying the effects of climate change.
The objectives of the course are to understand,
1. how the costs and benefits of mitigation are measured and how to simulate them in a numerical model;
2. the economics of climate change and policies;
3. the current landscape of domestic and international policy planning and implementation related to climate
change.
Learning outcomes
1. Articulate key issues relating to climate change;
2. Explain how economics can offer public policies aimed at mitigating the effects of climate change;
3. Undertake independent research in the area of the economics of climate change mitigation.
Course Content:
Part-A: Understanding climate economics
1.The science of Climate Change
a. Process, b. Projections
2. Emissions scenarios and options for emission reduction
a. Sources of greenhouse gas emissions; b. Trends and scenarios of future emissions; c. Options for emission
reduction
d. Beyond the Kaya identity
3. Abatement costs
a. The cost of emission reduction; b. Negative emissions; c. Negative abatement costs
Part-B: Policy instruments
4. Policy instruments for emission reduction
a. The justification for a public policy; b. Direct, market-based instruments; c. Second-best regulations
5. Impact of climate change
a. Total economic impacts; b. Impact and development; c. Marginal economic impact
6. Climate and development
a. Exponential growth; b. Poverty trap; c. Natural disasters
7. Adaptation policy and optimal climate policy
a. Adaptation versus mitigation; b. Adaptation and development
Part-C: International cooperation
8.International environmental agreements
a. Cooperative and non- cooperative abatement; b. Free-riding; c. International climate policies
Text Books:
Tol, Richard SJ. Climate Economics: Economic Analysis of Climate, Climate Change and Climate Policy. 2nd ed.
Cheltenham, UK: Edward Elgar. 2019.
Reference Books:
1. Kolstad, C. D., Intermediate Environmental Economics, Oxford University Press. 2011
2. Stern, Nicholas, and Nicholas Herbert Stern. The economics of climate change: the Stern review. Cambridge

Course No: HS5850
Course Name: History of Medicine in Colonial India
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
To enable the students understand: the growth of modern medical science and practice in colonial India; the social
and cultural dimensions of the colonial public health and medical policies; and of nature of the encounter between
diverse medical traditions
Course Content:
1. Western Ideas of Indian Environment – Medical Topography – Environmental Determinism, Tropical Paradigm –
Shifts in the discourses on race, climate and diseases
2. From Military/White personnel’s’ health to ‘Native’ and Public Health – the IMS (Indian Medical Service),
Challenge of Epidemics, Public Health Measures, Compliances and Resistances; Enclavism, Hill stations and
Sanatoria
3. Emergence of the local western medical profession – changing roles assigned to Indians in the public health
system, entry of Indians into the army and the provincial and central medical services, medical colleges; avenues
for private practice and employment in non-state sectors.
4. Colonial Medicine and Gender – Zenana Missions, Lock Hospitals, Scientific Midwifery, Women’s Medical
Institutions, WMS
5. (Colonial) State contribution Vs Public Philanthropy - Setting up of Funds, dispensaries, hospitals and colleges
on private initiative, the role of Princely States.
6. Medical Research - Tropical Medicine, Germ theory and Pasteurian paradigms, Bacteriological Research
Institutions
7. Encounter with indigenous systems – ‘accommodation’, marginalization, revivalist movements, hybridization;
implications for subsequent medical pluralism.

Course No: HS5855
Course Name: Memory, History and Literature
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The design and delivery of the course will be specially done to train students to study deconstructions of
commonly consumed historical knowledge as well as narratives of shared and collective memory. Students will be
specially trained in understanding the nature and function of fiction and fictional representations. Although primarily
based on literary studies, the course will also draw on cognitive psychology and cultural studies and in the process
offer interdisciplinary readings and training in memory studies to students.
Following are the objectives of the course
To train students to read fictional representations of history as alternative narratives of knowledge.
To train students to examine the interface between micro-memory (neural, psychological) and
macro-memory (collective, cultural) as represented in fiction.
To train students to examine the relationship between forgetting and fabulation as represented in
fiction.
To train students to examine the entanglement of memory and affect (empathy, trauma etc) as
examined in fiction.
To train students to examine the network of nostalgia and nation as represented in fiction.
Course Content:
Following are the modules to be followed in the course
History as alternative narratives of knowledge
The interface between micro-memory (neural, psychological) and macro-memory (collective, cultural) Forgetting
and fabulation as represented in fiction
Entanglement of memory and affect Nostalgia and nation
Text Books:
(Indicative list of primary texts to be taught in class):

‘Toba Tek Singh’ by Saadat Hasan Manto
The Book of Laughter and Forgetting by Milan Kundera Maus by Art Spiegelman

The Shadow Lines by Amitav Ghosh
The God of Small Things by Arundhati Roy
What the Body Remembers by Shauna Singh Baldwin ‘Iraqi Nights’ by Duniya Mikhail
The Corpse Exhibition by Hassan Blasim
