Course No: HS5880
Course Name: Corruption and Development
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course will introduce students to contemporary theories of corruption (with an emphasis on political
corruption) and its impacts on development, including perspectives from social and political philosophy. It will
attempt to use case studies to interpret and evaluate what is meant by corruption, how it is tied to broader social
processes and how it defines and shapes distinct political cultures.
Outcomes:
Students are expected to understand various interpretations of corruption from ancient to contemporary times,
across different social and political scales and contexts and also review multiple approaches to addressing it in the
context of sustainable development.
Course Content:
• Introduction: articulating corruption
o Scandals, countries and syndromes: the roles of shock, geography and development, and broad institutional
effects in describing corruption
o Contemporary case studies of political corruption from around 26 countries.
• An assemblage theory of corruption
o Describing the social: What is an apparatus?
o Corruption as social betrayal
• Corruption in the global South: politics of the belly
o The post-colonial context: revisiting scandals in Indonesia, Peru, Uganda
o The United States as post-colony: the Trump era
• Doing Something
o Diversion: History of settled farming to agroecology and alternative food movements
o Addressing climate change as corruption: The role of “transformation” in sustainability discourse
Text Books:
Heidenheimer, Arnold J., and Michael Johnston, eds. Political corruption: Concepts and contexts. Vol. 1.
Transaction Publishers, 2011.
Rajan, Sudhir Chella. A Social Theory of Corruption. Harvard University Press, 2020.
Reference Books:
Johnston, Michael. Syndromes of corruption: wealth, power, and democracy. Cambridge University Press, 2005.
Gabriel Zuckman, The Hidden Wealth of Nations: The Scourge of Tax Havens. University of Chicago Press, 2013.
Tellus Institute. DSTAIR: a decision support tool to analyze institutional reform. http://institutionalreform.org/

Course No: HS5910
Course Name: Contemporary India: A Sociological Perspective
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course introduces students to the sociological analysis of contemporary Indian society. It examines the history
of anthropology and sociology in India, problematizing their colonial legacy while discussing diverse theoretical
and methodological orientations. The course equips students with multiple theoretical frameworks used by
sociologists to analyze Indian society. Key themes include caste and modernity, globalization and Indian society,
and the emergence of the middle class.
Course Content:
Module I: Anthropology and Colonial Legacy
• Anthropology and the legacy of colonialism
• Orientalist constructions of Indian society and their critique
Module II: History and Theoretical Perspectives in Indian Sociology
• Brief history of Sociology/Anthropology in India
• Dominant theoretical perspectives in Indian Sociology:
o Indological approach
o Structural-functionalist perspective
o Marxist perspective
o Subaltern studies perspective
o Dalit perspective
Module III: Caste and Social Change in India
• The centrality of caste in Indian society
• Perspectives on the study of caste
• Caste and modernity
• Caste and identity mobilization
• Caste, inequality, and reservation policies
Module IV: Globalization and the Indian Society
• Theoretical overview on globalization
• Consumption and the emergence of the Indian middle class

Course No: HS5950
Course Name: Economic Analysis of Public Policy
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Decision making processes in designing public policies require a thorough understanding and analysis of the
economic, ethical and other implications of such policies being considered. Mere enumeration of costs and
benefits will not be sufficient to address questions such as: Are the total benefits larger than total costs? Who
benefits and to what extent? What are the budgetary implications of such policy decisions?
The objectives of the course are to enhance students’ conceptual understanding of fundamental issues in the
design, implementation and assessment of public policies. It is also intended to impart analytical skills to assess
the economic impact of policy interventions.
Students will acquire perspectives and analytical skill needed to undertake economic analysis of public policy
interventions, and contribute to rational policy making processes.
Course Content:
1. Policy Analysis, Politics and Ethics – Goals of Public Policy, Steps in Policy Analysis, Role of Policy Analysts
and Ethics for Policy Analysts
2. Economics for Policy Analysts – Review of Markets, Rational Behaviour, fundamental micro economic
concepts, role of incentives, concepts of efficiency, Imperfect markets, Role of Government;
3. Tools for Policy Analysis – Introduction to Benefit Cost Analysis; Decision making criteria, Types of policy
decisions, Cost-Effectiveness Analysis; Decision Tree models; Related concepts;
4. Valuation of non-marketed goods – methods for valuing non-marketed goods;
5. Economic Impact Analysis – Role of Survey methods, estimation of direct and indirect spending;
6. Public Policy Case Studies – Transportation, Pollution control, Etc.
The course will have theory lectures, case study discussions and group projects. Projects will involve where
possible field work where students will study a policy intervention in the field, gather data and report the outcomes.
Issues that arise in specific technology intensive domains (healthcare, telecom, energy, automation, internet) will
be explored using readings and case studies.
Text Books:
1. William K Bellinger, The economic analysis of public policy (Taylor & Francis, 2015)
2. Daniel Hausman, Michael McPherson and Debra Staz, Economic Analysis, Moral Philosophy and Public Policy
(CUP, 2016)
3. David Weimer and Aidan Vining, Policy Analysis: Concepts and Practice (Routledge, 2017)
Reference Books:
1. Catherine F Smith Writing Public Policy: Guide to communicating in the policy making process (OUP, 2018)
2. Peter H Ross, Mark W Lipsey and Gary T Henry, Evaluation: A systematic Approach (OUP, 2018)

Course No: HS5951
Course Name: Intellectual Property Rights: A Global and Indian Perspective
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
An understanding of IPR regimes in today’s world can-not be over-emphasized. Educations systems that
encourage students to be innovative, and develop products and services indigenously should provide an adequate
grounding in emerging IPR regimes globally and regionally.
The Objectives of this course are
a) To establish the need for and importance of creating Intellectual Property
b) Get an understanding of Policies around overall Global IPR and India’s Patent Organization
c) The science and business process to assess and identify patentable innovations of value
d) Get an understanding of the Patenting Process – domestic and international and Costs involved,
e) Understand the Maintenance, Protection, and enforcement of Patents, once granted
The objectives will be achieved through a mix of lectures, case studies, and sharing of experience by Faculty and
Industry Professionals.
Course Content:
1. The value of IP: Definition of IP; types – Process; Product; value of Standard Essential Patents (SEP) ; Patents
generated Globally and India’s share; contribution IPR towards a country’s GDP; Critical assessment of India’s
position in the Patent world and how it is impacting us
2. Role of Academia, Government and Industry in knowledge/ IP Creation; IP and Entrepreneurship – evaluate for
correlations
3. Global IPR and an India Perspective: Innovation policies and protection of intellectual property rights – Global
and Indian context – a historical perspective; IP Protection in India – review current laws and regulations;
Institutional mechanisms to facilitate knowledge creation, adoption and diffusion; Critical assessment – Is my idea
worth patenting?
4. How do you go about filing a Patent: Understanding of Territorial limitations; Process for filing a domestic patent;
International Process Direct or Paris route; PCT route – Pros and Cons; Process; Pros and Cons – Paris route Vs
PCT route; Importance of Timing; Costs involved – Advisory, legal, filing fees
5. . Enabling more IP/ Patent creation and generation:
6) Educational Policy – promoting thinking, ideation, innovation and value creation
7. Evaluate need for Legal and Financial Support for Innovators
8. Study the Impact of Flipping (IP moving from our country to another – when Startups shift their HQ from India to
other more start-up friendly countries) on IP; Need for Financial and Legal support for Patent Policing – Protecting
our Patents and enforcing laws when misused – domestic and internationally
Text Books:
1. Matthias Hillner, Intellectual Property, Design Innovation, and Entrepreneurship (Springer, 2021)
2. Abbe Brown., et al., Contemporary Intellectual Property: Law and Policy (OUP, 2019)
3. Tanya Apline and Jennifer Davis, Intellectual Property Law, Texts, Cases and Materials (OUP, 2021)
Reference Books:
1. Justine Pila and Paul Torremans, European Intellectual Property Law (OUP, 2019)
2. Rupinder Tewari and Mamta Bhardwaj - Intellectual Property, A Primer for Academia (Punjab University, 2021)

Course No: HS5952
Course Name: Governance and Institutions in India
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The aim of this course is to introduce the concept of governance in India and the institutions that are enshrined in
the Constitution of India to ensure an inclusive, equitable, sustainable and participatory system of government
guided by the objective of good governance based on an understanding of what constitutes public policy,
socio-economic development, and fundamental rights.
Outcomes:
At the completion of the course, students will be able to appreciate the nuances of the process of framing public
policy in India informed by an understanding of the social, political, legal, economic, ethical and environmental
factors that form the backdrop of the decision-making process in various policy-making bodies.
Course Content:
1. Philosophy of the Indian Constitution: Constituent Assembly Debates - Preamble, Fundamental Rights,
Directive Principles of State Policy - Constitutionalism in India - due process vs popular sovereignty -
Constitutional Amendments - Basic Structure - forms of Constitutions
2. Constitutional Politics: Democracy, Social Change, National Unity, Checks and Balances - rule of law, judicial
independence - liberal and republican constitutionalism; emergency powers and crisis of constitutionalism –
Federalism – centre state relations - role of Finance Commissions
3. Parliamentary Democracy in India: Institutional mechanism for checks and balances - ensuring good
governance – Separation of powers, executive, legislative and judiciary – RTI, Consumer Protection Act, Lok Pal,
Lok Ayukta, Ombudsman, Grievance Redressal – NITI Aayog - socio-economic development, Public Interest
Litigation
4. Process of Democracy: Constitutional provisions, Election Commission of India, Electoral Systems, Political
Parties and Party System, Conduct of Elections, Rules, Electoral Reforms.
5. Civil Society - Interest groups, Social movements, New social movements, Non-governmental Organisations
(NGOs)
6. Grassroots governance – Panchayati Raj, decentralization, Gandhian constructive programme – sustainable,
equitable, participatory and inclusive development
7. Law and Public Policy – Acts and legislations - Health, Education, Employment, Environment, Gender, Caste,
Housing, Water, Sanitation and Food – MGNREGA, NRHM, RTE, Swacchh Bharat, COVID-19, migrant labour
crisis during COVID-19
8. Globalization and its impact on public policy – social and economic impact -UN, World Bank, BRICS, IMF, WTO,
IPCC, SAARC and EU
Text Books:
1. Shivani Singh. 2019. Governance: Issues and Challenges. New Delhi: Sage.
2. Mookherjee, Dilip. 2008. Market, Institutions, Governance and Development. New Delhi: OUP.
3. Basu, Durga Das. 2021. Introduction to the Constitution of India. Gurgaon: Lexis Nexis.
4. Austin, Granville. 1999. The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
Reference Books:
1. Singer, Wendy. 2007. A Constituency Suitable for Ladies. New Delhi: Oxford University Press.
2. Austin, Granville. 2003. Working a Democratic Constitution. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
3. Bhushan, Prashant. 2017. The Case that Shook India. Gurgaon: Penguin Random House, India.
4. Vajpeyi, Ananya. 2012. Righteous Republic. Cambridge: Mass.: Harvard University Press.
5. Menon, Madhava, N.R. 2015. Nehru and Indian Constitutionalism. Mumbai: Indus Source Books.

Course No: HS5953
Course Name: Pollution, Public Health and Public Policy
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Given the current concerns about increasing environmental pollution and their impact on population health, it is
important for students to understand the challenges in designing effective regulatory policies to promote clean
environment and sustain better human health.
The objectives of this course are: (a) to provide students with knowledge related to the wider aspects of
environmental pollution, (b) to understand the steps involved in measurement, analysis and interpretation,
identifying sources of pollution, and (c) to understand their public health consequences and the need for various
regulatory policies to contain them.
The students will be familiarized with environmental chemicals, sources and measurement techniques. The course
will also enable them to link environmental chemicals and consequent public health impacts.
Course Content:
This course will cover topics relating
(1) environmental chemicals, measurement and analysis, identification of sources,
(2) environmental risk assessment, pollutant transport process in different medium, environment carrying capacity
and notion of sustainable development,
(3) exposure assessment and health impacts,
(4) International Conventions and national policies, and legal aspects of exposure to environmental chemicals,
(5) cost benefit analysis of environmental policies
(6) preventive environmental management.
Text Books:
1. Robert H Friis, Essentials of Environmental Health (Jones and Bartlett, 2018).
2. Joseph F Louvar and B Diane Louvar, Health and Environmental Risk Analysis: Fundamentals with
Applications (Prentice Hall, 2017).
Reference Books:
1. Evan K Paleologos, Environmental Risk Analysis (McGraw-Hill, 2001)
2. Francois Mancebo and Ignacy Sachs (Editors), Transition to Sustainability (Springer, 2015).
3. Kanchan Chopra, Development and Environmental Policy in India: The last few decades (Springer, 2017)

Course Name: Advanced Concepts in Film Studies
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The aim is to make the scholars familiar with advanced topics and practices in film studies. Scholars will be
encouraged to investigate the ways in which technologies and social changes have impacted, and continue to

social, economic and political contexts; and historical developments that have marked film as a medium, focusing
on historical case studies in order to think about changes and continuities throughout film history.

Course Name: History of Science and the Public
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
How has science and the scientific community created its authority and its relationships with other parts of
society? In today's "Knowledge Society" everybody should arguably know more about science, at the same time
as the authority of scientific knowledge and practice is questioned. While scientific communities and institutions
remain highly hierarchical, there has been a call for public engagement with research for the sake of democracy. In
the course we will examine how these different spheres of 'science' and 'the public' (or different publics) have been
created, how they are maintained and which functions they serve.
Outcomes:
The students will learn about the relationship between science and different sections of the public, and how this
relationship has developed in history. The students will learn how to argue in class, how to develop their own
semester project, how to give an oral presentation and to give comments to the presentations of other students,
and how to write a term paper.
Course Content:
• Demarcation of science from non-science
• History of science education
• Museums and public understanding of science
• Science and the media / science journalism
• Popular science movements
• Science and democracy
• Public engagement with research
• What everybody needs to know about science
• Amateur science
• Science and literature
• History of science and the public understanding of science

Course No: HS6020
Course Name: Uncertainty, Asset Pricing and Empirical Aspects of Financial Markets
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
(a) To provide an exposure to the students of the financial economic theories, since Markowitz (1952) to the most
recent ones.
(b) Related empirical developments of the concerned literature will also be discussed extensively.
Course Content:
Buying and Selling:
Assumption of income being exogenous will be relaxed for the theories of consumer’s optimization behavior and
how such income is rather determined endogenously will be discussed in details and concerned modified
discussion of her/his optimization behavior will be discussed.
2. Intertemporal Choice:
Simple two period intertemporal choices model will be introduced here and will further be extended for the case
involving more than two periods. Real life situation involving inflation will also be discussed.
3. Asset Markets:
Assets, including financial assets like bonds or corporate stocks, are goods that provide a flow of services,
including financial returns like interest or dividend payments, over time. In this chapter we will examine the
functioning of asset markets under conditions of complete certainty about the future flow of services provided by
the asset.
4. Uncertainty:
Complete certainty model of asset returns will be extended for the case if such return is uncertain, since
investment in financial markets always involve some risk. Operations of financial institutions such as insurance
and stock markets that can mitigate such risks, at least some extent, will also be introduced.
5. Risky Assets
Consumer’s optimum choice under uncertainty will be discussed extensively here, including her/his decision to
allocate income in consumption and in investment expenditure. The concerned investment decision will further be
extended to her/his decision of selecting an investment portfolio, instead of choosing merely a single asset.
6. Review of the Literature with Methodological developments
The first methodological breakthrough in this area came after the development of the theory of choice under
uncertainty by von Neumann and Morgenstern (1947). Later Markowitz (1952, 1959) and Tobin (1958) used this
theory to formulate and solve the portfolio selection problem. And, researchers developed methodologies to
estimate market line empirically in this regard. To improve the precision of estimated market lines, empirical
research on finance developed even further with the works of researchers such as Blume (1970), Friend and
Blume (1970), Black, Jenson and Scholes (1972) work with portfolios. We would like to discuss all these classic
works to provide a thorough understanding of the subject to the student(s). We will also discuss Mehra (2006) to
have an overall picture of the concerned literature in India, in general and specific issues that are important for
Indian financial market, in particular.
Since empirical research on the subject is largely based on the time series data, time series econometrics
eventually becomes an integral part of the subject. We would also like to engage with modern time series
econometric (to the extent possible) techniques to deal with such data.
Text Books:
1) Campbell, John Y., Andrew W. Lo, and A. Craig MacKinlay (1997), The Econometrics of Financial Markets,
Princeton University Press.
2) Cochrane, John H. (Revised Edition, 2005), Asset Pricing, Princeton University Press.
3) Hamilton, James D. (1994), Time Series Analysis, Princeton University Press.
4) Huang, Chi-fu, and Robert H. Litzenberger (1988), Foundations for Financial Economics, North Holland.

Blackwell, Oxford.

8) Von Neummann, J. and O. Morgenstern (1947): Theory of Games and Economic Behaviour, 2nd edition,
Princeton University Press, Princeton.
Reference Books:

Course No: HS6025
Course Name: Resources of Science and Technology in Sanskrit
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
To create an awareness of the tradition of science and technology that find expression in certain ancient Sanskrit
texts and to examine how they can be of use in the contemporary world.
a) Creating an awareness of ancient knowledge in the fields of Botany, Mathematics Architecture Metallurgy,
Medicine, and Yoga that is relevant to modern life
b) Paving the way for inter-disciplinary research in the field of Art, Architecture and Sciences.
Course Content:
Course contents:
This course will examine the ancient Sanskrit tradition of science and technology with a focus on the
methodological specificities that distinguished them from other intellectual and spiritual endeavours in ancient India
as well as from the modern scientific enterprises. It will also guide the students to comprehend some key features
of these ancient texts so that they would be able to hermeneutically decode such texts and can also place them in
larger linguistic and historical perspectives. It will examine the various branches of sciences such as Botany,
Mathematics, Architecture, Metallurgy, Medicine, and Yoga that were orally passed on for thousands of years from
generation to generation through and later by written documents in palm leaf manuscripts and paper. Experts in
the following branches of knowledge will provide information on the basics of some of these subjects:
1. Sanskrit basics to give the nuances of basic Sanskrit language structure to the students so that they get the
fundamental knowledge to read and understand the text.
2. Teaching the basic principles of arithmetic, algebra and geometry contained in ancient Sanskrit texts vis – a- vis
modern Mathematics.
3. To probe the ancient methods of construction of structures like temples, big mansions and the processes
involved in such grand endeavours.
4. To create an understanding of some of the methods in agriculture through organic and natural resources as
described in ancient texts like Krishiparashara.
5. Basic concepts of Yoga, which has gained popularity throughout the world for its contribution in its physical,
psychological, moral and spiritual development of man.
6. Basics of Ayurvedic principles such as dietetics, treatment of diseases, surgery and rejuvenation to be
introduced.
Lectures on some of the topics mentioned above would be delivered by experts in each field, not just with an intent
to showcase the details given in the ancient Sanskrit literature but to explore their continued validity and
successful adaptation in modern times.

Course No: HS6031
Course Name: Autobiography: Genre, History, and Futures
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course examines the history and approaches to self-construction and self-articulation that occupy critical
importance in our contemporary times. It engages with some of the key texts within the Western and Indian
tradition of autobiographical writing within their philosophical and historical context. It focuses on questions of
subjectivity, individuation, narrativity, and interiority. It asks the following questions: What are the limitations of the
self narrating itself? How do articulations of gender, sexuality, race and caste delimit the generic boundaries? How
does the genre of autobiography transform itself in the colony by interacting with indigenous modes of
self-narration? How does it negotiate with Indian thought and colonial modernity? The course will conclude with
discussions on some of the contemporary forms of autobiographical writing.

Biofiction, Digital Lives, Futures of Auto/biographical forms

Theory
Description:
The course offers a general introduction to the field of Disability Studies. It explores disability’s capacity to offer a

marker.
Outcomes:

connection between disabilities and disciplines such as psychoanalysis, literary criticism, anthropology, and
philosophy. Students may learn how disability, health and wellbeing become potential markers of interpretation.
Course Content:

body mind, rationality and intellectual labour
3. Stigma – Dehumanization and stigma; Erving Goffman and his contributions concerning social stratification

5. Disability and literary genres – Disability, life writing and self-expression; the idea of narrative prosthesis; literary
genres, bodies and transformation
6. Disability and rhetoric – The art of persuasion, care and politics; rhetoric, intimacy and mutuality
7. Deaf culture – The culture of hearing, sign languages and minority politics
8. Autism and neurodiversity – Neurodiversity; history of autism; autism and literary criticism
9. Disability, health and wellbeing – Health studies; mental health and wellbeing
10. Disability and disciplines – Disability as an interdisciplinary, and a transdisciplinary gestalt; disability and
narrative universes

Theory

Description:
The integration of technology into instructional design, curriculum design, assessment and evaluation practices,

shortcoming of the technology used in random of a course. They will able to use the technology appropriately in
pedagogical delivery of a course to retain quality education in the HE set up among other.

• The internal and external imperatives for technology use in higher education
• E-learning, M-learning
• Synchronous and asynchronous learning
• Computer assisted learning
• Computer supported learning
• Significance of technological change in HE
• Technology and Instructional design
• Blended learning
• Behaviourist, cognitivist, constructivist, and connectivist theory of learning
• Technology, freedom, and fairness
• Technology and social justice in education
• Shortcomings of technology-based education
• Impacts of technology on teachers
• Open educational resources.

Course No: HS6180
Course Name: Algorithms in Indian Astronomy
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course will introduce students to a number of advanced astronomical algorithms and their rationale as
described in the Indian astronomical texts. It will trace the development of increasingly sophisticated algorithms by
Indian astronomers over the course of history to compute and predict the occurrence of complex astronomical
phenomena. Thus, the course will enable students to gain a sound technical footing in the history and
development of astronomy in India.
Course Content:
1. Mathematical foundations of astronomy
a. Introduction to non-Euclidean geometry; spherical triangles and their properties
b. Indian sine and its computation
c. Celestial sphere and coordinate systems
2. Computation of mean planetary longitudes
a. Reckoning of time and the Indian luni-solar calendar
b. Finding the number of days elapsed since an epoch
c. Notion of mean and true sunrise; equation of time
3. Computation of true planetary longitudes
a. Epicycle and eccentric models
b. Manda samskara: Eccentricity correction
c. Sighra samskara: Conversion of heliocentric to geocentric longitudes
4. Computations involving shadow measurements
a. Finding the cardinal directions using a gnomon
b. Determination of terrestrial latitude and parallax correction
c. Ascensional difference and the rising times of rasis
5. Prediction of eclipses
a. Causes of eclipses and cycles associated with them
b. Determination of occurrence and duration of a lunar eclipse
c. Determination of occurrence and duration of a solar eclipse

Course Content:
The course is aimed at introducing students to the problems and prospects of Indian women, both historically and
conceptually. Historically the course surveys women’s status from ancient times till the present time while focusing

women across cultures. Instead of treating women as impediments to development or a problem to be solved the
course sensitizes students to women’s contribution to economy and nation building.

pre-independence India – Women in freedom struggle – GDI in India – Issues: caste, class, religion – Rural/urban
divide - Contemporary feminist movements - Sexuality and Indian Women - Encountering violence, dowry, rape –

Course No: HS6520
Course Name: Culture and Development
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
In normative development thought, culture is either a realm outside the sphere of development or the pre-history of
development that requires a forward march toward a society of consumption and well-being. This approach
defined development theory during development decades (except for a few articulations as in Sen, Boserup
among others) until the impasse in development theory in the 1980s and early 1990s. When the United Nations
announced the Decade for Cultural Development from 1988 to 1997, it brought culture to converse with
development practice in an institutional sense.
The course will introduce the students (preferably of higher semesters) to the way culture mediates our
understanding of development, and make a case for development that is as much a cultural process as is a
material outcome. Against the conventional wisdom that culture is too vernacular a practice to play any meaningful
role in the global process of development, this course is aimed at offsetting that residual status for culture in
development practice.
Outcomes:
The course will help students appreciate the multidimensionality of development practice and equip them with
critical vocabulary to see development as deeply embedded in cultural imaginaries. This engagement will help
them see development as a repository of values and as an everyday and iterative practice.
Course Content:
• Culture, the missing concept, in institutional development thought
• Discourses around culture and (modernist)-development, narrativization
• Power and knowledge, making of development and underdevelopment
• Beyond base and super-structure, faith-based development, culture, religion
• Politics of location, globalism, nationalism, localism
• Cultural globalization, representation, universality and the making of First/Third world
• Culturalism and multiple developments, a new social theory and development practice

Course Name: Introduction to Contemporary Tibet
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This is a seminar course for PhD students and senior MA students from the third year and above. The course
introduces Modern Tibet as a political, sociological and historical entity as it emerged in 1950s. The course will
broadly engage with issues of Tibetan identity, economy and socio-cultural development of Tibetan community
both within the TAR and outside. The reading material will be cross-disciplinary from anthropology, history,
sociology, international politics, and development studies. The course will focus on ethnic, linguistic and national
identities as they operate in the process of nation-building in the history of Modern Tibet from 1950s to
contemporary times. This will include a focus on articulation of political Tibet and contending formulations that
underlie current scholarly literature on the question of identity. Outcomes: At the end of the course, the students
are expected of have an in-depth understanding of Tibetan history, society and politics spanning the period from
early 19th century to the contemporary period.

Course No: HS6570
Course Name: Food Cultures
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Food requires gathering, growing, hunting, storage, distribution, preparation, display, serving, and disposal, all of
which are social activities. An anthropological study of food within a cultural system include economy, materiality,
distinction, inequality, gender, status, and food as a symbol. This course will serve as an introduction to the many
ways in which the gathering, growing, preparating and serving of food is one of the most universal acts in present
day culture, even as it is rife with particularities depending on geography, history and materiality. Through ten
modules intended at covering aspects of food cultures, it explores what it means to think about culture as food and
food as culture.
Course Content:
Through this course, students will be introduced to different ways of thinking about food as culture. Over the
course of thirteen weeks, we will locate food in different material, political and cultural contexts before asking what
it means to be the consumers of food in the current moment.
The course is organized through ten modules as follows: (A) Food and the anthropology of food: A brief history, (B)
The Tasting of Food: Meditations on the physical, chemical, and neurophysiological bases of taste, (C) Food and
gender (D) Food and labor (E) Nutritionism and society (F) Food, Industrialization and the Environment (G) Food
communication, consumption and entertainment (H) Food as symbol (I) Food, literature and writing (J) Field-visit
and project
The course will be organized via articles assigned every week from academic anthropological journals and popular
press. It will also include multimedia references such as television shows, documentaries and popular films. A
selection of reference books and articles is provided below.

Course No: HS6580
Course Name: Indian Cultural Studies
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Academic study of cultures in India has remained derivative of Western categories, assumptions and ideologies.
Ideas such as modernity, nationalism, development, cosmopolitanism etc. have all been applied readymade to
Indian experience thereby making Indian reality as either derivative or deviant examples.
The course aims at introducing students to distinct Indian ways of cultural expressions and offers pathways to
understand self and subjectivity in the context of localism, nationalism and globalism. In a departure from Western
frameworks, the course engages with Indian experience as articulated by its thinkers who provide a way of
thinking about Indianness (in all its diversity) and Indian experiences. However, it is not intended to completely
ignore the mediated and cross-pollinated nature of Indian thought. The course will cover key texts from the late
19th century to understand what constitutes Indian subjectivity, its difference, authenticity and life world, its
implications for nationhood and claims of particularism vis-à-vis universalism.
Outcomes:
The course is intended to equip the students with a theoretical idiom to investigate the ways in which Indian
thought since early 20th century shaped and transformed individual experiences as well as their place in the
cultural world. The students will also learn to articulate their individual and collective experiences through the idea
and vocabulary explored in the course.
Course Content:
1. Introduction: (Orientalist, colonial and contemporary representation of India)
2. Indian difference: (Aurobindo, Ramanujan, Bankimchandra, Malhotra and others)
3. Self and subjectivity: (Gandhi, Upadhyay, M.N. Roy, Ashis Nandy, Dharmapal and others)
4. Home, Nation and the World: (Nehru, Tagore, Ambedkar, Savarkar, Mazumdar, Malaviya and others)
5. Swaraj: (Lajpat Rai, Gandhi, Tilak, Rajaji, Alvares, Balagangadhar and others)
6. Art and aesthetics: (Coomaraswamy, Hiriyana, Radhakrishnan, Aurobindo, Naipaul, Devy and others)

Course No: HS7003
Course Name: Advanced Environmental Economics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This advanced level course is designed to guide students through the frontier areas of environmental economics.
The course begins with studying interaction between economy and the environment. Next module helps
understanding the welfare implications of national income and discusses the issues of sustainable development.
The impact of economic growth on environmental degradation is discussed next. Then the issues of externalities
and methods to regulate externalities are discussed. The impacts of uncertainty and information asymmetry on the
choice of policy instruments for regulating externalities are also examined. We then try to understand the methods
for economic valuation of environmental goods and services. The course concludes by discussing the optimal
extraction strategy for renewable and non-renewable resources
Course Content:
Module 1: Interaction between economy and the environment
• How does economy and the environment affect each other
• Justification of studying environmental economics
Module 2: Welfare implication of national income and sustainable development
• Concept of Hicksian income
• National income and its welfare implication
• Definations and indicators of sustainable development
Module 3: Economic growth and environmental degradation: Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) hypothesis
• Understanding of EKC
• Explanations for EKC hypothesis
• Limitations of EKC hypothesis
• Policy implications of EKC analysis
Module 4: Externalities and market failure
• Market as an institution
• Market: efficient and otherwise
• Externalities
• Coasian bargaining and efficient solution
Module 5: Incentive design
• Price rationing: Charges and subsidies
• Quantity rationing: tradable pollution permits
• Incentive compatibility
• Evaluation criteria: effectiveness, efficiency, equity
• Problems with emission taxation and permit system
Module 6: Environmental regulation and competitiveness
• Traditional wisdom about regulation competitiveness relationship
• Porter’s hypothesis
• Criticisms of Porter’s hypothesis
Module 7: Environmental efficiency and cost of pollution control
• Introduction to frontier approach of measuring efficiency
• Measuring environmental efficiency
• Cost of pollution control
Module 8: Theory and methods for environmental valuation
• What is economic value of environment
• Stated preference approach: contingent valuation and choice experiment
• Revealed preference approach: travel cost method, hedonic price theory
• Production function approach
Module 9: Optimal extraction of renewable and non-renewable resources
• Determination of price along the optimal extraction path for renewable and non-renewable resources
• Back stop technology
• Poverty –growth-environment relationship
Text Books:
1. Title: Environmental Economics: In Theory and Practice (2nd ed)
Author: Nick Hanley, Jason Shogren, and Ben White
Publisher: Pearson higher education

• Book: Hand Book of Environmental Economics for several year

This course will explore significant issues of urban land at multiple levels: societal aspects such as land as a
setting for housing, and large infrastructure projects including SEZs for the ‘Informal Sector’. It will include a focus
on the urban politics associated with land acquisition, land regularization, and land as a mode of financing. Finally,
the diverse meanings of land beyond property will be explored.
Outcomes:
Students will gain both a conceptual and policy-based understanding of land, its governance and politics. This will
allow an understanding of institutional issues to build technical managerial proficiency and analytical skills.
Course Content:
1. The Critical Significance of Urban Land in India and the Global South: The governance of land across regions
in India, and the Global South
2. Defining Land, Territory, Tenure: Introduction to land in specific contexts and as a general territorial system;
Land as Incremental settlement and transformation; Land in metro and small town settings
3. Land as History and as Practice: Land tenure as customary claims, and modern titles; The social embeddness
of land; Land as Myth
4. Land and Urban Planning. Land use zoning, non-conforming use, building bylaws; Advanced Locality
Management as Governance; Contemporary Planning instruments and ideas of Mixed Land use; Mega territory
planning and incentive zones; Land acquisition laws and reality;
5. Land as the basis for Infrastructure Governance: Land based financing for infrastructure development: Micro
and Macro instruments; Land regularization and development charges
6. Land for Pro-Poor Housing and Economy: Case of SRS and SRA Mumbai, CESS schemes of the MHADA;
Slum Upgrading, In-situ and plot reconstitution; Madhya Pradesh Land policy. International experiences: the
Kampong Improvement Program in Surabaya; Site and Services in India, Egypt.
7. Land as Politics: Land as contested territory. Politics of land acquisition and the price of land; The politics of
‘E-Tilting’; Debates over Resettlement and Rehabilitation.
Text Books:
1. Parnell, S., & Oldfield, S. (Eds.). (2014). The Routledge Handbook on Cities of the Global South. London:
Routledge.
2. Banerjee, B. (2002). Security of Tenure in Indian Cities: an overview of policy and practice. In A.
Durand-Lasserve, & L. Royston (Eds.), Holding their Ground: Secure Land Tenure for the Urban Poor in
Developing Countries (pp. 37-58). London: Routledge.
3. Hsing, Y. (2010). The Great Urban Transformation: Politics of Land and Property in China. New York: Oxford
University Press.
4. Benjamin, S. (2004, March). Urban land transformation for pro-poor economies. Geoforum, 35(2), 177-187.
Reference Books:

Course No: HS7008
Course Name: State and Development in Modern China
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course is aimed at using theories in both economics and political science to explain major issues in the
dynamics between China's political system and the path of its economic reform. In particular, the course would
enable students to understand in-depth the institutional context of China's growth and development experience.
Course Content:
Module 1: Introduction to theories of the state (Miliband-Poulantzas debate, the regulatory state, the capitalist
state, the developmental state).
Module 2: Theory and practice
Study of exceptional case studies that connote the relationship between the state and development (regulatory
state, the capitalist state, the developmental state) in the context of East Asian champions such as Japan, Korea,
Singapore, Taiwan, chiefly.
Module 3: Pre-reform economic structures in China
(Discussion on the command economy established in the 1950s in China, how the bureaucracy took over
functions left to markets in capitalist economies, the Great Leap Forward)
Module 4: Decentralization & State entrepreneurialism
Transformation of the Chinese economy since 1978 in agricultural and industrial development, enterprise reform,
foreign trade and foreign investment, chiefly. The module would probe the role of the state in Chinese economy.
Module 5: Political framework for China’s economic development
Understanding of the Chinese governing system and the inter-linkages between structure, power and Party
(Nomenklatura and cadre management, Party-business-relations)
Module 6: In perspective: State and development in China
Discussing how capitalistic is China today & what are the lessons for developing countries (including comparative
assessment with India).

Course No: HS7009
Course Name: Political-economy of modern China
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course provides immersion into understanding of modern China from an integrated political-economy
perspective. It would include coverage of the historical and institutional background of China’s politics, economics
and foreign policy. Detailed assessment of China’s ‘rise’ would be brought down to the present day, thereby
explicating major trends in China that impact contemporary global politics.
Course Content:
Module: Situating China in a global world [Weeks 1, 2, 3]
Understanding the traditional Chinese World Order, introduction to the Cultural Revolution, the pattern and Logic
of China’s Economic reform, role of ‘Plan’ Versus ‘Market’ in China’s Socialist Market Economy, Challenges Facing
the Chinese Economy
Module: China: regionalism and regionalization [Week 4, 5, 6]
Coverage of issue-areas such as China’s Regional Policy in East Asia and its characteristics, the South China Sea
Dispute and China-ASEAN relations, China and the BRICS initiative.
Module: India-China relations [Weeks 7, 8]
Sino-Indian Boundary Dispute: Genesis and developments leading to (and the aftermath of) the 1962 war,
India-China economic relations.
Module: China: major relationships and key issues [Weeks 9, 10, 11]
Concept of “The Responsible Power”, important dyadic relationships such as bilateral ties with the United States,
China’s engagement in Africa, issue-areas such China’s energy security, the Malacca dilemma and responses
Module: Cross-Strait relations [Weeks 12, 13, 14]
Peace and Security Across the Taiwan Strait, Economic interdependence and political divergence across the
Taiwan Strait, legal position of the PRC on the status of Taiwan
Module: China: looking ahead [Week 15, 16]
Interrogating the question - Does China Matter? How does one cope With China's Financial Power its role in world
economy, its fast productivity growth and rising innovation capacity? ?

Course Name: City in Literature and Cinema
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course aims to acquaint scholars with theories and concepts at the interface between cities on one hand and

? Representations of the city
-art and architecture in city
-city cultures and traditions
-crime , romance and relationships in the city
? Streets, social spaces and locations
-understanding key concepts vis-a-vis textual representations.

Course No: HS7021
Course Name: Infrastructure & Housing in Developing Countries: Emerging Challenges and Opportunities
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course explores advanced issues of urban infrastructure and housing from theoretical frames in order to think
through their societal aspects, the politics of policy and programs in India and other contexts of the Global South. It
will include new ways of thinking about the institutional aspects of partnerships within the context of governance,
frames of legal and institutional pluralism, and the politics of Mega Projects.
Outcomes:
Students of advanced studies will be made familiar with key theoretical frames and policy-oriented analysis for

course will help participants to gain both technical and policy-oriented proficiency with substantive theoretical
insights.
Course Content:

infrastructure and services, and shelter supply systems; the social and cultural embedding of Shelter as Space.

incremental versus those focusing on ‘one-shot’ complete provision systems.
3. Infrastructure within an Assemblage frame
4. Legal and Institutional Pluralism
5. City Politics & Governance Municipal and Higher level Parastatal authorities: 73rd and 74th CAA and actual
directives;
6. Practices of Urban Planning: History of planning, pandemics past and present, Land use zoning,
non-conforming use, building bylaws; Advanced Locality Management as Governance; Contemporary Planning
instruments and ideas of Mixed Land use; Mega territory planning and incentive zones; Land acquisition laws and
reality
7. Mega Projects: SEZs, Mega Infrastructures, Smart Cities, Splintering Urbanism

Course No: HS7200
Course Name: Regional Indian Literatures in Translation
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course introduces students to the multiplicity of works produced in the Indian languages in English translation.
It familiarizes students with the various translation theories and the subject of translation practice. This course
offers critical approaches to the complex representations of regional histories, identities, diverse cultural traditions,
and societal structures. The course also illustrates the many indigenous narrative traditions in the genres of short
story, drama, novel and poetry, illustrating the breadth and complexity of regional literatures in translation.
Outcomes:
Students will understand the multifaceted nature of realism and the notion of “earthiness” in regional works. They
will learn to analyze fictional images that express the physical, social and psychological realism in the regional
literatures of India. Students will understand the complex nature of cultural identities in regional Indian literature,
and will acquire skills to compare literary texts in terms of themes and traditions.
Course Content:
• History, Growth, and Role of Translation in India
• Translation: Theories, Approaches, and Key Terms
• Regional Representations of Gender, Class, Space
• Indian Romanticism, Anti-Colonial Literature, and Early Modernism
• The supernatural, and the feminine regional discourse
• Indigenous literary traditions: Sthalapurana in fiction, and folk literature
• Partition and Identities
• Representations of Patriarchy, Matriarchy, and Rural Indian Cultures
• Mapping Rural Spatiality in the Contemporary, and the Pitfalls of Social Climbing
Text Books:

Course No: HS7370
Course Name: 20th Century German Novels
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course is meant for PhD scholars working in the area of German Studies, or for those who find 20th century
German fiction relevant to their research work in areas such as Literary Studies and Philosophy. Its main objective
is to enable the learner to gain a broad literary historical perspective on 20th century German fiction, and to offer
the learner the possibility of in-depth engagement with works of fiction relevant to their research / research
interests.
Outcomes:
Successful completion of this course should give learners a literary historical overview of Novels/Fiction in
German-speaking countries through the 20th century, and a good understanding of fiction relevant to their
research.
Course Content:
• Common component will be a literary historical overview of German fiction over the course of the 20th century.
• Variable component will vary according to the research interest of the scholar/s taking the course. For example:
for a PhD scholar working on a contemporary woman writer, this component can be a survey of major landmarks
in Women's Writing in German Literature (Novels and Novellas).
• Other variable components can be the Modern German Novel, or the post-Holocaust German Novel, Novel in
the two Germanies from 1945-1990 and so on.
The course can be offered in German (using original texts) or in English (using available translations from German
Literature).

Course No: HS7540
Course Name: Advanced Topics in Economics of Innovation and Technological Change
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course is designed to provide students an advanced understanding of economics of innovation and
technological change. The special focus is on the technological change and innovation, innovation dynamics of
firms and industries.
Course Content:
Technology, Innovation and Market Structure
Industry structure; Determinants of market structure; Market structure and innovation; persistence of monopoly,
Schumpeterian hypotheses; Firm size and innovation, technological regimes and sectoral patterns of innovation.
Technology and Economic Growth
Industrial Revolution; Approaches to economic growth: Neo-classical and Evolutionary School- endogenous theory
of innovation; Nelson and Winter - evolutionary theory of technological change.
Diffusion of Technology and Strategic Management of Innovation
Technology Adoption; Diffusion of new technology; Economics of QWERTY, competing technologies,
path-dependence and technological lock-in; system competition and standardization; importance of network
externalities in the knowledge economy: economics of information technology, productivity paradox.
R&D, Patents, International Technology Transfer
The economics of the R&D and Patent System: Patent length and patent breadth, patent pools, patent races,
licensing, Reseach Joint Ventures, R&D spillover; Trade and International Transfer of technology; Multinational
Enterprises (MNEs) and Technology Spillovers.
Public Policy for Innovation and Diffusion
Role of institutions: National systems of innovation and Sectoral Systems of Innovation; The role of universities;
Financing of R&D: internal vs external finance, role of venture capitalists; Patent laws and innovation: Intellectual
property rights and innovation; spinoffs.
Text Books:
G. M. Peter Swann (2009) The Economics of Innovation, Edward Elgar.
Suzanne Scotchmer (2004). Innovation and Incentives. MIT Press
Reference Books:
Brownyn Hall and Nathan Rosenberg (eds.) (2010) Handbook of Economics of Innovation, Vol I &II, Elsevier.

Course No: HS7550
Course Name: Critical Theory in the Social Sciences
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course will critically examine core theories in the social sciences. Working through canonical understandings
of caste, race, class, and gender, it will discuss the challenges posed by an often Eurocentric body of work in
relation to understandings of non-Western societies.
Course Content:
(a) Core Theories in the Social Science
This will cover the canonical writings of Marx, Weber, Durkheim, Simone De Beauvoir, Jane Addams, and David
Harvey.
(b) Postcolonial, historiographic, and feminist critiques
Building on the first set of readings, we move onto critiques posited by Franz Fanon, Arjun Appadurai, Chandra
Mohanty, Judith Butler, and the Subaltern Studies scholars
(c) Case Studies from postcolonial and non-western societies
Here, we cover ethnographies that seek to both critique research and provide new lenses for looking at society.
(d) New Ethnographic Writing
In this module, we examine new forms of writing as a way of addressing critiques and providing new ways of
thinking about society
(e) Field Research
For the final segment, we examine the notion of field work or field study in the social sciences and interrogate
questions of authenticity and identity when understanding the researcher’s privilege.
Text Books:
(a) Morrisson, Kenneth. Marx, Durkheim, Weber: Formations of Modern Social Thought. Sage; 2012.
(b) Seidman, Steven and Jeffrey. C. Alexander (eds.). The New Social Theory Reader. Routledge; 2008.
(c) Guha, Ranajit (ed.). Subaltern Studies Reader. Oxford University Press; 1988.
Reference Books:
(a) Giddens, Anthony. Capitalism and Modern Social Theory. Cambridge University Press; 2013.
(b) Chakraborty, Dipesh. Provincializing Europe: Postcolonial Thought and Historical Difference (Princeton Studies
in Culture/Power/History). Princeton University Press; 2007.

Course No: HS7560
Course Name: Anthropology of Objects and Consumption
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
In this course, we examine studies on objects and consumption given their often marginalized status in
anthropocentric, production-oriented social science research. Through theories of both late capitalism, and
post-Fordist consumption oriented societies, we look at the primacy of objects and processes of consumption in
daily life.
Course Content:
(a) Theories of Consumption.
Here we look at theories that invert questions of production and refocus on questions of consumption through the
work of Daniel Miller.
(b) Questions of non-human life and materiality.
Working through Bruno Latour’s question of networks, the course examines the role that objects play in daily life.
(c) Theories of everyday life.
Primarily reading Michel de Certeau, we attempt a reading of society through an understanding of everyday
consumption and meaning-making.
(d) Popular Culture and Advertising.
Using advertising case studies and popular writing, we examine how objects function in popular consciousness.
(e) Non-anthropomorphic writing
In this last module, we look at forms of writing that attempt a staging of the world from a non-human point of view.
Text Books:
(a) Miller, Daniel. Consumption and its Consequences. Polity; 2012.
(b) Latour, Bruno. Reassembling the Social: An Introduction to Actor-Network-Theory. Oxford University Press;
2007.
(c) de Certeau, Michael. The Practice of Everyday Life. University of California Press; 2011.
Reference Books:
a) Latour, Bruno. An Inquiry into Modes of Existence: An Anthropology of the Moderns. Harvard University Press;
2013.
(b) Miller, Daniel. Stuff. Published by Polity; 2013.
(c) Miller, Daniel (ed.). Materiality (Politics, History, and Culture). Duke University Press; 2005.
(d) Miller, Daniel. A Theory of Shopping. Polity; 2013.

Course No: HS7570
Course Name: Historiography of Science, Technology and Medicine
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The objective of the course is to provide graduating students and research scholars of history of science,
technology and medicine (HSTM) with a theoretical and historical understanding of their academic field. HSTM has
emerged as an academic discipline with its own distinctive historiography. We will discuss how historians of STM
have studied and written about the origin, transformation, circulation and co-production of scientific, technological
and medical knowledge and practices.
Learning outcomes:
In the course, the students will learn about the meaning and importance of historiography and how to place their
own evolving work within the larger historiography of HSTM. The students will learn about the most important
historiographical traditions, the relationship between theory and practice, the local and the global, and the
importance of textual, oral, visual and material cultures of HSTM. They will also learn how to write a literature
review in HSTM.
Course Content:
1. Introduction – what is the history of science, technology and medicine? How does HSTM relate to other
academic disciplines? Why is it important?
2. The origins and development of history of science – history of science before Kuhn, Thomas Kuhn, paradigm
shifts and Scientific Revolutions, Ludwik Fleck, thought styles and thought collectives, Boris Hessen and internal /
external history of science
3. History of science, technology and medicine, and science and technology studies – the origins of Science,
Technology and Society and Science and Technology Studies; Sociology of Scientific Knowledge, Actor Network
Theory and Social Construction of Technology, and its interaction with HSTM
4. From HSTM as knowledge to HSTM as practice – the turn towards practice, circulation and coproduction of
knowledge and practice, visual and material cultures of STM
5. Eurocentrism and HSTM as global history – a critique of Eurocentric history of STM, the Needham Question,
colonial and postcolonial HSTM
6. History of science, technology and medicine in India – historiographical approaches and trends in HSTM in
India
Text Books:
1. Arnold, David. Science, Technology and Medicine in Colonial India. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press,
2000.
2. Biagoli, Mario (ed). The Science Studies Reader. New York: Routledge, 1999.
3. Kuhn, Thomas. The Structure of Scientific Revolutions. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1962.
4. Sismondo, Sergio. An Introduction to Science and Technology Studies. Second Edition. Chichester:
Wiley-Blackwell, 2010.
Reference Books:
1. The Cambridge History of Science. 7 Volumes. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2002–2018.
2. Arnold, David. Everyday Technology - Machines and the Making of India's Modernity. Chicago: University of
Chicago Press, 2013.
3. Basalla, George. "The Spread of Western Science." Science 156 (1967): 611-622.
4. Doel, Ronald E., and Thomas Söderqvist (eds). The Historiography of Contemporary Science, Technology and
Medicine. New York: Routledge, 2006.
5. Edgerton, David. The Shock of The Old: Technology and Global History Since 1900. London: Profile Books,
2006
6. Fleck, Ludwik. Genesis and Development of a Scientific Fact. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1979 (First

The course familiarizes PhD students with the historiography of one of the most important time periods in the

Description:
The course will introduce the students to the sub-field of Borderland Studies within an interdisciplinary focus

Border as conceptual category

4. India’s Himalayan borders as conflict and contact zones.
5. De-centring the border: Flows, networks, communities along the Himalayas.
6. Contemporary articulations of state-making & citizenship in India’s Himalayan borders.

Course No: HS8370
Course Name: Sociolinguistics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course investigates interaction between language and society. It aims at bringing together studies of
grammatical systems and their usage in languages in a social and cultural context. It emphasizes on
sociolinguistic issues that consider variables like social class, gender, ethnicity and cultural variations. This course
familiarizes students with an array of concepts that include language identity, ideology, views and attitude.
Outcomes: This course builds knowledge of language situations that include indigenous/minority languages in
India and beyond. It informs students about the causes of language endangerment and its effects. It enables
discussions related to language policy and planning as well as language assessment and revitalization. It also
equips students with analytical abilities through hands-on training in order to conduct a pilot study by formulating
and testing hypotheses, collecting data, analysing them and drawing generalizations in sociolinguistic research.
Course Content:
• Introduction to Sociolinguistics: Defining sociolinguistics; Some fundamental concepts: Language, dialect and
idiolect; Pidgin and creole; Language and colonization; Influence of society and culture in language use; Language
policy and linguistic rights; India as a linguistic area.
• Language change: Variation and change; Perspectives of language change (Anthropological, Prescriptivist,
Sporadic and Systematic); Diachronic vs. Synchronic changes; Sound change; Lexical change; Syntactic change;
semantic change; Changes in the form of speech
• Multilingualism: Concepts of multilingualism; Multilingualism in education; Scholastic achievements, cognitive
flexibility and social tolerance; Code mixing and code switching; Language endangerment and revitalization;
Language indigeneity; English as a part of Linguistic Ecology; Politics of language in India
• Language Technology and Development: Importance of technology in the development of language; Community
based language development; Technology and language in the context of changing goals and needs of society,
culture and politics in India; Adapting new technologies to strengthen endangered languages
Text Books:
Meyerhoff, M. (2011). Introducing Sociolinguistics. London: Routledge.
Akmajian, A., Farmer, A. K., Bickmore, L., Demers, R. A., & Harnish, R. M. (2017). Linguistics: An Introduction to
Language and Communication. MIT Press.
Reference Books:
Chomsky, N. (2006) Language and Mind, New York: Cambridge University Press.
Fishman, J. A. (1970). Sociolinguistics: A Brief Introduction. Rowley, Mass.: Newbury House.
Kachru, B., Y. Kachru, and S. N. Sridhar (Eds.). (2008) Language in South Asia, New York: Cambridge
University Press.
Montgomery, M. (1986). An Introduction to Language and Society. New York/London: Routledge.
Romaine, S. (2001). Language in Society: An Introduction to Sociolinguistics. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
Sproat, R. (2010). Language, Technology, and Society. London: Oxford University Press.
Yule, G. (2010). The Study of Language (4th Edition), Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

Course No: HS8390
Course Name: Advanced Macroeconomic Theory
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The primary objective of this course is to bring PhD/MS students to the frontier of current research in
macroeconomics. Topics include generation models, the real business cycle, the open economy, economic growth,
and India specific issues like inflation, deficit financing etc.
Course Content:
New growth theory
Real Business cycle theory
Traditional Keynesian theory of fluctuations
Relation between Unemployment and rate of change in money wage rates.
Microeconomic foundations of incomplete nominal adjustment
Advanced theories of consumption
Capital theory and Investment Behaviour
Investment, Budget Deficits and Fiscal Policy
Text Books:
Romer D Advanced Macroeconomics, 3rd cd., McGraw-Hill, 2006 References:
Barro R and Xavier Sala-Martin, Economic Growth, McGraw-Hill (1995)
Blanchard O J and Stanley Fischer, Lectures on Macroeconomics, The MIT Press(1989)
Cooley Thomas, Frontiers of Business Cycle Research, Princeton University Press (1995)
Sargent Thomas, Dynamic Macroeconomic Theory, Harvard University Press (1987)
A list of Journal articles will be distributed for each topic

Course No: HS8770
Course Name: English Language Teaching
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course intends to locate language teaching/learning in the theoretical framework of second/foreign language
learning/teaching. This course familiarizes the learners with the correlation between language structures and
social functions. It demonstrates relevance of language teaching methods in real classroom transactions with
specific reference to comprehensive evaluation of learners’ proficiency.
Outcomes:
The course yields an appreciation of the role of theory and practices in language learning and teaching; an ability
to see through the nature and structure of target language; and the correlation between context, cognition, and
computation in learning; that eventually leads to effective language testing and mapping of proficiencies.
Course Content:
• Theoretical framework and perspectives in language teaching
• Diverse Learners and multilingual classrooms
• Socio-cultural context in learning/teaching English in India
• English Structures
• Linguistics skills in focus
• Theories in second language learning/teaching
• Translanguaging
• Approaches, methods, and techniques in language teaching
• Post Method
• Evaluation and Grading
• Literacy Engagement and Motivation: Rationale, Research
• Teaching and Assessment
Text Books:
1. Richards, J.C. and Rodgers, T.S. Approaches and Methods in Language Teaching, London: Cambridge
University Press, 2001
2. Lapp, D. and Fisher, D. (Eds.) Handbook of Research on Teaching the English Language Arts, London:
Routledge, 2017
Reference Books:
1. Brindley, Susan (ed). Teaching English, London: Routledge, 1993
2. Richards, J. C. & Richards, Jack Croft Curriculum Development in Language Teaching, London: Cambridge
University Press, 2001.

Indian Institute of Technology
Course Details Report
Course No: ID1100
Course Name: Concepts in Engineering Design
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
--
Course Content:
The purpose of this course is to introduce to the undergraduate student the fundamental principles of Engineering
Design which is very important and relevant in the context of to-day’s engineering professionals. The course will
be generic to all engineering disciplines and will not require specialized preparation or pre-requisites in any of the
individual engineering disciplines.
The first eight lectures will introduce the students to the following aspects of design.
1. Philosophy of Engineering Design.
2. Engineering Design Process.
3. Identification and Analysis of needs.
4. Organization of Design Concept.
5. Design Methods.
6. Considerations in Engineering Design.
7. Design decisions.
8. Development of design.
Case studies from field situations and real products will be used to illustrate these principles. Software support will
be provided for self-learning by students.
Text Books:
--
Reference Books:
1. Dandy G. C. and Warner, R.F., "Planning and Design of Engineering Systems" Unwin Hyman, 1989.
2. Eric Laithevaite, (1989), "Invitation to Engineering", Basil Blackwell Inc., Oxford, U.K., 1984.
3. Florman, S.C., "Existential Pleasures of Engineering", St. Martin's Press, New York, 1976.
4. George E.Dieter, "Engineering Design, A Materials and Processing Approach", McGraw Hill International Book
Co., (62:744 DIE (148 532), 1983.
5. Henry Petroski, "To Engineer is Human -The Role of Failure in Successful Design", St. Martin Press
(62.744.004.6 Pet, 167795), 1985.
6. lITO, "Design Thinking Visual Fundamental+ Human Features", (62:744 ING 106961).
7. Lawrence, P. Grayson, Joseph M. Biedenbac (Eds.), "Engineering Education for 215 century" ASEE, 1980,
62:744 DIE (148532), 1980.
8. Morris Asinow, "Introduction to Design", Prentice Hall, (62:744 ASI 23501), 1962.

Course No: ID1200
Course Name: Ecology and Environment
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Objective: To sensitise students to the concepts of Sustainability and its relevance and application to different
fields of Sciences and Engineering.
Course Content:
The course is divided into different modules that are taught by different teachers:
This a two credit course – with two instruction classes every week for 14 weeks.
The modules and the current set of teachers are as follows:
1. Introduction to Sustainability: Dr. B.S. Murty (Civil Engg.)
• Introduction
• Definition of Sustainability
• Sustainability Goals,
• Climate Change
• Case Studies (Eg: Dams, Chemicals, e-waste, IOT, Landfill siting etc)
2. Ecology : Dr. Susy Varughese (Chemical Engg.)
• Ecology – definitions of Ecological Systems
• Biodiversity and Examples
• Historical Impact of Economy on Ecology
• Restoration / Ecological Engineering
3. Energy: Dr. Srinivas Jayanti (Chemical Engg.)
• Energy Demand / Resources
• Pollution from Energy generation
• Energy and Climate Change (Global Warming)
• Energy and Sustainability
• Long Range and Short Range Solutions, (Global vs. India)
4. Water Quality and Waste Management: Dr. Ligy Philip (Civil Engg.)
• Water Quality and Treatment
• Waste Management and Treatment
• Case Studies
5. Water Management and Resources: Dr. B. S. Murty (Civil Engg.)
• Urban Drainage
• Water Resource Management
• Impact of Climate Change
6. Sustainability – Economics/Ethics : Dr. Sudhir Chella Rajan (Humanities and Social Sciences)
• Sustainability and Economics
• Sustainability and Ethics
• Urban Planning Sprawl and Sanitation
• Transportation
• Energy and Smart Grid
• Water , Waste and Governance
7. Environmental Management and Life Cycle Assessment: Dr. R. Ravi Krishna (Chemical Engg.)
• Risk Assessment - Definition
• Pollutant Pathways / Safety/ Exposure
• Liability
• Life Cycle Assessment and Environmental Management
• Case Study
Wrap up – Emphasis on Climate Change and Adaptation
Course Structure:
• Online Recorded Video Lectures
• Live sessions for interaction / Q&A
• Assignments and Poster
• Two Exams – Online on Moodle

Course Name: Emergency Management
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The main objective of the course is to prepare the students for the unexpected health emergency. At the end of the

first aid provision; Types of Disaster: Natural, Environmental, Political, Pandemic; Management: Assessment and
management of first aid incidents - Patient Assessment System; Mass Disaster Management: Prevention,
Preparedness, Relief, and Recovery, Disaster Plans and Procedures; Individual Emergency Management: Airway
Management, Advance Life Support, Recovery Position; The roles and responsibilities of a first responder - Role
of a good Samaritan/citizen, The need to minimize the risk of infection, When and how to call for help; Specific
Emergency Management: Rural Emergency; Wilderness Emergency; Athletic Injuries; Altitude Illness; First aid
equipments and their safe use; Technology for First Aid Training; International organizations on Emergency
Management.

Course No: ID3100
Course Name: First level Creative Engineering Project
Course Type:
Project
Description:
This course is proposed to be an umbrella under which students can work with interested faculty on short-term
creative engineering projects, working on feasible solutions to real-world problems. The level of the project is
expected to involve the material from the first four semesters of the curriculum.
Course Content:
This course will encompass identifying and formulating problems for design and seeking solutions to the real world
challenges through observations, analysis and understanding.
The proposed mechanism of interaction between the faculty and students is as follows:
• A faculty member/student can propose a student project outlining the motivation, objectives, expectations of
student time commitment and deliverables. A document with this content may be developed in collaboration with
the students and shall act as a memorandum for the course.
• The students are expected to work in a self-motivated and self-monitored mode. However, they are encouraged
to interact periodically with the faculty mentor and discuss progress documented in the form of periodic reports.
• The Advisor, co-curricular affairs shall be designated the course co-ordinator. The Advisor along with the faculty
mentor will meet with the students at least twice during the course of the semester to assess progress.
• The Advisor, co-curricular will ensure that the Center for Innovation space and resources are available to the
students and faculty should they choose to use the same.
• The faculty mentor shall assign a letter grade upon completion of the project based on a rubric that was agreed
upon at the start of the semester.
• The students may work in teams but the role and contribution of each of the team members shall be clearly
outlined in all reports submitted to the extent that such progress may be assessed for individual letter grade.
• At the end of the project, all students are expected to turn in a final report containing the complete details of the
project for archival purpose. All project reports may be archived at cfi.iitm.ac.in in a keyword searchable format for
future students’ use. While delivering project goals is important, the overarching objective of this course is to
ensure that the students benefit technologically and realize the importance of planning, discipline and
professionalism in the creative engineering process. This shall form the guiding principle for awarding letter
grades.

As relevant to the proposed project
Reference Books:
As relevant to the proposed project

Course No: ID5010
Course Name: Advanced Materials and Processes
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
(i) To introduce elementary chemical and physical principles underlying recent advances in materials
fabrication/synthesis, design, and processing.
(ii) Examination of cases in advanced materials research and nanotechnology.
Course Content:
(a) Physical and engineering principles for Advanced Materials Science:
Current classification of applied materials, introduction to quantum chemistry and statistical thermodynamics of
materials, bonding in inorganic and organic materials, bonding-structure-property correlations in recently
developed glassy, hybrid (eg. liquid crystals-composites) and polymeric materials (eg. conducting polymers),

Green manufacturing” as an emerging paradigm (Anastas’ criteria), vacuum and thin film technologies,

special case, nanomaterials - synthesis/fabrication and methods of deployment in devices, overview of tools for
integrated computational materials engineering.

The basic physico-chemical and processing principles for the following materials will be covered. (High Tc
superconductors, solar energy and battery materials, optical and magnetic materials, ferroics, biosensor surfaces
and interfaces, self-cleaning surfaces, coatings, functional self-assemblies, organic and inorganic electronic
materials, industrial catalysts).

Course No: ID5011
Course Name: A Hybrid Course on Water Quality – An approach to People’s Water Data
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The learners will be able to:
Identify the major contaminants in drinking water and their impact on health.
Understand water quality (WQ) standards across the world and in India.
Learn ways of measuring major WQ parameters.
Design a field measurement of WQ.
Overlap the data with geospatial information.
Learn the concept of hydroinformatics.
Measure WQ parameters in the field.
Develop a survey and incorporate the data on online platforms.
Model the data generated and assess their use.
Course Content:
The course will be delivered in the form of lecture modules, assignments, discussions, and field measurements.
Evaluation will assess comprehension of the theory and implement the understanding in the form of
measurements. The students will have four week-long interaction with citizens on their water quality along with
measurements leading to ‘People’s Water Data’. Understanding the concepts, data and field realities are expected
to kindle an entrepreneurial interest in them.
Specific components of the course may be taught by different teachers.
The teaching modules:
A. Water quality: Concepts
Water cycle: An introduction; Clean water: A discussion of potable water; Microbial, chemical, heavy metals,
radiological and particulate matter pollution; Measurements and units; Accuracy and precision; Sampling and
guidelines
B. Water quality: Parameters
Water quality parameters: Common parameters such as temperature, pH, conductivity, dissolved oxygen,
alkalinity, oxidation-reduction potential, turbidity and their implications; Microbial contamination in drinking water
and its implications; Common chemical contaminants such as ammonia, nitrate, chloride, BOD and TOC, in
drinking water; Pesticides, weedicides, and specific examples; Emerging contaminants such as pharmaceuticals,
personnel care products, PFAS, etc.; Heavy metals in drinking water and implications; Arsenic in water as an
example; Turbidity and its implications; Radiological parameters; Limits of contaminants in water: Guidelines and
their origin; Enforcement agencies and their role: Legal guidelines; Microbial diversity in water and antimicrobial
resistance
C. Water quality measurements
Measuring water quality: Instrumentation for common WQ parameters; Calibration, validation of accuracy, quality
control of sensors and kits, use of standards; Physical and chemical disinfection: Measurement methods; Heavy
metals: Measurement methods; Turbidity measurements; Ultra-trace measurements; Risks of wastewater
contamination in WQ
D. Water quality survey (source and household)
Field test kits (FTKs); Geo-spatial coordinates, their detection and incorporation in data; Survey research: An
introduction; Statistical analysis of water data; Common water purification methods and technologies at the
household level and in rural communities; Field measurements: Guidelines to the specific techniques being used;
Hydroinformatics: An introduction
E. Measurement, behaviour and impact
Water related practices in the household; Behavioural obstacles to improving water quality; The role of
measurement and information in changing behaviour
F. Work in the field
Training, data and analysis with FTKs and equipment; Analysis of data; Innovations using water quality data: A
discussion
Text Books:
1. N. F. Gray, Drinking water quality: Problems and solutions, 2nd edition (2008), Cambridge University Press.
2. John Dezuane, Handbook of drinking water quality, 2nd edition (1996), Wiley.
3. Stephanie Fraser, Water quality: Assessment and management, 1st Edition (2019), Callisto.
4. Crittenden, J. C., Trussell, R. R., Hand, D. W., Howe, K. J., & Tchobanoglous, G. Stantec's, MWH’s Water
