Course Name: Multivariable Calculus
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
In this basic course on multivariable calculus we introduce the concepts of differential and integral calculus over
Euclidean spaces R^n and their submanifolds. This is a foundational course for learning manifold theory,
differential topology and analysis on manifolds.
Course Content:
Differentiability in Rn , directional derivatives, Chain rule, Inverse function theorem, Implicit function theorem,
Lagrange multiplier method.
Riemann integral of real-valued functions on Euclidean spaces, Fubini’s theorem, Partition of unity, change of
variables.
Differential forms on Rn , simplices and singular chains, Stokes’ theorem for integral of differential forms on chains
(general version) on Rn , closed and exact forms, Poincaré lemma, Classical Green’s theorem, divergence
theorem and Stokes’ formula as applications of general form of Stokes’ theorem.
Arbitrary submanifolds of Rn not necessarily open, differentiable functions on submanifolds, tangent spaces,
vector fields.
Text Books:
1. Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, Third Edition, McGraw Hill International Editions,
Mathematical Studies 1976; Paper-back Indian Edition 2017.
2. S. Kumaresan, A Course in Differential Geometry and Lie groups, Hindustan Book Agency, Trim 22, 2002.
Reference Books:
1. W. Fleming, Functions of Several Variables, Second Edition, Springer-Verlag, 1977.
2. J. Munkres, Analysis on Manifolds, Addison-Wesley, 1991.
3. M. Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds, A Modern Approach to Classical theorems of Advanced calculus,
W.A.Benjamin, Inc.,1965.
Course No: MA5380
Course Name: Topology
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
In this basic course on topology we introduce the concept of topological spaces and give several examples where
they naturally occur. We develop classical constructions to form new topological spaces. We introduce
characterizing properties like connectedness, compactness and separation axioms and prove important basic
results. The knowledge of topological spaces and their properties are indispensible in several branches of pure
and applied mathematics. This foundational course is necessary and sufficient for a beginning graduate student to
take further courses on algebraic and differential topology.
Course Content:
Topological Spaces: open sets, closed sets, neighbourhoods, bases, subbases, limit points, closures, interiors,
continuous functions, homeomorphisms.
Examples of topological spaces: subspace topology, product topology,metric topology, order topology, topological
groups.
Quotient topology, examples of quotient topology: construction of cylinder, cone, suspension, Moebius band, torus,
orbit spaces.
Connectedness and Compactness: Connected spaces, Components, Local connectedness, Compact spaces,
Local compactness, Tychnoff Theorem.
Separation Axioms, Urysohn lemma, Urysohn Metrization theorem,Tietze Extension theorem, One-point
compactification, paracompactness and partition of unity.
Text Books:
1. J. Dugundji, Topology, UBS, 1999.
2. M. A. Armstrong, Basic Topology, Springer, 2005.
Reference Books:
1. J. R. Munkres, Topology: A First Course, Prentice Hall, 1975.
2. G. F. Simmons: Introduction to Topology and Modern Analysis, Tata McGraw-Hill, 1963.

Course No: MA5390
Course Name: Ordinary Differential Equations
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The prime objective is to introduce theory and concepts of ordinary differential equations. The course discusses
various solution techniques (including series methods) for linear and nonlinear ODEs and also for system of
differential equations. The course intends to give understanding of the properties of solutions to the students and
make them able to anlyze it. It provides a strong foundation for many other mathematics courses.
Course Content:
Existence-Uniqueness for systems: Picard’s theorem, Non-local existence theorem. (6 lectures)
Second Order Equations: General solution of homogeneous equations, Non-homogeneous equations, Wronskian,
Method of variation of parameters, Sturm comparison theorem, Sturm separation theorem, Boundary value
problems, Green's functions, Sturm-Liouville problems. (15 lectures)
Series Solution of Second Order Linear Equations: ordinary points, regular singular points, Legendre polynomials
and properties, Bessel functions and properties. (15 lectures)
Systems of Differential Equations: Algebraic properties of solutions of linear systems, The eigenvalue-eigenvector
method of finding solutions, Complex eigenvalues, Equal eigenvalues, Fundamental matrix solutions, Matrix
exponential. (4 lectures)
Text Books:
1. E.A. Coddington, An Introduction to Ordinary Differential Equations, PHI Learning 1999.
2. Tyn Myint U, Ordinary Differential Equations, Elesvier North- Holland, 1978.
Reference Books:
1. M. Braun, Differential Equations and Their Applications, 3rd Ed., Springer-Verlag, 1983.
2. G.F. Simmons, Differential Equations with Applications and Historical Notes, 2nd Ed.,McGraw- Hill, 1991.
3. P.J. Collins, Differential and Integral Equations, Oxford University Press, 2006.
4. W.E.Boyce and R.C. Di-Prima, Elementary Differential Equations and Boundary Value Problems, John Wiely &
Sons, 2001.
5. R.P. Agarwal and D. O'Regan, An Introduction to Ordinary Differential Equations, Springer- Verlag, 2008.

Course No: MA5400
Course Name: Probability Theory
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course is a first course on Probability Theory. First, probability spaces seen as measure spaces with total
mass equal to unity. Then the student will learn different notions of convergence of sequences of random
variables, culminating in the strong law of large numbers. Finally, the topic of convergence in distribution will be
studied in detail, culminating in the central limit theorem.
Course Content:
Probability: Axiomatic Definitions, Three Definitions of Probability, Independent Events, Arithmetical Density,
Counting and Probability.Random Variables, Distributions and Expectations, Discrete and Continuous Random
Variables, Borel Fields and General Random Variables.Conditioning and Independence, Sequential Sampling,
Mean Variance and Transforms.Poisson Process, Law of Large Numbers, Central Limit Theorem, Stirling's
Formula and De-Moivre's Theorem.Introduction to Random Walk, Markov Chain and Martingale.
Text Books:
K. L. Chung and F. AitSahlia, Elementary probability theory, fourth edition, Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics,
Springer-Verlag, New York, 2003.
Reference Books:
1. Feller, William. An Introduction to Probability Theory and its Applications. Vol. I and II. New York, NY: Wiley,
1968-1971.
2. Dudley, R. M. Real Analysis and Probability. Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 2002.
3. Jacod, Jean; Protter, Philip. Probability essentials. Second edition. Universitext. Springer-Verlag, Berlin, 2003.
4. Walsh John B. Knowing the Odds: An Introduction to Probability. American Mathematical Soc. 2012.

Course No: MA5430
Course Name: Algebra II Ring Theory & Field Theory
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The objecive of this course is two-fold. First, to introduce modules over commutative and non-commutative rings
and do some of the interesting properties of simple and semi-simple modules. Secondly, do advanced topics in
ring theory and field theory as a continuation of Algebra I.
Course Content:
Module Theory: Right and Left modules ; Examples over Z , polynomial rings and other simple rings ; Quotient
modules ; module homomorphisms ; homomorphism theorems.
Ring Theory: Structure Theorem of modules over a PID ; a polynomial ring over a UFD is again a UFD ; basic
properties of Noetherian rings and modules ; Universal Property of a Polynomial Ring; Quotient field and
localization for integral domains.
Field Theory : Criteria for Irreducibility ; Classical Straightedge and Compass construction and examples ; normal
and separable extensions.
Basic Non-Commutative Algebra: Linear Maps and Modules over non-commutative rings ; Simple and
Semi-simple modules and rings.
Text Books:
1. D. S. Dummit and R. M. Foote: Abstract Algebra, 2nd Edition, John-Wiley, 1999.
2. S. Lang: Algebra 3rd Edition, Addison-Wisely, 1999.
Reference Books:
1. J.A. Gallian: Contemporary Abstract Algebra, 4th Ed., Narosa, 1999.
2. M. Artin: Algebra, Prentice Hall inc 1994.
3. I.N. Herstein: Topics in Algebra, John-Wiley, 1995.
4. T. A. Hungerford: Algebra, Graduate Texts in Mathematics, Vol. 73, Springer-Verlag, 1980.

Course No: MA5440
Course Name: Combinatorics and Number Theory
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
To acquaint the students with the basics of combinatorics and number theory. It aims at giving a glimpse of
discrete mathematics, especially those topics that could not be covered in Fundamentals of Discrete Mathematics,
but are used mostly in applications.
Course Content:
Combinatorics: Numbers and counting, partitions and permutations, principle of inclusion and exclusion, pigeon
hole principle, recurrence relations, generating Functions.
Number Theory: Primes, divisibility and the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, prime number theorem, Euclidean
algorithm, congruences, ring of integers mod n, chinese remainder theorem, arithmetic functions, Fermat's last
theorem, Mobius inversion formula, quadratic residues, quadratic reciprocity law, binary quadratic forms, continued
fractions, Pell's equation, Diophantine equations.
Text Books:

Learning, 2003.
2. I. Niven, H.S. Zuckerman, and H.L. Montgomery. An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, Wiley, 1991.

Course No: MA5450
Course Name: Functional Analysis
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
In this course we focus on the basic theory of infinite dimensional vector spaces equipped with a norm or an
inner-product. It has numerous applications in both pure and applied mathematics. This theory provides the
framework for the theory of harmonic analysis, differential equations, representation theory, operator
theory/algebra, quantum probability, quantum mechanics etc.
Course Content:
Unit I: (14 lectures)
Normed linear spaces, Banach spaces; Classical examples: C([0,1]), lp, c, c0, c00, Lp[0,1]; Continuity and
boundedness of linear operator; Quotient spaces; Finite dimensional normed spaces; Riesz lemma,
(non)compactness of unit ball; Seperability with examples;
Unit II: (10 lectures)
Hahn Banach extension theorem, Open mapping theorem, Closed graph theorem, Uniform boundedness principle.
Unit III: (16 lectures)
Hilbert spaces, Projection theorem; Orthonormal basis, Bessel inequality, Parseval equality; Dual, Duals of
classical spaces-c0, lp, Lp[0,1]; Riesz representation theorem, Adjoint of an operator; Double dual, Weak and
weak* convergence;
Text Books:
1. M. Fabian, P. Habala, P. Hajek, V. M. Santalucia, J. Pelant and V. Zizler, Functional analysis and
infinite-dimensional geometry. (Canadian Math. Soc, Springer 2001).
2. M. T. Nair, Functional analysis. (PHI-Learning, New Delhi, Fourth Print 2014).
Reference Books:
1. B. Bollobas, Linear analysis (Cambridge Univ. Press 1999).
2. J. Conway, A course in functional analysis. (Springer 2007).
3. C. Goffman and G. Pedrick, A first course in functional analysis, (Prentice-Hall 1974).
4. P. D. Lax, Functional analysis (Willey interscience 2002).
5. B.V Limaye, Functional analysis (New Age International 1996).
6. M. Reed and B. Simon, Methods of Modern Mathematical Physics, Vol I. (Academic press, 1980).

Course Type:
Theory
Description:

Course No: MA5490
Course Name: Fluid Dynamics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course is devised to introduce the fundamental aspects of fluid flow behaviour. Some of the basic ideas that
will be taught in this course include, steady state mechanical energy balance equation for fluid flow systems,
estimation of pressure drop in fluid flow systems and performance characteristics of fluid machinery.
Course Content:
Kinematics of Fluid flow, Laws of fluid motion, Inviscid incompressible flows, two and three-dimensional motions,
Airfoil theory, inviscid compressible flows;
Viscous incompressible flows, Navier-Stokes equations of motion and some exact solutions; Flows at small
Reynolds numbers; Boundary layer theory.
Text Books:

Course No: MA5540
Course Name: Probability and Statistics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Probability theory is the branch of mathematics that deals with modelling random processes (uncertainty). It plays
a fundamentally important role due to its direct application in many real life problems. It also forms the
fundamental basis for many other areas in the mathematical sciences including statistics, modern optimisation
methods and risk modelling. This course provides an introduction to probability theory, random variables and
Markov processes.
Course Content:
Probability calculus- Random variables- Standard discrete and continuous distributions- Expectation- Moments-
Law of large numbers. Data presentation- Frequency distributions and their characteristics- sampling distributions-
Point and interval estimation- Tests of hypotheses- Large and small sample tests.Curve fitting- Simple correlation
and regression.
Text Books:
1. Introduction to probability by Dimitri P. Bertsekas and John N.Tsitsiklis, 2nd edition.
2. Mathematical Statistics with Applications by John E. Freund
Reference Books:
1. Introductory Statistics by Sheldon M.Ross , Third edition.
2. Fundamentals of applied probability and random processes by OliverC. Ibe, 2nd edition.

Course No: MA5720
Course Name: Numerical Analysis of Diff. Equations
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The objective is to study the basic theory and application of various numerical methods for
solving ordinary and partial differential equations.
Course Content:
Ordinary Differential Equations: Initial value problems- basic theory and application of multistep methods (explicit
and implicit), stability analysis- zero stability, absolute stability, relative stability and intervals of stability, eigenvalue
problems, predictor- corrector methods, Runge-Kutta methods, boundary value problems-shooting methods.Partial
Differential Equations: (a) Parabolic Equations:Explicit and implicit finite difference approximations to
one-dimensional heat equation, Alternating Direction Implicit (ADI) methods. (b) Hyperbolic equations and
Characteristics: Numerical integration along a characteristic, equations, numerical solution by the method of
characteristics, finite diference solution of second order wave equation. (c) Elliptic equations: finite difference
methods in polar coordinates, techniques near curved boundaries, improvement of accuracy- direct and iterative
schemes to solve systems, methods to accelerate the convergence. (d) Convergence, consistency and stability
analysis.
Text Books:
1. S S Sastry, Introductory methods of Numerical Analysis, 5th Edition, Prentice Hall of India, 2012.
2. G D Smith, Numerical Solution of PDE: Finite Difference Methods, Clarendon Press, 1985.
Reference Books:
1. M K Jain, S R K Iyengar and R K Jain, Numerical Methods for Scientific and Engineering Computation,
5th edition, New Age International, 2007.
2. G Evan, J Blackledge and P Yardley, Numerical methods for PDEs, Springer, 2009.

Course Name: Fast Matrix Algorithms
Course Type:
Theory
Description:

HODLR matrices, HSS matrices, Generalised Rybicki Press method, Fast Fourier Transform, Non-uniform fast

including HODLR, HSS, H matrices (4 lectures)
7. Fast direct solvers (5 lectures)
8. Fast Fourier transform (2 lectures)
9. Non-uniform fast Fourier transform (3 lectures)
10. Butterfly algorithms (3 lectures)
11. Randomized numerical linear algebra (5 lectures)

Course Name: Mathematics of Fractals
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
One might think of fractals as just complex shapes and beautiful pictures generated by computers. They are much
more than that. In fact, in an abstract sense, anything that occurs randomly and is irregular may turn out to be a
fractal. Fractals arise in places as tiny as the membrane of a cell and as gigantitic as the solar system. In this
course, the student will be taught the mathematical theory of fractals. Certain selected applications will be dealt
with, as the course progresses.

Hausdorff measure and dimension, Fractal Interpolation Functions, Hidden Variable FIF, Fractal Splines, Fractal
Surfaces, Measures on Fractals, Complex Dynamics, Mandelbrot Set, Julia Set and Fatou Set.

Course No: MA6041
Course Name: GIAN 191003K02: Fractal Geometric Measure Theory and Applications
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The course is to provide the student with a profound knowledge of fractals through geometric measure theory. The
course content supplements and complements courses in measure theory, analysis, topology, and probability
theory. It enables the participants to employ new and powerful methods to compute different types of dimensions
associated with fractal objects. It starts with some simple but very important examples of fractal sets and introduce
some notions of fractal dimensions. It presents some basic methods of to compute various types of dimensions.
Then it will cover the basic geometric-measure theory: Radon measures, metric-outer measures, and their
properties. Covering theorems: (5r-covering theorem, Vitaly covering theorem, Besicovitch covering theorem).
Differentiation of measures and using these results for the characterization of the absolute continuity of a
measure. Density estimates for Radon measures and their consequences for the positivity of the Hausdorff
measure and Packing measure. It will cover notions of the dimension of measures, the dimension of projection and
the product of fractal sets and the dimension of the slices of fractal sets. Some aspects of discrete dynamical
systems and Birkhoff’s Ergodic Theory will be covered as these tools are required to study fractal sets. The
Hutchison Theorem will be discussed for the computation of the Hausdorff dimension of self-similar fractals with
well-separated cylinders. The fractal dimensions of the most well-known self-similar and self-affine fractals. Also,
the course will cover overlapping constructions of fractals, Hochman’s Theorem, the absolute continuity of
Bernoulli convolutions, Dimension theory of self-affine fractals: Self-affine carpets, sub-additive pressure,
self-affine function graphs, Multifractal analysis of self-similar measures and Large deviation multifractal analysis.
Moreover, the course will give the students to classify and analyze various non-linear phenomena and complex
structure in sciences and engineering through fractal dimensions.
Course Content:
IteratedFunction Systems (IFS), Separation conditions, Hausdorff- and Packing measures. Fractal dimensions,
Mass-distribution Principle and Frostman’s Lemma, Covering theorems, 5r-covering theorem, Vitaly covering
theorem, Differentiation of measures, Lebesgue density Theorem, Density Theorems for Hausdorff and Packing
measures, Hausdorff- and Packing- and Lq and entropy dimension of a measure, Dimension estimates for the
projection of fractal sets, Dimension estimates for the products and slices of fractal sets, The dimension of fractal
function and fractal graphs, Multifractal analysis of measures, Multifractal analysis of self-similar measures,
Large-deviation multifractal analysis, Application of Large deviation multifractal analysis in Internet traffic, Fractal
interpolation functions and their properties, Recurrent fractal functions, Bounds of box-counting dimensions of
fractal functions, Application of Fractal Functions in Differential and Integral Equations.
Text Books:
1. B. Barany, K. Simon, B. Solomyak, Self-similar and Self-affine Sets and Measure, Vol-276, Mathematical
Surveys
and Monographs, AMS, Providence, 2023.
2. P. Mattila, Geometry of Sets and Measures in Euclidean Spaces, Cambridge University Press, 1995.
3. F. Przytycki, M. Urbanski, Conformal Fractals: Ergodic Theory Methods, Cambridge University Press, 2010.
4. K. J. Falconer, The Geometry of Fractal sets, Cambridge University Press, 1985.
5. K. J. Falconer, Techniques in Fractal Geometry, John Wiley & Sons, 1997.
Reference Books:
1. C. J. Bishop, Y Peres, Fractals in Probability and Analysis, Cambridge University Press, 2017.
2. P. Massopust, Fractal Functions, Fractal Surfaces, and Wavelets, 2nd edition, Academic Press, 2016.

Course Name: Introduction to Lie Algebras
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
To prepare the students in basics of Lie algebras.

Course No: MA7557
Course Name: Random Graphs and Complex Networks
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Complex networks are huge real life networks like Neural, Social, Communication networks or The World wide
web. The study of these are hindered by their immense size. The only feasible approaches are studying the local
structure or use the idea of random graphs and asymptotes. This course aims to prepare the interested student to
delve in to the fascinating area which is a current topic of huge interest.
Course Content:
Introduction to graphs and connectivity, Complex networks with real world examples: Internet, Social networks,
Brain, collaboration network.
Scalefreeness and small world properties. Random graphs and the need for it. Useful probabilistic methods and
results.
Phase transition in random graphs: The evolution of clusters. The giant component and Central limit theorem.
Criticality properties and bounds.
Models suitable for Complex networks with related results: 1. Generalized random graphs, 2. Configuration model
and 3. Preferential attachment models.
Text Books:
R. van der Hofstad, Random Graphs and complex networks, Vol:1, Cambridge University Press, 2016.
Reference Books:
R. van der Hofstad, Random Graphs and complex networks, Vol:1 & 2, (Class notes), 2013-2014, e-copy available
from the author.

Course No: MA7870
Course Name: Game Dynamics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course aims to equip interested phd students with fundamentals of single and multipopulation game dynamics
which is an active area of research with applications in Biology, Economics and Learning. The objective is to make

Course Content:

Course No: MD1004
Course Name: Medical Biochemistry
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
1. To understand the biochemistry of human body fluids
2. To learn the disorders of carbohydrate, protein and lipid metabolism
3. To appreciate enzymology and disease associated with it
4. To acquire knowledge on organ specific biochemical tests
5. To understand the significance of nutritional biochemistry in human health
Course Content:
Introduction to medical biochemistry, Scope of clinical biochemistry
Biochemistry of body fluids – Blood, Lymph, cerebrospinal fluid, synovial fluid,
pleural fluid, peritoneal fluid, amniotic fluid, saliva, sweat, tears and urine
Disorders of carbohydrate metabolism – Diabetes Mellitus, Galactosemia, Glycogen
storage diseases, hereditary fructose intolerance, Hunter syndrome, Hurler syndrome,
mucopolysaccharidoses.
Disorders of protein metabolism – Phenylketonuria, Maple syrup urine disease,
Homocystinuria, Tyrosinemia, Alkaptonuria, Lysomal storage disorders.
Protein folding disorders - Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's
disease, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, cystic fibrosis, Gaucher's disease, Spinal muscular
dystrophy, Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Transthyretin amyloidosis.
Disorders of lipid metabolism - Hyperlipidemia, Hypercholesterolemia, Familial
hypercholesterolemia and Familial combined hyperlipidemia, lipoprotein lipase
deficiency, Tangier disease, abetalipoproteinemia.
Purine metabolism disorders – Lesch- Nyhan syndrome, adenosine deaminase
deficiency, X – linked agammaglobulinemia, Hyperuricemia and gout.
Pyrimidine metabolism disorders – Orotic aciduria, Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase
deficiency, 5- fluorouracil toxicity, Tyrosinemia type 1.
Enzyme classification and nomenclature, enzyme kinetics and mechanism of enzyme
action. Clinical significance of the following enzymes - transaminases (ALT & AST),
creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, alkaline phosphatase, carbonic anhydrase,
aldolase, amylase, lactase, lipases, Glucose -6- phosphate dehydrogenase, glutamate
dehydrogenase, choline esterase.
Overview of organ specific tests.
Cardiac function – Troponin, creatinine kinase (CK), myoglobin, natriuretic peptides
(BNP, NT – proBNP).
Kidney function - creatinine, urea, electrolyte balance, filtration rate, glomerular
filtration rate (GFR).
Liver function – ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin.
Bone health – ALP, calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone (PTH), 25,
hydroxyvitamin D.
Pancreas – Glucagon, insulin, c-peptide, blood glucose
Gastrointestinal function – Fecal occult blood, stool tests for fat, stool tests for
reducing substances, stool tests for parasites
Inflammatory markers – C – reactive protein (CRP), Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
(ESR), Interleukin – 6, Interleukin – 1 beta, Tumor necrosis factor alpha, white blood
cell count (WBC)
Lung Health – Spriometry, Diffusion capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide
(DCLO), Arterial blood gases (ABG), Bronchodilator response test, serum surfactant
protein D (SP-D).
Brain Health – Neurofilament light chain (NfL); Amyloid-beta (Aß); Tau protein,
Homocysteine, S100B, Brain derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)
Complete blood profile
Nutritional Biochemistry: Fat soluble vitamins – general characteristics,
classification, vitamin storage in the human body, daily requirements, avitaminoses,
coenzyme Q, stigmasterol. Water soluble vitamins – Vitamin B complex, Vitamin C,
Choline, Inositol, Para-aminobenzoic acid, Alpha – lipoic acid, Carnitine, Bioflavanoids,
Vitamers (Isotels). Essential trace elements – Iron, Zinc, iodine etc., and their functions
in the body; dietary sources of trace elements; factors affecting absorption and utilization
of trace elements trace elements deficiency and diseases. Recommendations for daily
intake of fat and water soluble vitamins and trace elements. Vitamin and essential
minerals deficiency disorders.
Enzyme assays – ALT, AST, Creatinine kinase
Blood glucose levels, HbA1c measurement, complete lipid profile, Electrolyte analysis – sodium,
potassium and chloride levels in blood. RFT and LFT, Thyroid function tests, vitamin analysis –
vitamin B12 and folate. Calcium and phosphate measurement in blood. Blood haemoglobin, transferrin
and ferritin

Course Type:
Theory
Description:

Course Name: Medical Genetics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
1. To understand the genetic and epigenetic etiology of human diseases
2. To appreciate the structure of DNA, chromosome and significance of human genome project

4. To acquire knowledge on Gene therapy and gene delivery systems

Introduction to Clinical Genetics; History of Human Genetics; Pedigrees- gathering family

Course No: MD3002
Course Name: Basics of Pharmacology
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
1. To understand the pharmacological concepts such as pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of drugs. As
well pharmacotherapy.
2. To appreciate the mathematical modelling of pharmaco -kinetics and –dynamics.
3. To acquire skills to calculate the combinatorial efficacy of therapeutic drugs and predict their outcome.
4. To distinguish among the body of pharmacological agents and substances, based on their generic name,
pharmacological classification, mechanism of action, clinical effects and side effects (adverse events and
severe adverse events).
5. Define various models representing rates and order of reactions and calculate pharmacokinetic parameters
(eg, zero- and first-order) from experimental data based on these models.
6. To attain hands on skill in pharmacological investigations (in vitro and pre-clinical)
Course Content:
i) Introduction, definitions and scope of pharmacology
ii) Routes of administration of drugs –(Enteral route – Oral, Sub lingual &
Rectal, Parenteral – Intra venous, intra muscular, subcutaneous, intra-arterial,
intra thecal, Topical – dermal, transdermal, Ophthalmic, Otologic, Nasal)
iii) Pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion)
iv) Pharmacodynamics (physiological receptors, specificity of drug responses,
signalling pathways, mechanism of drug action)
v) Factors modifying drug effects (route of administration, rate and degree of
absorption, rate of elimination, effect of other drugs, tolerance, idiosyncrasy
and allergy)
vi) Drug toxicity – (Acute, sub- acute and chronic toxicity)
vii) Pre-clinical evaluations – (in vitro and in vivo studies – Animal
Mathematical Pharmacology:
i) Models to analyse the efficacy of combination therapy
ii) Target Mediated Drug Disposition (TMDD) model
iii) Mathematical analysis of ligand – receptor system
iv) Pharmacokinetic – pharmacodynamic modelling and simulation
v) Mathematical analysis of the pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PKPD)
behaviour of therapeutic agents
vi) Mathematical models in drug design and development
vii) Free Energy Calculations in Rational Drug Design
Chemotherapy
i) Introduction – General principles of anti-microbial therapy, Sulfonamides and
co-trimoxazole – Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics, Uses
ii) Penicillin’s and Cephalosporin’s – Classification of drugs, Mode of action,
Mechanism of resistance, Anti-bacterial Spectrum, Dosage.
iii) Tetracycline and Chloramphenicol - Mode of action, anti-bacterial Spectrum,
Dosage.
iv) Macrolides, Amino glycosides, Polyene & Polypeptide antibiotics -
Classification of drugs, Mode of action, Anti -bacterial Spectrum, Dosage.
v) Quinolines and Fluroquinolines - Classification of drugs, Mode of action,
Anti-bacterial Spectrum, Dosage.
vi) Antifungal antibiotics - Classification of drugs, Mode of action, Anti-fungal
spectrum, Dosage.
vii) Antiviral agents - Classification of drugs, Mode of action, Dosage, Uses
viii) Chemotherapy of tuberculosis and leprosy – First line and second line Drugs,
Mode of action, Dosage, Uses
ix) Chemotherapy of Malaria – Classification of drugs, Pharmacokinetics and
Pharmacodynamics, Dosage, Guidelines for Prophylaxis and therapy for
malaria
x) Chemotherapy of protozoal infections (amoebiasis, Giardiasis) - Classification
of drugs, Mode of action, Dosage.
xi) Pharmacology of Anthelmintic drugs - Classification of drugs, Mode of
action, Dosage
xii) Chemotherapy of cancer (Neoplasm’s) – General Principles in
Pharmacotherapy for cancer, Classification of drugs, Pharmacokinetic and
Pharmacodynamic Parameters, Dosage, Uses.
Cardiovascular drugs: Classification, mode of action and dosage of the following
i) Antihypertensive
ii) Anti-anginal drugs
iii) Anti-arrhythmic drugs
iv) Drugs used for therapy of Congestive Heart Failure
v) Drugs used for hyperlipidaemias
CNS drugs:
i) Adrenergic and anti-adrenergic drugs – types of Adrenergic receptors,
endogenous catecholamine Classification of drugs, Pharmacokinetics and
pharmacodynamics, Uses.
ii) Cholinergic and anticholinergic drugs - types of cholinergic receptors,
Classification of drugs, Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, Uses
iii) Neuromuscular blockers – Classification of drugs & uses
iv) Mydriactics and miotics - Classification of drugs & uses
v) Drugs used in myasthenia gravis - Classification of drugs, Mode of action,
Dosage
vi) Drugs used in Parkinsonism - Classification of drugs, Mode of action, Dosage
Renal Drugs – Diuretics & anti-diuretics
Text Books:

Course No: MD5006
Course Name: Stem Cell Technologies and Regenerative Medicine: From Bench to Bedside
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course is designed to provide a comprehensive understanding of stem cell biology, advanced stem cell
technologies, and their applications in disease modeling, therapeutics, and personalized medicine. The course will
be split into five major units, covering theory, laboratory work, research projects, and clinical translation. It will offer
students a robust foundation in both the scientific principles and practical applications of stem cell technology for
the treatment of diseases, organ regeneration, and precision medicine.
Learning Objectives:
1. Foundational Knowledge of Stem Cell Biology:
• Understand the types and functions of stem cells, including embryonic, adult, and induced pluripotent stem cells
(iPSCs).
• Grasp the processes of cellular differentiation and niche-based regulation in tissue maintenance and
regeneration.
2. Competency in Disease Modeling and Precision Medicine:
• Employ stem cells and iPSC-derived organoids to model diseases and study conditions such as
neurodegenerative disorders and cancer.
• Understand and analyze patient-specific models for drug testing and therapeutic development in personalized
medicine.
3. Skill in Advanced Stem Cell Techniques:
• Practice core stem cell techniques, including cell culture, differentiation, 3D organoid creation.
4. Application of Stem Cells in Translational Research:
• Analyze the translation of stem cell research from lab to clinical settings, focusing on case studies of therapies
for cardiovascular, neural, and pancreatic tissues.
• Understand clinical pathways and considerations for moving stem cell research into therapeutic applications.
5. Understanding of Ethical, Regulatory, and Commercial Contexts:
• Evaluate ethical considerations and regulatory frameworks relevant to stem cell therapies, including patient rights
and safety standards.
• Explore the commercial landscape, including patenting, intellectual property, and market challenges in the
biotech industry.
Course Content:
Unit 1: Stem Cell Biology and Disease Modeling
1 Stem Cell ( Types and Potency
Embryonic SCs, adult SCs , and induced pluripotent SCs (
Stem cell differentiation and self renewal mechanisms
Niche regulation of stem cells
2 Molecular Mechanisms in Stem Cell Biology
Signaling pathways controlling stem cell fate (Wnt, Notch, Hedgehog,
BMP)
E pigenetic regulation of stem cells and reprogramming
3 Disease Modeling with iPSCs and Organoids
Generating iPSCs from patient cells
Using stem cell models for studying cancer, neurodegenerativedisorders, and genetic diseases
Case studies: Dise ase modeling for Parkinson s, Alzheimer s, diabetes,
and cystic fibrosis
4 High Throughput Screening for Drug Discovery
Stem cells in drug testing and personalized medicine
Organoids for screening drug efficacy and toxicity
Role of stem cells in high throughput genetic screens
Unit 2:
Stem Cell Therapeutics and Regenerative Medicine
1
Stem Cell Isolation and Culture Techniques
Isolation and culture of different types of stem cells (ESCs, iPSCs,
A SCs)
Maintaining pluripotency and differentiation of stem cells
Characterizing stem cells using flow cytometry,
immunohistochemistry, and transcriptomics
2 Organoid Development and Analysis
Protocols for generating brain, liver, and heart organoids from SCs
Functional analysis of organoids: Imaging, molecular assays, and
electrophysiology
3 Cryopreservation and Biobanking
Biobanking protocols for long term storage of SCs and organoids
Importance of biobanking in research and clinical applications
Unit 3:
Advanced Techniques in Stem Cell Research (3 Credits)
1 Stem Cell Isolation and Culture Techniques
Isolation and culture of different types of stem cells ( A SCs, iPSCs)
Maintaining pluripotency and differentiation of stem cells

Unit 4: Clinical Applications and Translation (1.5

Personalized iPSC lines and organoids for drug testing

Course No: MD5008
Course Name: Control Systems in Biomedical Systems and Devices
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
1. To teach modern control fundamentals
2. Establish a framework for control design for medical devices
3. Give examples and enhance the understanding of controls in physiology
Course Content:
1 Models of physiological systems, feedback and feedforward control, cross
coupling among feedback paths, positive and negative feedback loops, basics of proportional (P),
integral(I) and derivative(D) actions.
2 Introduction to linear systems and state space modelling of physical systems. Analysis of state
space models, Controllability and Observability. 5
3 Design of control systems : Understanding system performance specifications, synthesis of PID
controller for given specifications, lead-lag compensation, Ziegler-Nichols tuning method, design
for pole-zero cancellation and issues, control system design using state-space approach, pole
placement through state-feedback, optimal control, parameter variation and sensitivity analysis.
4 Model predictive control and applications?? Introduction to MPC and Receding Horizon Control,
Prediction Models: Linear, Nonlinear, and Physiological Models, Formulation of the MPC
Optimization Problem, Design of Cost Functions and Weighting Matrices, Constraint Handling in
Inputs, Outputs, and States, Solvers and Real-Time Optimization Techniques, Stability and
Feasibility in MPC, Applications of MPC in Medical Devices
5 Introduction to machine learning in control, Overview of AI control paradigms, Learning-based vs.
model-based design trade-offs. Introduction to RL concepts including Markov Decision Processes,
value functions, and policy optimization. Application of RL to dynamic systems control with focus
on exploration-exploitation trade-off, reward design, and safety. Case studies in robotic
prosthetics, glucose regulation, and adaptive therapy control.
Text Books:
1 C. Cosentino and D. Bates, ‘An Introduction to Feedback Control in Systems Biology’, CRC Press, 2011.
2 Sean Mayne, Control system and reinforcement Learning, Cambridge, 2022
3 Marco Schoen, Introduction to Intelligent Systems, Control, and Machine Learning using MATLAB

Course No: MD5010
Course Name: Mechanical Design for Biomedical Devices
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This elective introduces mechanical engineering students to the principles and practices of designing mechanical
systems for
biomedical devices. The course emphasizes real-world clinical needs, regulatory requirements, and
multidisciplinary teamwork.
Students will learn to translate clinical requirements into mechanical design specifications, select appropriate
materials and
manufacturing methods, and develop functional prototypes. The course culminates in a team-based design project
addressing an
actual clinical challenge.
• Understand the role of mechanical design in biomedical devices
• Apply mechanical engineering principles to solve medical challenges
• Integrate clinical, regulatory, and user-centered considerations into design
• Select and justify material choices based on biocompatibility and performance
Course Content:
Introduction to Biomedical Device Design (2 weeks)
• Overview of biomedical devices: From simple tools to complex implants
• Clinical needs assessment: Identifying problems and user requirements
• Regulatory landscape: FDA, CE, ISO standards and compliance
Mechanical Engineering Fundamentals for Biomedical Devices (8 weeks)
• Mechanical systems in medicine: Mechanisms, fluidics, kinematics
• Material selection: Biocompatibility, durability, and manufacturing considerations
• Ergonomics and human factors: Designing for patient and clinician usability
Design Process and Methodologies (2 weeks)
• Design controls and risk management: Ensuring safety and reliability
• Prototyping techniques: Rapid prototyping, 3D printing, and iterative design
• Testing and validation: Bench testing, preclinical evaluation, and standards
Case Studies and Industry Practices (2 weeks)
• Analysis of existing medical devices: Orthopedic implants, surgical tools, wearable devices
• Economic and manufacturing considerations: Cost, scalability, and quality control
Team Project: Design, Build, and Test (semester long project)
• Team formation and project selection: Addressing real clinical needs
• Concept generation and selection: Brainstorming, feasibility, and design reviews
• Detailed mechanical design: CAD modeling, simulation, and tolerance analysis
• Prototype fabrication and assembly: Hands-on build using available resources
• Testing and iteration: Functional testing, risk mitigation, and design refinement
• Final presentation and documentation: Oral and written reports
Text Books:
1. Foundations and Strategies for Medical Device Design (McGraw Hill)
Reference Books:
1. Biomedical Engineering and Design Handbook (Myer Kutz)
2. Design of Biomedical Devices and Systems (Paul H. King, Richard C. Fries, Arthur T. Johnson)

Course No: ME2200
Course Name: Materials and Design
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Fundamental understanding of the correlation between the structure and properties of materials forms an integral
part of any successful design. The main objective of this course is to provide a basic knowledge concerning the
internal structure of materials, their mechanical properties and various methods to quantify their mechanical
integrity and failure criteria. Phases and heat treatment methods to tailor the properties of Fe-C alloys, which
forms perhaps the most important set of engineering
Course Content:
Crystal Structure: Unit cells, Mettalic crystal structures, Ceramics. Imperfection in solids: Point, line, interfacial and
volume defects; dislocation strengthening mechanisms and slip systems, critically resolved shear stress.
Mechanical Properties: Tensile, compression and torsion tests; Young’s modulus, relations between true and
engineering stress-strain curves, generalized Hooke’s law, yielding and yield strength, Considere criterion,
ductility, resilience, toughness and elastic recovery; Hardness: Rockwell, Brinell and Vickers and their relation to
strength.Static failure theories: Ductile and brittle failure mechanisms, Tresca, Von-mises, Maximum normal stress,
Mohr-Coulomb and Modified Mohr-Coulomb; Fracture mechanics: Introduction to Stress-intensity factor approach
and Griffith criterion. Fatigue failure: High cycle fatigue, Stress-life approach, SN curve, endurance and fatigue
limits, Marin factors, effects of mean stress using the Modified Goodman diagram; Methods to analyse multiaxial
fatigue. Fracture with fatigue: Paris law. Phase diagrams: Interpretation of binary phase diagrams and

Course No: ME2201
Course Name: Kinematics and Dynamics of Machinery
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course teaches the kinematics and rigid-body dynamics of kinematically driven machine components. It is
assumed that you have a basic understanding of the concepts of displacement, Velocity, acceleration, static force
equilibrium and dynamic equilibrium.
Course Content:
Introduction - Basic concepts of mechanisms and machines, kinematic pairs, chains, kinematic inversion and
mobility concepts with emphasis on 4R and 3R1P mechanisms; Grashof and non-Grashof 4R mechanisms
Kinematic Analysis of Mechanisms – Use of Velocity and Acceleration diagrams, Graphical Velocity analysis using
instantaneous centres, Analytical velocity and acceleration analysis using loop closure equations
Kinematic Synthesis - Three position graphical synthesis for motion and path generation
Dynamic analysis - Analytical approach, Slider-crank mechanism dynamics, Turning moment diagrams for IC
engines, Flywheel design for engines and punch presses; Two-plane balancing, Multi-cylinder IC engine balancing
Cams: Nomenclature, follower motion types, graphical and analytical disc cam profile synthesis for roller and flat
face followers
Gears: Involute Geometry and gear parameters, fundamental law of gearing and conjugate action, spur gear
contact ratio and interference/undercutting, epicyclic and regular gear train kinematic analysis

Course No: ME3101
Course Name: Heat Transfer
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The aim of the course is to help students build a solid foundation in the heat transfer exposing them to the three
basic modes namely conduction, convection and radiation. Rigorous treatment of governing equations and
solution procedures for the three modes will be provided together with solving problems of practical interest in heat
transfer. The course will also briefly cover boiling and condensation and a treatment of two kinds of problems in
heat exchangers namely analysis and design.
Course Content:
Modelling of situations involving conduction heat transfer with convection and or radiation boundary conditions for
one dimensional and two dimensional conduction followed by a solution by a of the governing equations to obtain
the temperature field for both steady and unsteady heat transfer. (2) Approximate solution to unsteady conduction
heat transfer in a few geometries by the use of charts. (3) Performing scale analysis for forced and free
convection heat transfer problems to identify pertinent dimensionless parameters governing convection. (4)
Approximate solutions to laminar boundary layer equations (momentum and energy) for both internal and external
flow (5) Estimating heat transfer rates in laminar and turbulent flow situations using appropriate correlations for
simple geometries for free and forced convection, boiling and condensation. (6) Calculation of radiation heat
transfer between surfaces using radiative properties, view factors and the radiosity method. (7) Analysis and
design of heat exchangers with both the LMTD and the NTU method. Course Contents: Introduction Steady
State Conduction in one and two - dimensional systems - One dimensional unsteady state conduction ; analytical
and numerical methods Convection: Basic equations, Boundary layers; Forced convection : External and internal
flows, correlations, Natural convection Radiation heat transfer: Basic laws, Properties of surfaces, view factors,
network method and enclosure analysis for gray diffuse enclosures containing transparent media, Engineering
treatment of gas radiation Boiling and condensation Analysis of heat exchangers
Text Books:
1. A. Bejan, Heat Transfer John Wiley, 1993
2. J.P.Holman, Heat Transfer, Eighth Edition, McGraw Hill, 1997.
3. F.P.Incropera, and D.P. Dewitt, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, John Wiley, Sixth Edition, 2007.
4. Massoud Kaviany, Principles of Heat Transfer, John Wiley, 2002
5. Yunus A Cengel, Heat Transfer : A Practical Approach, McGraw Hill, 2002

Course No: ME3305
Course Name: Manufacturing Technology-II
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
• To explore the basic support functionalities needed in a machine to enable manufacturing process to shape
materials.
• To explore ways to inspect the geometric shape (form, fit, and finish) made by manufacturing processes.
Course Content:
Rigid positioning of tools and parts: Tool and work holding devices, Jigs and fixtures.
Movement of tools and parts: Overview of tool-work relative kinematics, Linear motion, Rotary motion, Mechanical
synchronization of linear and rotary motion (machine kinematics), Programmable positioning and synchronization
of linear and rotary motions (electric motor drives, CNC, programming of tool paths).
Movement of parts between machines: Material transport systems, Part identification and data capture, Robotics.
Manufacturing factory: CAD/CAM, CAPP; Process route modeling, Layout optimization, Economics of
manufacturing, Case studies & industrial applications; Automation in manufacturing cells, assembly lines; Digital
and smart manufacturing (Industry 4.0).
Measurement: Definition of metrology, Measurement standards- geometrical dimensional and surface finish;
Geometrical measurements – Form measurements: straightness, flatness, roundness, cylindricity; Dimensional
measurements: linear and angular measurements with applications; Surface roughness measurement and
evaluation; Form and finish measurement systems: Profile and form testers and CMM, GD&T: Geometrical and
dimensional tolerances, limits and fits, Gauging: design and selection.
Text Books:
• Mikell P. Groover, Automation, Production Systems. and Computer-Integrated Manufacturing, 4th Edition,
Pearson
• I.C. Gupta, A Text Book of Engineering Metrology, Dhanpat Rai Publication
• William Boyes , Handbook of Jig and Fixture Design, 2nd Edition
• The Fourth Industrial Revolution, Klaus Schwab
• A.B. Chattopadhay, Machining and Machine Tools, Willey Publication.
Reference Books:
• Kalpakjian and Schmid, Manufacturing processes for engineering materials (5th Edition)-Pearson India, 2014
• Schuler Metal forming Handbook

Course No: ME4003
Course Name: Applied Mechanics of Materials
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Seeking motivation from the basic Strength of Materials course, the objective is to introduce the student to a few
advanced topics (mentioned below). Each of these topics has practical applications in a wide variety of
engineering problems. For example, contact mechanics forms the basis for tribology, deformation of flat plates is
essential to understand the mechanics of thin films and fracture mechanics for analysing failure of components
with pre-existing flaws. Before these topics are discussed, the necessary mathematical preliminaries will be
introduced.
Course Content:
Basic elasticity: Necessary foundations; Stress, Strain, equilibrium equations, compatibility, generalized Hooke’s
law and plane problems in elasticity, Airy’s stress function
Basic contact mechanics: Elastic half space problems in elasticity- Line and point loads, Normal contact of elastic
solids - Hertz theory. Several examples that highlight the general procedure to calculate the stress distributions
when two bodies are in contact will be discussed
Theory of flat plates: Kinematics, equilibrium equations, assumptions involved solutions to rectangular and circular
plate problems. Distributions of stresses, strains, and displacement will be obtained for thin and thick plates for a
variety of boundary conditions.
Basic fracture mechanics: Griffith theory of fracture, elastic stress field around a crack tip, energy release rate.
Calculation of stress intensity factors and strain energy release rates for several problems of engineering interest
will be discussed.
Text Books:
1. Arthur. P. Boresi, Advanced mechanics of materials, John Wiley and Sons, Sixth edition, 2003
Reference Books:
1. K. L. Johnson, Contact Mechanics, Cambridge University Press, 1985.
2. C. T. Sun and Z. H. Jin, Fracture Mechanics, Academic Press, 2012

Course No: ME4010
Course Name: Control Systems
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
To provide a basic understanding of the concepts and techniques involved in designing control schemes
fordynamic systems. At the end of this course, one should possess in-depth knowledge of concepts from
classicalcontrol theory, understand the concept of transfer function and use it for obtaining system response,
analyzedynamic systems for their stability and performance, and design controllers (such as
Proportional-Integral-Derivative) based on stability and performance requirements
Course Content:
ntroduction to Control, Classification of Dynamic Systems, Closed Loop Control System with
Feedback,Mathematical Preliminaries – Complex Variables, Laplace Transform. Standard Inputs, Free and
ForcedResponse, Transfer Function, Poles and Zeros. Response to various Inputs, Effect of Poles, Notion of
BoundedInput Bounded Output (BIBO) stability. Effect of Zeros, Closed Loop Transfer Function,
DynamicPerformance Specification, First Order Systems. Second Order Systems, Unit Step Response of
UnderdampedSecond Order Systems, Concepts of Rise Time, Peak Time, Maximum Peak Overshoot and Settling
Time.Controllers – Proportional (P), Integral (I) and Derivative (D) Blocks, Examples of PID controller
design.Routh’s Stability Criterion, Use in Control Design, Incorporation of Performance Specifications in
ControllerDesign, Analysis of Steady State Errors. Root Locus and its Application in Control Design.
FrequencyResponse, Bode Plots, Nyquist Plots. Nyquist Stability Criterion, Relative Stability – Gain and Phase
Margins.Control System Design via Frequency Response – Lead, Lag and Lag-Lead Compensation
Text Books:
1. Control Systems Engineering, 8th Ed, 2019, Norman S. Nise,2. Modern Control Engineering, 2015, K. Ogata
Reference Books:
None

Course No: ME4201
Course Name: Fundamentals of Tribology
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
This course aims to establish a fundamental understanding of tribological engineering exploring areas as diverse
as component surface distress to bearing performance, with emphasis on engineering applications. It will focus on
the relationships of friction, wear and lubrication, and how these relate to the development of reliable and
sustainable engineered solutions for tribological contacts such as bearings, gears and etc. It will include the
detailed analysis of the tribological properties of materials, and wear mechanisms.
Course Content:
Introduction and history of tribology, the nature of engineering surfaces, surface roughness parameters,
measurement techniques of surface topography, contact types, Hertzian contact pressure for line and point contact
surfaces. Friction: definition, the laws of friction, theories of friction, friction of metals, ceramic, lamellar solids and
polymers. Wear: definition, types, the Archard equation for adhesive and abrasive wear, wear of brass,
unlubricated wear of metals, wear regime maps for metals, mechanisms of adhesive wear of metals, lubricated
wear of metals, fretting wear of metals, wear of ceramics and polymers, abrasive wear effect on particle properties
and wear testing methods. Lubrication : lubricant properties-viscosity, viscosity index, temperature and pressure
effects on viscosity, lubricant composition, lubricants and additive types, lubrication selection, Reynolds’ one and
two dimensional equations, Navier-Stokes equations, boundary, elastohydrodynamic and hydrodynamic lubrication
regimes, chemical and physical absorption, Langmuir theory, additive chemistry, grease and solid lubricants.
Applications : Bearings, Gears, Clutches, Brakes, Piston, Cylinder and case studies
Text Books:
[1] I.M. Hutchings, Tribology: Friction and wear of Engineering Materials, Edward Arnold, London, 1992.
[2] J.A. Williams, Engineering Tribology, Cambridge University Press, UK, 2005
[3] B. Bhushan, Introduction to Tribology, John Wiley Sons, New York, 2002.
Reference Books:
[1] A Cameron, Basic Lubrication Theory, Wiley Eastern Ltd., New Delhi, 1987.
[2] F.P. Bowden and D. Tabor, Friction and Lubrication, Methuen & Co. Ltd., London, 1967.
[3] M.M. Khonsari and E. Richard Booser, Applied Tribology: Bearing Design and Lubrication, Wiley Publication,
New York, 2008.

Course No: ME5001
Course Name: Prognostics and Health Management of Machine Tools
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
To learn about sensor signal acquisition and data preprocessing techniques
To learn and understand and implement various signals processing methods for feature extraction
To learn about various feature selection techniques
To learn about data driven prognostics models, model or physics based prognostics models
To learn to integrate the decision making models for maintenance planning and scheduling of manufacturing
Course Content:
History and technological development in diagnostics of machine tools, need for prognostics, definition of
prognostics, ISO 13381-1 definition of diagnostics vs prognostics, prognostics requirement evaluation, steps
involved in prognostics system design, data availability analysis for prognostics modeling option selection,
challenges in prognostics. : cutting force, vibration, acoustic emission, spindle motor current and cutting
temperature signal analysis, feature extraction techniques, time and frequency domain statistical features, feature
selection techniques, Future fusion, prognostics metrics for feature selection : linear and non-linear regression
models, Weibull models, log-linear models, logistic regression models, artificial neural network models, model
accuracy evaluation: mathematical and analytical model for cutting force, cutting temperature, material removal
rate and surface quality and integrity - grinding, EDM process, fatigue concepts for life estimation, risk calculation,
concepts of condition based maintenance models. Case studies: sensor selection and signal acquisition, feature
extraction, feature selection, data based model building and model accuracy evaluation, physics based model
building, model updating procedures.
Text Books:

publications-2011.

Press, 2003.

Engineering Systems, 2006, John Wiley & Sons, Ltd

2006.

Course No: ME5010
Course Name: Hybrid and Electric Vehicle Technology
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
To understand and evaluate different Hybrid & Electric power train architectures, energy storage and management
technologies as regards performance, be able to model them and propose appropriate solutions.
Understanding of hybrid electric drive systems and factors affecting their efficiency and performance. Ability to
simulate and size the major components of a hybrid drive system given a set of constraints
Course Content:
• Introduction to Hybrid and Electric Vehicle architecture- series, parallel, series-parallel, micro-hybrid and
complex HEV layouts. Benefits, Power flows, losses, energy usage and drive quality. Basics of EV, HEV, PHEV
and Fuel Cell vehicles. (6 Lectures)
• Components of Hybrid Electric Drives: Different kinds of motors like induction, permanent magnet, switched
reluctance, their characteristics and thermal analysis of motors. Different control methods for motors used in
hybrid and electric drives. PHEV Architeciures.Fuel Cells, hybrid fuel cell systems and control.( 1 0 Lectures)
• Energy storage devices; types of batteries, their characteristics, charging systems and energy management.
Super capacitors, flywheels and hydraulic accumulators. High voltage electrical architectures and integration of
power electronic systems. Rectifiers, buck converters, bi directional DC-DC converters, voltage and current source
inverters, Battery chargers for HEVs and PHEVs. Thermal Management of power electronic devices. (12 Lectures)
• Hybrid vehicle modelling: Engine characteristics, vehicle model, modelling power train subsystem like motors,
energy storage devices and transmissions. Gradability requirements, gear ratios. Dynamic modelling of the power
train. Modelling hydraulic hybrids.Sizing the components of a hybrid / electric vehicle based on application and
range. Optimization algorithms, Energy recovery, regenerative braking and energy management. (10 Lectures)
• Comparison with conventional vehicles as regards emissions and fuel economy and well to wheel performance.
Recent Electric and Hybrid vehicle technologies case studies. (4 Lectures)
Text Books:
1. Hybrid Electric vehicles, Principles and Applications with Practical Perspectives.Chris Mi, M. Abdul Masrur and
David WenzhongGao,Wiley, USA, 2011.
2. Advanced Hybrid Powertrains for Commercial Vehicles. Haoran Hu, Rudy Smaling, and Simon J. Baseley. SAE
Publications (Product Code: R-396).
3. Hybrid Powered Vehicles, Second Edition. John M. German, SAE Publications (Product Code: T-125)
4. Electric and Hybrid-Electric Vehicles. Ronald K. Jurgen, SAE Publications (Product Code: PT-143.SET)
5. History of the Electric Automobile: Hybrid Electric Vehicles. Ernest H. Wakefield, SAE Publications (Product
Code: R-187)

Course No: ME5011
Course Name: Plasticity and damage mechanics
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
• To provide fundamentals of phenomenological plasticity and damage theories and its application to
manufacturing process.
• To develop the skillset for writing user-defined material subroutines for Finite element models
• To expose the use of optimization technique for parameter identification
Course Content:
Introduction to mechanics of deformation- concept of continuum, stress, strain and constitutive relation for
elasticity
One dimensional plasticity- Temperature and strain rate effect- one dimensional rate dependent constitutive
models; Physically based (dislocation density) models for strain hardening
Phenomenological modelling of multiaxial plastic deformation; Axioms of continuum plasticity theory; Isotropic and
Anisotropic yield criteria; Isotropic and kinematic hardening; Analysis of representative yield criteria and hardening
models- vonMises, Hill48 and Barlat 89 models
Introduction to failure- Geometric instability- Local neck- Continuum damage models- Uncoupled damage models-
BW criterion, Modified Mohr Coulomb criterion; GTN models- Issues related to non-proportional loading-
Application of damage models for specific problems in manufacturing- such as machining and incremental sheet
forming
Identification of material parameters- Direct method (linear simultaneous equations) and multi-objective
evolutionary algorithm
Introduction to UMAT- User defined material model- Fundamentals of writing UMAT- implementation of elastic and
elastoplastic UMAT
Text Books:
1. Hosford, W F., Fundamentals of Engineering Plasticity. Cambridge University Press, 2013.
2. Dixit, P M and Dixit, U S Plasticity- Fundamentals and Applications, CRC Press, 2015
3. Srinivasa, A R and Srinivasa, M S, Inelasticity Of Materials: An Engineering Approach And A Practical Guide,
World Scientific Publishing , 2009
4. Kachanov, L M Introduction to continuum damage mechanics, Springer, 1986
5. Hertzberg R W, Vinci R W and Hertzberg, J L Deformation and Fracture Mechanics of Engineering Materials,
Wiley ,2020
Reference Books:
1. Khan, A S and Huang, S, Continuum theory of Plasticity, John Wiley
2. Kachanov, L M , Fundamentals of the theory of Plasticity, Dover, 2013

Course Name: Metal forming analysis and tool design
Course Type:
Theory
Description:

friction model); Shear friction theory (Sticking friction model); Lubrication in metal forming applications; Stribeck

strain indentation); Slip line field analysis- Hodograph (Plane strain extrusion and drawing); Finite element

Theory

To provide adequate foundation on basic mathematical skills to PhD scholars in Mechanical Engineering. The

Numerical Solutions of Non-linear Equations Integration by Trapezoidal and Simpson’s rule

Course No: ME5020
Course Name: Professional Communication Skills
Course Type:
Others
Description:
This course is designed to improve the English communication of Mechanical Engineering students by raising their
awareness of common mistakes in English grammar and develop their communication through fluency and
confidence-building real-life speaking tasks and writing tasks.
Course Content:
Introduction: Understand the basic nature, scope, and principles of communication, understand barriers to
communication and techniques to overcome them, Understand encoding non - verbal communication;
Grammar and vocabulary: aware of the common mistakes in everyday English grammar, learn and practise the
accurate use of the grammatical devices required for everyday communication in an appropriate real-life context,
understand techniques of expanding vocabulary.
Functional language in everyday contexts: give and respond to suggestions, delegate and accepting tasks, give
and respond to opinions, agree and disagree, make interruptions and clarifications.
Sound and Intonation in Oral Communication: understand IPA (International Phonetic Alphabet), understand
rhythm and intonation in oral communication.
Oral Communication - Group Discussion: earn the techniques of group discussion, discuss changing scenarios in
social and academic aspects by participating in group discussion.
Oral Communication - Interview Skills: develop and practice Interview Skills, participate in mock Interviews,
receive feedback and consolidate understanding.
Oral Communication - Technical Presentation Skills: understand the structure, format, and useful functional
language of making technical presentations, make demo technical presentations, receive feedback and
consolidate understanding.
Writing Skills I - Email Writing: understand the structure and functional language to write business emails,
understand a range of tones and registers in business emails.
Writing Skills II - Report Writing: understand the structure and functional language to write a Technical Report.
Reading Skills: discuss and determine specific strategies (Planned, Comprehensive, and Active) as a starting point
for academic reading, be guided to set realistic short-term and long-term goals in Academic writing.
Writing Skills - Academic Writing: understand the structure of a Research Paper in Mechanical Engineering and
allied linguistic devices for the same.
Leadership and Soft Skills: develop and practice techniques and strategies to improve decision making skills, team
management skills, and allied soft skills.
Text Books:
Instructor developed course material.
Reference Books:
1) Simply Said: Communicating Better at Work and Beyond. Jay Sullivan. Tylie, 2018
2) Common Errors in Everyday English. Saumya Sharma, Oxford University Press, 2017
3) Academic Writing for Graduate Students: Essential Skills and Tasks. J. Swales and C. Feak. Michigan
University Press. 2012.

Course Name: Data Science for Mechanical Engineers
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The principal objective of the course is to give the students a broad overview of data science tools and techniques
that can be applied to subfields of mechanical engineering.
Course Content:
1. Foundations of Data Science – Tools and Techniquesa) Introduction to Data and Data Science – History and

problem, Multiple Regression, Polynomial Regression, Introduction to regularization in practice, Goodness of fit,
Examples from Mechanical Engineering. (5 hours) 2. Modeling Uncertaintya) Probability Theory – Requirement for
modeling uncertainty in mechanical engineering, Random Variables, Probability Distribution, Joint and conditional
probability, Moments of distributions – Expectation, Variance, Standard Probability Distributions and their
relevance to problems encountered in practice in Mechanical Engineering. (6 hours) b) Essentials of Statistical
Modelling – Relationship between probability theory and statistical practice, Statistical Measurement, Descriptive
Statistics, Inferential Statistics, Hypothesis testing, Connection between modeling errors and regression, Statistical
understanding of regularization, Applications and examples in Mechanical Engineering, (6 hours) 3. Machine
Learninga) Introduction to Machine Learning -- Insufficiency of statistical approaches for practical problems in
Mechanical Engineering, Introduction to Learning based models. (1 hr)Machine Learning Algorithms such as b)
Linear Classification Algorithms – Logistic regression, Multiclass problems, Gradient Descent based approaches
(5 hrs) c) Tree Based Models – Decision Trees, Ensemble Models – Random Forests, XGBoost (4 hrs) d)
Unsupervised Techniques – Relevance to mechanical Engineering, k-Means, PCA, t-SNE (4 hrs) e) Artificial
Neural Networks – Neural Networks as Universal Models, Forward Model of an ANN, Need for Deep Learning (3

Course No: ME5101
Course Name: Advanced Heat & Mass Transfer
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The aim of the course is to help students build a solid foundation in heat transfer exposing them to the three basic
modes namely conduction, convection and radiation. Rigorous treatment of governing equations and solution
procedures for the three modes will be provided together with solving problems of practical interest in heat
transfer. The course will also briefly cover boiling and condensation and a treatment of two kinds of problems in
heat exchangers namely analysis and design. Outcome
(1) Modelling of situations involving conduction heat transfer with convection and or radiation boundary conditions
for one dimensional and two dimensional conduction followed by a solution of the governing equations to obtain
the temperature field for both steady and unsteady heat transfer.
(2) Approximate solution to unsteady conduction heat transfer in a few geometries by the use of charts.
(3) Performing scale analysis for forced and free convection heat transfer problems to identify pertinent
dimensionless parameters governing convection.
(4) Approximate solutions to laminar boundary layer equations (momentum and energy) for both internal and
external flow
(5) Estimating heat transfer rates in laminar and turbulent flow situations using appropriate correlations for simple
geometries for free and forced convection, boiling and condensation.
(6) Calculation of radiation heat transfer between surfaces using radiative properties, view factors and the radiosity
method.
(7) Analysis and design of heat exchangers with both the LMTD and the e-NTU method.
Course Content:
Introduction and Review of Heat Transfer Fundamentals
Conduction
Review of One-dimensional Steady state conduction
Heat Transfer from Extended Surfaces
Two Dimensional Steady State Conduction in Cartesian and Cylindrical Coordinates
Transient Conduction
Convection
Velocity and Thermal Boundary layers
Laminar and turbulent boundary layers - Blasius solution, Similarity solutions, Integral technique.
Heat transfer correlations for External flows
Developed flow inside ducts and pipes- Nusselt number for constant heat flux and constant wall temperatureturbulent
flow in pipes
Natural convective heat transfer from a heated plate
Radiation
Basics - black and gray body radiation - radiation in enclosures
Fundamentals of condensation and boiling- pool boiling curve- flow boiling
Basics of mass transfer- mass averaged and mole averaged velocities and fluxes- Fick’s law of diffusion
Text Books:
1. F.P.Incropera, D.P. Dewitt, T.L Bergman and A.S Lavine, Principles of Heat and Mass Transfer, John Wiley, Sixth
Edition, 2018.
2. Yunus A Cengel, Heat Transfer : A Practical Approach, Second Edition, McGraw Hill, 2008.
Reference Books:
1. A. Bejan, Heat Transfer John Wiley, 1993.
2. J.H.Lienhard V and J.H.Lienhard IV A Heat Transfer Textbook, Fourth Edition, 2011, Dover Publications, New
York (free online edition available for download).
3. J.P.Holman, Heat Transfer, Eighth Edition, McGraw Hill, 1997.
4. Massoud Kaviany, Principles of Heat Transfer, John Wiley, 2002.

Course No: ME5103
Course Name: Incompressible Fluid Flow
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
To gain a post-graduate level understanding of the fundamental concepts of incompressible fluid flows including
turbulent flows.
Course Content:
1. Introduction and Basic Concepts - Definition of fluid and concept of continuum; Properties of fluids; Flow field,
streamlines, path lines and streak lines; Kinematics of fluid motion; Eulerian and Lagrangian formulations
2. Governing Equations of Fluid Flow - Reynolds transport theorem; Mass and momentum conservation;

3. Potential Flow - Stream function and velocity potential; Elementary plane flows; Superposition of elementary
plane flows; Concept of lift and drag
4. Boundary Layer Theory - Concept of boundary layer; Derivation of boundary layer equations; Boundary layer
flow over a flat plate; Boundary layer flow with non-zero pressure gradient; Flow separation and drag; Free shear
flow
5. Turbulent flows - Characteristics of turbulent flows; Concept of averaging; Reynolds Averaged Navier Stokes
(RANS) equations; Turbulent internal flows; Turbulent external flows

Course No: ME5131
Course Name: Nanoscale Thermofluidics: Theory and Computation
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
*To enhance the understanding of students about crucial concepts in Fluid Mechanics and Heat Transfer by
showing their molecular origin,
*To upskill students to use nanofluidic simulation tools to approach engineering problems from a unique viewpoint,
*To help students quantify the influence of nanoscale thermal fluctuations and intermolecular interactions on
various processes at a larger scale.
Course Content:
* Module 1 (theory; 4 hrs)
Course introduction
• Relevance of nanofluidics simulations in today’s engineering scenarios Macroscopic modelling of fluid flows – a
recap
• A quick peek into continuum hypothesis, material derivative, governing equations of fluid dynamics and heat
transfer, various boundary conditions, some canonical problems in fluid dynamics and heat transfer, and their
characteristics.
* Module 2 (theory; 6 hrs)
Microfluidics
• Brief introduction to fluid flow at smaller (micron) scales, changes to assumptions and consequent modifications
to governing equations.
Nanofluidics – essential theory
• The discrete nature of materials, failure of continuum hypothesis and break-down of constitutive laws at
nanoscale,
• Limitations of experimental and continuum simulation techniques, and
• The origin of thermophysical properties of fluids (diffusivity, viscosity, surface tension, density distribution at
interfaces etc.) from their molecular motion.
* Module 3 (theory + practical; 15 hrs)
Computational nanofluidics
This module will cover:
• Detailed discussion on MD and a brief account of fluctuating hydrodynamics
• Introduction to programming in LAMMPS and data post-processing. Equilibrium simulations of simple liquids and
gases
By the end of this module, students will be able to:
• Simulate a basic molecular system using the standard Lennard-Jones potential in LAMMPS, and
• Determine their thermophysical properties under equilibrium conditions.
* Module 4 (theory + practical; 15 hrs)
Thermofluidics at nanoscale – some crucial concepts
• Modifications to canonical fluid flow and heat transfer problems at nanoscale due to non-continuity, thermal
fluctuations, and intermolecular interactions,
• Explore the molecular origin of several boundary conditions at solid/fluid and fluid/fluid interfaces (slip/stick,
constant temperature, and constant heat flux),
• Quantify and recognize the consequence of viscous dissipation in fluid flow.
Text Books:
? M. P. Allen and D. J. Tildesley, Computer Simulation of Liquids (Oxford University Press, Oxford, 2017).
? J. S. Rowlinson and B. Widom, Molecular Theory of Capillarity (Clarendon Press, Oxford 1982).
? J. M. Ortiz de Zárate and J. V Sengers, Hydrodynamic Fluctuations in Fluids and Fluid Mixtures (Elsevier,
Amsterdam, 2006).
Reference Books:
? Jean Pierre Boon and Sidney Yip, Molecular Hydrodynamics (Dover Publications, 2013).
? Perumanath et al. Physical Review Letters 131, 164001 (2023)
? Zhao et al. Journal of Fluid Mechanics 861:R3 (2019)
? Zhang et al. Physical Review E 92, 052403 (2015)

Course Name: Finite Element Analysis
Course Type:
Theory
Description:

Course No: ME5205
Course Name: Theory of Vibration
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
The primary objective of this course is to enable you to build and solve mathematical models of vibrating systems.
The emphasis is on linear systems subject to sinusoidal or periodic excitations. The course requires a math
background in Fourier series, solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and basic linear algebra (including
eigenvalue problems).
Course Content:
Building Vibration Models - Assumptions and approximations; Practical case study - deriving the
equations of motion; highlight need for single degree-of-freedom (SDOF) models
SDOF Models - Free vibration without and with damping; viscous and other damping types; Forced
vibration - harmonic force, rotating unbalance/base excitation, vibration isolation; periodic forcing and concept of
frequency response function (FRF); General Excitation - Impulse response, Step and pulse type forces, shock
response spectrum
Multi degree-of-freedom (MDOF) Models - Deriving equations of motion for complex models; Concept of mode
shapes and associated mathematical properties; Use of modal superposition to obtain forced vibration response;
Concept of proportional or Rayleigh damping; More on FRFs and their uses; Vibration absorber application
Continuous system Models - Equations of motion for transverse vibration of strings, torsional vibration of shafts,
axial and beam bending vibrations; forced vibration of continuous systems using modal
Superposition; Approximation methods – Rayleigh-Ritz and Galerkin based solutions.
Text Books:
1. W. T. Thomson, M. D. Dahleh and C. Padmanabhan, 2008, Theory of Vibration with Applications, Pearson
Education India: New Delhi.
2. L. Meirovitch, 2001, Elements of Vibration Analysis, Tata McGraw-Hill: New Delhi.

1. B. Balachandran, E. B. Magrab, 2009, Fundamentals of Vibrations} Cengage Engineering: New Delhi.
2. V. Ramamurti, 2012, Mechanical Vibration Practice and Noise Control, Narosa: New Delhi.

Course No: ME5210
Course Name: Applied Mechanics of Materials
Course Type:
Theory
Description:
Seeking motivation from the basic Strength of Materials course, the objective is to introduce the student to a few
advanced topics (mentioned below). Each of these topics has practical applications in a wide variety of
engineering problems. For example, contact mechanics forms the basis for tribology, deformation of flat plates is
essential to understand the mechanics of thin films and fracture mechanics for analysing failure of components
with pre-existing flaws. Before these topics are discuss
Course Content:
Basic elasticity: Necessary foundations; Stress, Strain, equilibrium equations, compatibility, generalized Hooke’s
law and plane problems in elasticity, Airy’s stress function Basic contact mechanics: Elastic half space problems in
elasticity- Line and point loads, Normal contact of elastic solids - Hertz theory. Several examples that highlight the
general procedure to calculate the stress distributions when two bodies are in contact will be discussedTheory of
flat plates: Kinematics, equilibrium equations, assumptions involved solutions to rectangular and circular plate
problems. Distributions of stresses, strains, and displacement will be obtained for thin and thick plates for a variety
of boundary conditions. Basic fracture mechanics: Griffith theory of fracture, elastic stress field around a crack tip,
energy release rate. Calculation of stress intensity factors and strain energy release rates for several problems of
engineering interest will be discussed.
Text Books:
1. Arthur. P. Boresi, Advanced mechanics of materials, John Wiley and Sons, Sixth edition, 2003
Reference Books:
1. K. L. Johnson, Contact Mechanics, Cambridge University Press, 1985. 2. C. T. Sun and Z. H. Jin, Fracture
Mechanics, Academic Press, 2012

Theory

properties.
Module 4: Sound in Enclosures and Waveguides

sounds; Sound fields in large enclosures; reverberation equations; concept of direct and reverberant fields;
